"""Batch 315: Daba's Character Chronicle gate closes (Psychological Profile
approved, Game Plan closed), and his second wave (Chronicles LI-LIII) locks --
the three next-wave candidates offered in his Game Plan, all picked by Abad
to run "as a wave": the open "what does he want for himself" psychological
question tested directly (LI), the corpus's first genuine physical threat to
his S-tier rating (LII), and a pure texture entry showing 1804's semi-dormant
present (LIII, deliberately touching nothing about MCD-1569's unspecified
Book 1 trigger).
"""
import json
from datetime import date

LEDGER_PATH = "canon-ledger.json"
SOURCE = (
    "Original invention, chat-drafted 2026-09-28, extending Daba's own "
    "50-Chronicle launch wave (Batch 296) and his gate profile "
    "(docs/lords-of-cian/character-profiles/daba.md)."
)

with open(LEDGER_PATH, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    ledger = json.load(f)

existing_ids = {r["id"] for r in ledger["rules"]}

NEW_RULES = [
    {
        "id": "MCD-1869",
        "category": "daba-character-chronicle",
        "statement": (
            "Daba Chronicle LI, 'The Day With No Name in It' (full text at "
            "docs/lords-of-cian/chronicles/daba-chronicle-li-the-day-with-no-name-in-it.md). "
            "First entry of Daba's second Character Chronicle wave, developing the "
            "psychological question flagged as genuinely open in his gate profile -- whether he "
            "wants anything for himself distinct from 1804's survival. Mika (present since "
            "Chronicle I) tells him she has bought a house, half a day's walk from the coast "
            "road, for no operational reason -- simply asking him to come see it. Pressed to "
            "articulate a want he has never had practice naming, Daba arrives at one certain, "
            "specific answer: the only thing he has ever wanted for himself is for the list of "
            "names 1804's doctrine exists to answer to stop growing. He does not go see the "
            "house by the entry's close, but does not decline either -- the door stays "
            "deliberately, genuinely open, a first real data point on an otherwise-unresolved "
            "question rather than a resolution of it. No new named characters."
        ),
        "status": "locked",
        "source": SOURCE,
    },
    {
        "id": "MCD-1870",
        "category": "daba-character-chronicle",
        "statement": (
            "Daba Chronicle LII, 'The Ground That Almost Wasn't Enough' (full text at "
            "docs/lords-of-cian/chronicles/daba-chronicle-lii-the-ground-that-almost-wasnt-enough.md). "
            "Second entry of the wave -- the first Chronicle in the entire 53-entry corpus to put "
            "Daba's S-tier rating (CC-135) under genuine physical threat, since he holds no "
            "variant biology or density scaling and his rating comes entirely from guerrilla "
            "mastery and tactical discipline. Closing a safehouse at Threnfall personally after "
            "it is traced by a patient, unnamed Trust Compliance captain and eleven enforcers, "
            "Daba survives only by applying his own core doctrine (density is not power if the "
            "terrain neutralizes it, MCD-1567/1568) to save his own life for the first time, "
            "escaping through a disused well and drainage culvert rather than confronting the "
            "perimeter directly. He is genuinely wounded -- an injury decided by luck, not "
            "skill, the first time in his own life that distinction has applied -- and is saved "
            "on arrival at a second safehouse by Wrenna's counting-as-containment response, a "
            "discipline he built into her without ever fully explaining why. Reuses Bren and "
            "Wrenna. No new named characters; the antagonist captain and his enforcers are "
            "deliberately unnamed. Does not touch or dramatize the separate, still-undramatized "
            "Harek Vondel defeat reserved at MCD-1855."
        ),
        "status": "locked",
        "source": SOURCE,
    },
    {
        "id": "MCD-1871",
        "category": "daba-character-chronicle",
        "statement": (
            "Daba Chronicle LIII, 'What a Quiet Year Looks Like' (full text at "
            "docs/lords-of-cian/chronicles/daba-chronicle-liii-what-a-quiet-year-looks-like.md). "
            "Third entry of the wave, closing it -- a deliberate pure-texture entry with no "
            "threat and no plot advance, showing 1804's mature, semi-dormant present day to day: "
            "Kether's refined seven-day recruit vetting, Wrenna running two cells and keeping an "
            "unprompted personal margin-note habit in her reports, Deryn Kettel's ordinary "

        ),
        "status": "locked",
        "source": SOURCE,
    },
]

new_ids = [r["id"] for r in NEW_RULES]
assert len(new_ids) == 3
assert len(set(new_ids)) == len(new_ids), "duplicate IDs within the new-rules batch"
collisions = existing_ids & set(new_ids)
assert not collisions, f"ID collision with live ledger: {collisions}"

ledger["rules"].extend(NEW_RULES)

batch_note = (
    "Closes Daba's Character Chronicle Launch Protocol gate for a second wave: the "
    "Psychological Profile drafted last batch was approved as drafted ('Approve as drafted, "
    "keep going'), and the Game Plan's three next-wave candidates -- testing the open 'what "
    "does he want for himself' question, the corpus's first genuine physical threat to his "
    "S-tier rating, and a pure semi-dormant-present texture entry -- were all picked by Abad to "

    "gate with 53 total Chronicles."
)
ledger["batches_completed"].append(

        "note": batch_note,
    }
)

ledger["ledger_version"] = f"{round(float(ledger['ledger_version']) + 0.1, 1):.1f}"
ledger["last_updated"] = str(date.today())

with open(LEDGER_PATH, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    json.dump(ledger, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
    f.write("\n")

print(f"OK. Total rules: {len(ledger['rules'])}. Ledger version: {ledger['ledger_version']}. "
      f"Batches: {len(ledger['batches_completed'])}.")

# Daba Chronicle XXVII: The Second Name No One Spoke

*Locked canon, Batch 296, 2026-09-18 (`MCD-1597`). Entry 27 of 50 in Daba's own Chronicle series,
launched under the Character Chronicle Gameplan's own protagonist-series model. Dramatizes a
structural innovation Daba builds specifically against `MCD-1567`'s stated risk -- blind succession,
where each cell's second-in-command is chosen and prepared without ever being told they hold the
role, so a cell's leadership survives a loss without any single person's capture being able to
expose the whole chain. Extends `MCD-1569`'s account of Daba building 1804's durability "before he
can see the full shape of what it will eventually need to answer." Introduces Yeva Tolan, a cell
leader, and Marn, her chosen second, both collision-checked clean. No other new named characters.
Abad's approval: "rate 50 Chronicles in batches using as many agents as needed to make it
efficient."*

---

Yeva Tolan had led the river cell for three years when she stopped coming back from a routine crossing, and for eleven days no one in 1804 outside Daba himself knew whether she was dead, taken, or simply delayed by weather the way couriers were delayed a dozen times a season without anyone thinking twice about it. The not-knowing was, by design, almost the whole of the danger. A network built to survive its own losses could not afford to grind to a halt every time one of them might have happened.

The river cell did not grind to a halt. Three days into the silence, a man named Marn who had spent those three years hauling nets and carrying messages and being, by every outward appearance, the least remarkable member of Yeva's crew, opened a sealed instruction he had carried folded into the lining of his coat since the week he joined, and began running the cell exactly as though he had always led it.

He had not known, until that morning, that he was meant to.

This was the piece of the design Daba had never once explained to anyone but the person it applied to, and had built into the network quietly enough that even Sael, who knew more of its architecture than anyone but Daba himself, had not known Marn carried it. Every cell of any real size had a second, chosen by its leader and confirmed by Daba alone, prepared through months of small unexplained tests -- extra responsibility handed over on ordinary days, decisions quietly checked afterward against what the leader herself would have made -- without the second ever being told the tests meant anything at all. The instruction itself, sealed and unopened until the moment it was needed, held nothing more than a place, a time, and the plain fact of what had happened. No plan. No orders. Only permission, and the confirmation that the cell's work was not to stop.

"Why not tell them?" Sael had asked him once, years before Yeva Tolan ever led anyone, back when the idea was still an argument between the two of them in the cellar. "A man who knows he's the second can prepare properly. Study the role instead of stumbling into it."

"A man who knows he's the second is a second name," Daba had said. "And a second name is one more thing that can be pulled out of someone under the wrong kind of pressure. If Marn never knows he's Yeva's second, there's nothing in his head worth taking from him. He can be caught, questioned, broken open entirely, and give up nothing about the river cell's future because there's nothing there to give up. He only becomes dangerous to us the moment he's needed -- and by then it's already too late for anyone to have gotten to him first."

It cost something, and Daba never pretended otherwise. A cell run for eleven days by a man discovering the shape of his own new authority as he went was a cell run less smoothly than it would have been under months of open preparation. Marn made two decisions in that stretch that Yeva, when she finally did return -- delayed, as it happened, by nothing more dramatic than a washed-out crossing and a week spent waiting for the water to drop -- judged too cautious, and one that she judged exactly right, better than she might have made herself. He gave the cell nothing to be ashamed of and nothing to be proud of beyond the plain fact that it had not stopped.

Yeva found Daba the week after her return, not to complain but to ask the question that mattered more. "Who's mine now, if it happens again? Does he know?"

"No," Daba said. "And it isn't Marn a second time. A man who's already been tested once is a man people start watching for a reason, even without meaning to. I've chosen someone else. You won't know who until you need to."

She did not press him for the name, understanding, by then, exactly what the not-knowing was worth. She only nodded, and went back to her river, and the cell went on being exactly as unremarkable as it had always needed to be -- one more ordinary crew moving ordinary cargo along an ordinary water, carrying inside it a second, unspoken name that would only ever matter on the one day it was finally called on to.
# Daba Chronicle XXVIII: The Banner He Would Not Take

*Locked canon, Batch 296, 2026-09-18 (`MCD-1598`). Entry 28 of 50 in Daba's own Chronicle series,
launched under the Character Chronicle Gameplan's own protagonist-series model. Dramatizes a
growth-temptation moment -- a chance to absorb a much larger, already-organized militia in a single
stroke -- and the hard, costly call to decline it, holding doctrine over mass even against real
internal disagreement, extending `MCD-1567`'s founding principle and `MCD-1569`'s account of Daba
building 1804 "before he can see the full shape of what it will eventually need to answer."
Introduces Bramm Oskell and the Ashfield Banner, both collision-checked clean; reuses Nessa. No
other new named characters. Abad's approval: "rate 50 Chronicles in batches using as many agents as
needed to make it efficient."*

---

The Ashfield Banner numbered close to six hundred fighters by the time Bramm Oskell came to find Daba himself, which made it, by a wide margin, the largest organized resistance force operating anywhere near the districts 1804 had spent years learning to move through unseen. Oskell was not a subtle man, and he did not pretend to be one during the two hours he spent laying his offer out across a borrowed table -- his Banner would take 1804's name, his fighters would answer to 1804's discipline where it made sense to, and in exchange 1804 would gain, overnight, six hundred bodies, a dozen fortified positions, and a reputation loud enough that the Trust would have to answer it with something more than a clerk's shrug.

"You'd be the largest resistance force in the Sovereign Trust's whole northern reach," Oskell said. "Not the quietest anymore. The largest. There's a version of fighting them where quiet stops being the smartest thing to be."

Nessa argued for it that same night, in the cellar that had stopped being a cellar in any literal sense years before but had kept the name out of habit, and argued for it harder than Daba had heard her argue for anything since the naming. Six hundred fighters meant districts that could finally be held rather than merely visited. It meant grain moved by the wagonload instead of the handcart, wounds treated in real infirmaries instead of borrowed back rooms, a hundred families protected openly instead of a dozen protected in secret. She did not accuse him of anything. She only laid the arithmetic in front of him, plainly, the way she laid every hard number in front of him, and let him sit with what it cost to refuse it.

"You've spent years telling me small is how we survive," she said. "Tell me honestly this isn't just fear of the thing getting big enough to matter."

Daba did not answer quickly, because it was not a small question and he had learned, long before Nessa ever asked him anything, not to give easy answers to questions that deserved better. He thought of Marn, discovering a role he'd never known he held. He thought of Rhyne, learning a second craft at real cost to the one she loved. He thought, longer than either of those, of the number the network carried as its own name, and of how easily six hundred fighters under one recognizable banner became, to anyone counting from the Trust's side of the ledger, a target with a return address.

"Oskell's Banner is six hundred people who can be seen," he said finally. "Everything we've built is built on the fact that nobody can find the whole of us in one place, because there isn't a whole of us anywhere to find. The day we take his name, we stop being a hundred separate nights that never look like anything, and we start being one army with a known shape. Every position he's fortified is a position the Trust already knows to watch. Every fighter who answers to us by name is a fighter whose capture tells them something true about who we are. We wouldn't be absorbing his strength. We'd be inheriting his exposure."

# Daba Chronicle LIV: The Window That Faced the Water

*UNLOCKED / PENDING APPROVAL. Daba Chronicle LIV, first entry of a third wave. Close-third on
Daba, no dedicated narrator. Pays off Chronicle LIII's closing line ("he did not go that night
either. But he thought, for the first time, that he might") without fully resolving the larger
open question of what he wants for himself — a real, concrete step forward rather than a
retraction or a final answer. Reuses Mika. No new named characters.*

---

He went on a day nothing required him to.

That was the whole of the decision, in the end — not an argument won, not a crisis that happened
to route him past the coast road, just an ordinary morning with an empty ledger and no name added
to anything, and Daba found that an empty ledger, once he let himself notice it, was its own kind of
permission he had never given himself before.

The house was smaller than he'd pictured it, which surprised him more than it should have, given
that Mika had described it to him plainly and he had simply failed, in all the months since, to
build the real thing out of her words instead of some larger shape his own mind had substituted
without telling him. One story. A door that didn't latch quite square in its frame. A kitchen with
exactly the kind of window Mika had promised, facing water that was, this far up the coast, more
grey than blue, and utterly unremarkable, and somehow more interesting to look at than he'd expected
anything to be that asked nothing of him in return.

Mika didn't make a production of his arrival. She handed him a cup of something bitter she called
tea and was, by her own cheerful admission, still learning to brew correctly, and let him stand at
the window for as long as he wanted without narrating what he should be feeling about it.

"You don't have to say anything," she said, eventually, when the silence had gone on long enough
that she judged it needed permission rather than patience. "I didn't buy this to make you perform
gratitude at it."

"I'm not performing anything." He turned the cup once in his hands, not drinking, just holding it.
"I'm trying to work out what this is, exactly. What room it's supposed to occupy."

"It doesn't have to occupy a room. It can just be a house."

"Everything I've ever kept has had a function." He said it without complaint, the way he might
report a tide table. "The ledger. The list. The network. Even you, when we started — you had a
function, and I was honest about that at the time, and you were honest back."

"And now?"

"Now I don't know what function this is. A window. Bad tea. You, not doing anything to earn the
visit." He set the cup down, untouched, on the sill. "I keep waiting to feel like I'm spending
something. Time I owe somewhere else. And I don't. That's the part I don't have a category for."

Mika came and stood beside him at the window, close enough that their shoulders nearly touched, not
quite. "Maybe that's what it's for. Not a function. Just the absence of the feeling that everything
has to be one."

He stayed the whole day, which was longer than he'd told himself he would, and shorter than Mika,
watching him from the doorway as he finally sat down at her kitchen table and let a silence pass
between them that had nothing urgent inside it, privately hoped it might someday become. He did not
promise to come back on any schedule. He did not, this time, need Mika to tell him the door stayed
open — he had walked through it once, on a day nothing required, and understood, in the plain
arithmetic he trusted more than any feeling, that a door walked through once could be walked through
again, and that this, too, was now simply true, filed alongside every other true thing he kept.

He left before dark, because the ledger back in the district would not read itself, and because he
had not, in fact, stopped being the man who counted things — only added, for the first time, one
more entry to the small private column of things that were not debts, and did not need to be repaid,
and existed, as far as he could tell, simply because he had let them.

The list of names had not grown that day either. He noted that too, on the walk back, the two facts
sitting side by side in his own accounting without contradiction: a debt that stayed unpaid, and a
window that faced the water, both true, both his, both worth keeping.

---

*Continuity notes (not narrative): a real, concrete step forward on the open psychological question
from Section 2 of `daba.md` — he goes, he stays a full day, he leaves without a schedule for
returning — without asserting a final resolution (whether this becomes a habit, whether he ever
lets it compete with the network's own claims on him, stays open). Deliberately mirrors Chronicle
LI's own "arithmetic" language (the list, the count, what's owed and what isn't) to show growth
without abandoning his established voice. No new named characters — Mika reused throughout.*

# Daba Chronicle LV: The Name Daba Never Spoke

*UNLOCKED / PENDING APPROVAL. Daba Chronicle LV, second entry of the third wave. Close-third on
Daba, no dedicated narrator. Extends the blind-succession structure Daba built for individual cells
(`MCD-1597`, "Yeva Tolan"/"Marn," Chronicle XXVII) to the network's own top, a question forced open
by his own near-death in Chronicle LII. Reveals, for the first time, whether Daba built the same
structure in for himself — and names Kether as the answer. Reuses Kether, Bren, Wrenna. No new
named characters.*

---

Bren asked the question three weeks after Threnfall, on an evening when the wound across Daba's
ribs had closed enough to stop demanding daily attention and had started demanding, instead, the
kind of quiet reckoning that came after a body healed faster than the mind that had watched it
nearly fail.

"You built Yeva a second," Bren said. "You've built every cell of any size a second, going back
years. Who's yours?"

Daba did not answer right away, which Bren had learned, across years of proximity, to read
correctly — not evasion, calculation.

"There isn't one," he said finally.

"That's not true, or it's the worst decision you've ever made, and I don't think you make the
worst decision available to you when the stakes are the whole network."

"There wasn't one," Daba corrected, "until Threnfall taught me there needed to be. The doctrine
protects every cell against my own logic. I never applied it to myself, because the network's
whole architecture was built around the assumption that I was the one constant piece — the person
who held the shape of the thing in his own head, the one loss the design itself couldn't route
around. Making a second for myself meant admitting the design had a hole in it exactly where I'd
always told everyone else there couldn't be one."

"And now?"

"Now I've spent three weeks doing the only thing I know how to do with a fact I don't like." He
met Bren's eyes. "I counted it honestly, and built the fix."

He had already chosen her, in the two weeks since, the same way he chose every second: not by
announcement, not by test she would ever recognize as a test, but by the accumulation of small,
unexplained authority handed over on days that looked ordinary from the inside. He had let Kether
run the vetting process end to end for a month without his own review sitting behind it. He had
asked her, twice, to make a call on a resource dispute between two cells that would once have come
to him directly, and had watched her resolve both without asking him a single question afterward
about whether she'd gotten it right. He had, three days ago, without telling her why, handed her the
key to the back room that held the annual list — the one place in the entire network he had never
let another living person enter alone.

She had not asked why. She had simply taken the key, and returned it that evening, and said nothing
at all about what she had or hadn't read inside, which told him more about her fitness for the role
than any test he could have designed on purpose.

"Kether," Bren said, when Daba finally told him, and did not sound surprised so much as satisfied,
the way a man sounds when a suspicion he'd never voiced is finally confirmed. "She doesn't know."

"She doesn't know. And she won't, unless it's needed, for exactly the reason Marn never knew about
the river cell until the morning he had to. If I'm taken, or if the well at Threnfall had gone the
other way three weeks ago, there's nothing in Kether's head worth extracting, because she doesn't
know she's carrying anything at all. She only becomes dangerous the moment she's needed, and by
then it's already too late for anyone to reach her first."

"That's the same argument you made about Yeva's cell."

"It's the same argument because it's still true. I only ever thought it stopped applying to me
because I mistook being necessary for being exempt." He was quiet a moment, turning the fact over
the way he turned every fact, checking its edges. "I nearly proved myself wrong at Threnfall
without meaning to. I'd rather prove myself right on purpose, before the ground makes the choice
for me a second time."

Wrenna, told of it days later — not the name, only that the structure now existed, matching what
she already understood of how the network protected itself — asked the one question that mattered
to her particularly.

"Does she know how close you came? At Threnfall?"

"No," Daba said. "She knows a safehouse was lost and I was wounded closing it. She doesn't know the
numbers. Nobody outside this room knows the numbers but you and Bren, and that was never going to
change just because I finally admitted the hole in my own design."

"Because telling her would make her carry it."

"Because telling her would make her watch me differently, and a second who watches her own leader
for signs of the next near-miss is a second who's already half doing the job before she's ever
asked to. I need Kether running the network the way she's always run it — clear-headed, unwarned,
entirely her own — right up until the one morning it turns out she has to."

The list that night carried no new name, same as it had for most of the year now, and Daba closed
the back room's door on a fact that had cost him three weeks of honest reckoning to admit and had
taken him, in the end, less than a month to fix once he let himself see it clearly: that the
doctrine he had built to survive everyone else's death had never, until Threnfall forced the
question, been asked to survive his own.

---

*Continuity notes (not narrative): extends the blind-succession structure locked at `MCD-1597`
(Yeva Tolan/Marn) to Daba's own position for the first time — a genuine escalation prompted
directly by Chronicle LII's near-death, closing a real structural gap in 1804's own design that the
corpus had never previously addressed. Kether is confirmed as his chosen, unwitting successor;
per the mechanism's own established rule, she does not learn this, and does not learn the true
margin of Threnfall's danger either. Reuses Kether, Bren, and Wrenna, all already established. No
new named characters.*

# Daba Chronicle LVI: What Vetting Cannot See

*UNLOCKED / PENDING APPROVAL. Daba Chronicle LVI, third entry of the third wave, closing it.
Close-third on Daba, no dedicated narrator. A genuine doctrine-limit entry — the network's
elaborate vetting process, dramatized repeatedly across the corpus as the source of its own
safety, fails for the first time not through betrayal but through an honest, non-malicious human
error from someone who passed it faithfully. New named character: Sarel Doune, collision-checked
clean. Reuses Kether. No other new named characters.*

---

Sarel Doune had carried messages for 1804 for four years, had passed the same year-long vetting
every courier passed, had never once, in any test Kether or Daba himself had run against her,
shown a flicker of the carelessness that got people killed. She was, by every measure the network
possessed, exactly the kind of person the doctrine was built to find and trust.

She mentioned the safehouse's approximate location to her own sister over a family dinner, three
towns away from anywhere 1804 operated, in a sentence she did not remember saying an hour later and
would not have recognized as dangerous if she had.

It was not a betrayal. Sarel never told anyone anything she understood to be a secret; she told her
sister, in the ordinary shorthand of two people who had shared a childhood and every worry since, that
she'd been staying near the old grain road lately for work she couldn't discuss, work that kept her
safe, work her sister shouldn't ask about — and her sister, three months later, repeated the
fragment to a man she was courting, a man who repeated it, admiringly, to a friend who happened to
work Compliance intake and had learned, over years in the job, to file even the smallest loose
threads for later use.

Nothing came of it directly. The safehouse in question had already been abandoned for other reasons
by the time the fragment finished its slow crawl through three unrelated conversations and landed,
finally, on a desk that could have used it and, by pure administrative bad luck, filed it under the
wrong district and let it sit unread for a season. But Daba traced the whole chain back afterward,
the way he traced everything, and what he found unsettled him more than any deliberate leak could
have.

"She passed every test we have," he said to Kether, laying the traced conversation out on the
table between them. "Year-long observation. Repeated, unexplained pressure. Every measure we run
against a person to see whether they'll hold a secret under strain, and she held every one of them.
And she still said something she shouldn't have, to someone she loved, in a moment that had no
strain in it at all."

"Because there wasn't any strain," Kether said. "We test people against pressure. We don't test
them against comfort."

"That's exactly it." Daba turned the paper over, though there was nothing on the back of it worth
reading, the gesture only a place to put his hands while his mind worked the problem. "Every test I
have ever designed assumes the danger comes from someone trying to break a person open. It never
once accounted for a person breaking themselves open, gently, out of love, in a sentence that felt
like nothing at the time it was said."

"You can't vet against love."

"No," he agreed. "You can't. Which means the doctrine has a hole in it that no amount of watching
will ever close, because the hole isn't in the watching. It's in the fact that every person we trust
also loves someone we've never vetted at all, and we have no method — none — for reaching the people
they love without becoming exactly the kind of intrusive, controlling apparatus this network was
built to stand against."

Kether was quiet a while, turning that over the way he'd taught her to turn everything over. "So
what do we do."

"I don't know yet." He said it plainly, without the discomfort the admission would once have cost
him — Chronicle L's own honest confession to Wrenna had, in its own way, made this kind of sentence
easier to say aloud. "I could tighten the vetting further. Add a new test for exactly this failure
mode. And it would catch nothing, because the failure mode isn't a weakness in a person's
discipline. It's the ordinary cost of a person having a sister she loves. I'd be punishing the part
of Sarel that makes her worth trusting in the first place to guard against a danger her own
goodness creates."

He did not tell Sarel what had happened, in the end, or how close the chain had come to mattering
before administrative bad luck buried it in the wrong district's files. He judged, and told Kether
plainly that he was judging rather than knowing for certain, that telling her would only teach her
to fear her own sister's dinner table, and that the cost of that fear would very likely exceed the
cost of the risk itself.

"We watch the chain, not the person," he said finally, arriving at the only answer the arithmetic
actually supported. "We can't close the hole. We can only get faster at noticing what falls through
it before it lands somewhere that matters. That's not the doctrine failing. That's the doctrine
finding the edge of what doctrine can do at all."

The list carried no new name because of Sarel Doune, that season or any after. But Daba added, for
the first time in the network's own internal accounting, a category that had never existed before
in any of his careful record-keeping: not a debt, not a name, just a plain, unresolved fact, filed
where he kept the things he had decided to live with rather than solve — that the network's safety
had always depended, in some measure it could never fully audit, on the ordinary, ungovernable love
of people for people who had never signed anything at all.

---

*Continuity notes (not narrative): a genuine doctrine-limit entry, the corpus's first honest,
non-malicious vetting failure — distinct from Chronicle XXXIX's growth-temptation register and
Chronicle XXXVI's grief-arithmetic register, this is specifically about a blind spot in the
vetting mechanism itself (`MCD-1567`'s "cross-trained dispersed cells... doctrine over mass"
extended here to its own limit: doctrine cannot vet against love). No harm actually results,
deliberately, since the point is the exposed structural gap rather than a catastrophe -- matching
the project's established preference for testing a limit cleanly rather than manufacturing
unnecessary stakes. New named character Sarel Doune, collision-checked clean; her sister and the

## Chronicle LIV: "The Window That Faced the Water"

*Pays off LIII's ending — he actually goes.*

He went on a day nothing required him to.

That was the whole of the decision, in the end — not an argument won, not a crisis that happened to route him past the coast road, just an ordinary morning with an empty ledger and no name added to anything, and Daba found that an empty ledger, once he let himself notice it, was its own kind of permission he had never given himself before.

The house was smaller than he'd pictured it, which surprised him more than it should have, given that Mika had described it to him plainly and he had simply failed, in all the months since, to build the real thing out of her words instead of some larger shape his own mind had substituted without telling him. One story. A door that didn't latch quite square in its frame. A kitchen with exactly the kind of window Mika had promised, facing water that was, this far up the coast, more grey than blue, and utterly unremarkable, and somehow more interesting to look at than he'd expected anything to be that asked nothing of him in return.

Mika didn't make a production of his arrival. She handed him a cup of something bitter she called tea and was, by her own cheerful admission, still learning to brew correctly, and let him stand at the window for as long as he wanted without narrating what he should be feeling about it.

"You don't have to say anything," she said, eventually, when the silence had gone on long enough that she judged it needed permission rather than patience. "I didn't buy this to make you perform gratitude at it."

"I'm not performing anything." He turned the cup once in his hands, not drinking, just holding it. "I'm trying to work out what this is, exactly. What room it's supposed to occupy."

"It doesn't have to occupy a room. It can just be a house."

"Everything I've ever kept has had a function." He said it without complaint, the way he might report a tide table. "The ledger. The list. The network. Even you, when we started — you had a function, and I was honest about that at the time, and you were honest back."

"And now?"

"Now I don't know what function this is. A window. Bad tea. You, not doing anything to earn the visit." He set the cup down, untouched, on the sill. "I keep waiting to feel like I'm spending something. Time I owe somewhere else. And I don't. That's the part I don't have a category for."

Mika came and stood beside him at the window, close enough that their shoulders nearly touched, not quite. "Maybe that's what it's for. Not a function. Just the absence of the feeling that everything has to be one."

He stayed the whole day, which was longer than he'd told himself he would, and shorter than Mika, watching him from the doorway as he finally sat down at her kitchen table and let a silence pass between them that had nothing urgent inside it, privately hoped it might someday become. He did not promise to come back on any schedule. He did not, this time, need Mika to tell him the door stayed open — he had walked through it once, on a day nothing required, and understood, in the plain arithmetic he trusted more than any feeling, that a door walked through once could be walked through again, and that this, too, was now simply true, filed alongside every other true thing he kept.

He left before dark, because the ledger back in the district would not read itself, and because he had not, in fact, stopped being the man who counted things — only added, for the first time, one more entry to the small private column of things that were not debts, and did not need to be repaid, and existed, as far as he could tell, simply because he had let them.

The list of names had not grown that day either. He noted that too, on the walk back, the two facts sitting side by side in his own accounting without contradiction: a debt that stayed unpaid, and a window that faced the water, both true, both his, both worth keeping.

---

## Chronicle LV: "The Name Daba Never Spoke"

*Extends the blind-succession structure to Daba's own position — for the first time.*

Bren asked the question three weeks after Threnfall, on an evening when the wound across Daba's ribs had closed enough to stop demanding daily attention and had started demanding, instead, the kind of quiet reckoning that came after a body healed faster than the mind that had watched it nearly fail.

"You built Yeva a second," Bren said. "You've built every cell of any size a second, going back years. Who's yours?"

Daba did not answer right away, which Bren had learned, across years of proximity, to read correctly — not evasion, calculation.

"There isn't one," he said finally.

"That's not true, or it's the worst decision you've ever made, and I don't think you make the worst decision available to you when the stakes are the whole network."

"There wasn't one," Daba corrected, "until Threnfall taught me there needed to be. The doctrine protects every cell against my own logic. I never applied it to myself, because the network's whole architecture was built around the assumption that I was the one constant piece — the person who held the shape of the thing in his own head, the one loss the design itself couldn't route around. Making a second for myself meant admitting the design had a hole in it exactly where I'd always told everyone else there couldn't be one."

"And now?"

"Now I've spent three weeks doing the only thing I know how to do with a fact I don't like." He met Bren's eyes. "I counted it honestly, and built the fix."

He had already chosen her, in the two weeks since, the same way he chose every second: not by announcement, not by test she would ever recognize as a test, but by the accumulation of small, unexplained authority handed over on days that looked ordinary from the inside. He had let Kether run the vetting process end to end for a month without his own review sitting behind it. He had asked her, twice, to make a call on a resource dispute between two cells that would once have come to him directly, and had watched her resolve both without asking him a single question afterward about whether she'd gotten it right. He had, three days ago, without telling her why, handed her the key to the back room that held the annual list — the one place in the entire network he had never let another living person enter alone.

She had not asked why. She had simply taken the key, and returned it that evening, and said nothing at all about what she had or hadn't read inside, which told him more about her fitness for the role than any test he could have designed on purpose.

"Kether," Bren said, when Daba finally told him, and did not sound surprised so much as satisfied, the way a man sounds when a suspicion he'd never voiced is finally confirmed. "She doesn't know."

"She doesn't know. And she won't, unless it's needed, for exactly the reason Marn never knew about the river cell until the morning he had to. If I'm taken, or if the well at Threnfall had gone the other way three weeks ago, there's nothing in Kether's head worth extracting, because she doesn't know she's carrying anything at all. She only becomes dangerous the moment she's needed, and by then it's already too late for anyone to reach her first."

"That's the same argument you made about Yeva's cell."

"It's the same argument because it's still true. I only ever thought it stopped applying to me because I mistook being necessary for being exempt." He was quiet a moment, turning the fact over the way he turned every fact, checking its edges. "I nearly proved myself wrong at Threnfall without meaning to. I'd rather prove myself right on purpose, before the ground makes the choice for me a second time."

Wrenna, told of it days later — not the name, only that the structure now existed, matching what she already understood of how the network protected itself — asked the one question that mattered to her particularly.

"Does she know how close you came? At Threnfall?"

"No," Daba said. "She knows a safehouse was lost and I was wounded closing it. She doesn't know the numbers. Nobody outside this room knows the numbers but you and Bren, and that was never going to change just because I finally admitted the hole in my own design."

"Because telling her would make her carry it."

"Because telling her would make her watch me differently, and a second who watches her own leader for signs of the next near-miss is a second who's already half doing the job before she's ever asked to. I need Kether running the network the way she's always run it — clear-headed, unwarned, entirely her own — right up until the one morning it turns out she has to."

The list that night carried no new name, same as it had for most of the year now, and Daba closed the back room's door on a fact that had cost him three weeks of honest reckoning to admit and had taken him, in the end, less than a month to fix once he let himself see it clearly: that the doctrine he had built to survive everyone else's death had never, until Threnfall forced the question, been asked to survive his own.

---

## Chronicle LVI: "What Vetting Cannot See"

*A genuine, non-malicious failure exposes a real limit of the doctrine itself.*

Sarel Doune had carried messages for 1804 for four years, had passed the same year-long vetting every courier passed, had never once, in any test Kether or Daba himself had run against her, shown a flicker of the carelessness that got people killed. She was, by every measure the network possessed, exactly the kind of person the doctrine was built to find and trust.

She mentioned the safehouse's approximate location to her own sister over a family dinner, three towns away from anywhere 1804 operated, in a sentence she did not remember saying an hour later and would not have recognized as dangerous if she had.

It was not a betrayal. Sarel never told anyone anything she understood to be a secret; she told her sister, in the ordinary shorthand of two people who had shared a childhood and every worry since, that she'd been staying near the old grain road lately for work she couldn't discuss, work that kept her safe, work her sister shouldn't ask about — and her sister, three months later, repeated the fragment to a man she was courting, a man who repeated it, admiringly, to a friend who happened to work Compliance intake and had learned, over years in the job, to file even the smallest loose threads for later use.

Nothing came of it directly. The safehouse in question had already been abandoned for other reasons by the time the fragment finished its slow crawl through three unrelated conversations and landed, finally, on a desk that could have used it and, by pure administrative bad luck, filed it under the wrong district and let it sit unread for a season. But Daba traced the whole chain back afterward, the way he traced everything, and what he found unsettled him more than any deliberate leak could have.

"She passed every test we have," he said to Kether, laying the traced conversation out on the table between them. "Year-long observation. Repeated, unexplained pressure. Every measure we run against a person to see whether they'll hold a secret under strain, and she held every one of them. And she still said something she shouldn't have, to someone she loved, in a moment that had no strain in it at all."

"Because there wasn't any strain," Kether said. "We test people against pressure. We don't test them against comfort."

"That's exactly it." Daba turned the paper over, though there was nothing on the back of it worth reading, the gesture only a place to put his hands while his mind worked the problem. "Every test I have ever designed assumes the danger comes from someone trying to break a person open. It never once accounted for a person breaking themselves open, gently, out of love, in a sentence that felt like nothing at the time it was said."

"You can't vet against love."

"No," he agreed. "You can't. Which means the doctrine has a hole in it that no amount of watching will ever close, because the hole isn't in the watching. It's in the fact that every person we trust also loves someone we've never vetted at all, and we have no method — none — for reaching the people they love without becoming exactly the kind of intrusive, controlling apparatus this network was built to stand against."

Kether was quiet a while, turning that over the way he'd taught her to turn everything over. "So what do we do."

"I don't know yet." He said it plainly, without the discomfort the admission would once have cost him — Chronicle L's own honest confession to Wrenna had, in its own way, made this kind of sentence easier to say aloud. "I could tighten the vetting further. Add a new test for exactly this failure mode. And it would catch nothing, because the failure mode isn't a weakness in a person's discipline. It's the ordinary cost of a person having a sister she loves. I'd be punishing the part of Sarel that makes her worth trusting in the first place to guard against a danger her own goodness creates."

He did not tell Sarel what had happened, in the end, or how close the chain had come to mattering before administrative bad luck buried it in the wrong district's files. He judged, and told Kether plainly that he was judging rather than knowing for certain, that telling her would only teach her to fear her own sister's dinner table, and that the cost of that fear would very likely exceed the cost of the risk itself.

"We watch the chain, not the person," he said finally, arriving at the only answer the arithmetic actually supported. "We can't close the hole. We can only get faster at noticing what falls through it before it lands somewhere that matters. That's not the doctrine failing. That's the doctrine finding the edge of what doctrine can do at all."

The list carried no new name because of Sarel Doune, that season or any after. But Daba added, for the first time in the network's own internal accounting, a category that had never existed before in any of his careful record-keeping: not a debt, not a name, just a plain, unresolved fact, filed where he kept the things he had decided to live with rather than solve — that the network's safety had always depended, in some measure it could never fully audit, on the ordinary, ungovernable love of people for people who had never signed anything at all.

Here's the real survey. I checked the actual files and ledger rather than working from memory — a few things are more/less done than CLAUDE.md's prose history suggested.

## What's genuinely untouched — biggest gaps first

**1. Six of eight Tier 1 Character Chronicle protagonists have never been started at all.** Ozmund (120 Chronicles) and Lauris (109) are the only two launched. Ezio Valcari, Fermand Aurelias, Valen Sinisterblade, Sephtis, Anansi, and Orlok — all named as Tier 1 in the Character Chronicle Gameplan — have zero profile doc, zero walkthrough, zero anything. This is the single biggest block of unbuilt material in the project.

**2. Ten of the eleven Batch-312 villains have no Chronicle dramatizing their defeat.** Only Renfel Auberon got one (Kanja Chronicle III). Harek Vondel, Orven Castellan, Halveth Ashcombe, Rannic Sorvell, Brakon Skevik, Ilsevet Sorrenta, Vex Thurlow, Ossa Drem, Kruger Sennit, and Callas Modrin are all locked as characters with a defeat already specified in their rule text, but nobody's written the scene. Batch 312 explicitly flagged this as "a distinct future wave."

**3. The Character Chronicle Launch Protocol backfill is stalled partway through.** I checked the actual files, not just the status table:
- **5 of 11 aliases** (Bane, Blue-Collar Titan, Captain, Crow King, Sovereign Ghost) have a Rules Walkthrough drafted but no Psychological Profile or Game Plan — gate still reads NO.
- **6 aliases** (Trench Monarch, Industrial Myth, Scourge, Iron Bastard, Lord of Embers, Storm That Walks) have nothing at all.
- **All 20 territories + Arturo** have zero profile docs despite having 2–13 Chronicles each.
- That's the rest of the "34 backfills" Abad ordered on 2026-09-20 ("Backfill everything") — started, then abandoned mid-way.

**4. Real inconsistency worth flagging, not just building around:** Lauris's own profile doc (`character-profiles/lauris-letitia.md`) still reads **"Gate cleared: NO"** even though her Chronicle I was drafted, presented, and locked with your explicit "lock it" (Batch 292), and she now has 109 Chronicles. Either that header is just stale and should say YES, or the gate was cleared conversationally without ever updating the doc. Worth a quick look before more Lauris material gets built on top of it.

**5. Five further Character Chronicle tiers were surveyed in the Gameplan doc but never sequenced:** Avatars/Titans, antagonists, T.D.K.'s Five Champions, dockside crew, and minor named figures. No characters picked yet.

**6. Smaller open threads**, all explicitly flagged as open but not queued: a second SBD/SEALBLACK archive-expansion wave (Batch 311 left this open, same multi-batch pattern as the Maw Codex), a fourth Daba wave, a second Kanja-version wave (27 of the Twenty-Two Victories still undramatized from Kanja's own POV), and `OPEN-012`'s forgotten map codes (deliberately parked).

**7. Drive sync gap:** the Kanja-version track has no Drive folder yet — its 3 Chronicles exist only in git/ledger.

59	The roughly two months between Operation 40 and Lauris's recruitment by Ezio Valcari were the only period since her birth in which she held no institutional affiliation. She moved between fourteen Aerelin-prepared safe-houses, terminating three Directorate tracking teams without incident, and spent the interval securing the relocated engineered-Karesian cave systems (Site K-Theta's 200, per MCD-190) for long-term concealment. Knowledge of the cave systems is staged within the Lords of Cian: Sephtis learns of them within roughly two years of Lauris's recruitment, Ezio within roughly five years; Kanja and the wider crew do not know of them as of the present-day timeline, a detail reserved for a future book.

61	### MCD-194 | World Mechanics
62	Ezio Valcari, having observed Lauris's Directorate career from a distance for roughly two decades, arranged her recruitment meeting through Aerelin's mediation at a private coastal residence. Fermand Aurelias accompanied Ezio and withdrew to a side room, leaving the two to speak alone. Lauris's biological-signature sense registered Ezio's body as inconsistent with his public 'non-combatant theorist' identity -- density and structural-resonance markers she recognized as Karesian-related -- and the two explicitly agreed not to discuss it; the arrangement still holds as of the present-day timeline, and Lauris has never raised what she has since observed of his hidden capability in the field. Ezio briefed her on Anu Un Ra's broader operational history via Sephtis's archives, converting her Operation-34 discovery into full strategic context, and offered her the Attia role. She accepted on three conditions, all agreed without modification: her independent agenda regarding engineered Karesian subjects (the Drowning Vault's 120, the withheld Operation 38 facility, her Kares Prime preservation commitments) takes precedence over Lords of Cian operational requirements when the two conflict; her relationship with Aerelin and the Kareth War-Order network stays on terms she controls rather than the movement's central command; and her authority over her own combat deployment decisions is absolute.

Kanja forged it in eleven continuous days at the Karkosa's forge, using pattern-welded steel infused with Drakma from Mao Volcano's caldera during an unrelated supply stop. The completed breaker measures roughly 720mm, leaf-bladed, and weighs roughly three times what the same design would weigh for a Cian-born wielder -- calibrated specifically to her grip strength and combat-progression curve rather than to standard ergonomics.

She told Kanja: 'This breaker carries the discipline that my Sister-Hold trained me in for six hundred years... After today, the discipline's name on Cian will be the breaker's name. The discipline's previous name on my homeworld is no longer in operational use. I am, in functional terms, transferring the naming authority to your forge. The naming authority belongs to you. I accept the transfer.' Kanja accepted: 'The discipline's name on Cian is Attia's Rite. The forge accepts the naming authority. The forge will hold it until you require its return.' Since the exchange, Kanja has also become her equipment's primary maintenance authority on Cian, periodically refining and recalibrating the Spine of Dagon and the Aristocrat alongside Attia's Rite.

Act III, the Five Champions' first open war: Baryon's march against the Unchained Kingdom (repelled), Kanja's naval engagement against Ever-Haunt forces redirected toward the Foldtide, and Bolo Troth's attempt to retrieve Archon Meridian colliding with Ezio's investigation. # Ezio Valcari — Profile & Game Plan

**Status:** walkthrough drafted
**Track:** Character Chronicle (Tier 1)
**Gate cleared:** NO — no Chronicle prose may be drafted or presented until this file reaches "game plan approved."

This file is the standing gate artifact for this character, per the Character Chronicle Launch
Protocol locked in `CLAUDE.md`. It is the single source of truth for who this character is before
any Chronicle is written or rewritten — not a summary produced after the fact.

---

## 1. Rules Walkthrough

Every locked rule touching Ezio Valcari, pulled from `canon-ledger.json` and organized thematically.
Ezio is a genuine backfill case in the same sense Daba was: he has never had his own Chronicle
series, but he is an extensively demonstrated recurring supporting character across 31 Kanja
Industrial Myth Alias Chronicles (plus one Lord of Embers crossover) and 4 of Lauris Letitia's own
Character Chronicles. The profile below must synthesize that demonstrated characterization, not
invent a competing one.

### Biography / stats
- `CC-027` / `WC-016` — publicly known as a theorist/spymaster, but classified as an elite
  close-quarters combatant capable of killing a room in three seconds. This capability is a closed
  secret known only to Valen, Sephtis, Kanja, Anansi, and Lauris (`CC-111` amends the list to
  confirm Lauris knows). Valen actively protects Ezio's cover.
- `CC-026` / `WC-016` / `CC-108` — first cousin of Valen Sinisterblade, of House Valcari, sharing
  the "Sinister Bloodline" martial tradition; Valen personally and familially trained him in the
  Sinister Bloodline's War-Side tradition (extends `CC-035`), not merely a shared lineage.
- `CC-028` — 75 years old (present-day/Book 1 timeline), with 750 years of wisdom-equivalence
  gained through training under Sephtis.
- `MCD-373` — roughly sixteen years old at the Furnace District Strike (Kanja's own age 21 at that
  battle, `MCD-244`) — his earliest demonstrated appearance in the corpus.
- `CC-030` — one-third of "the revolutionary trio": Ezio (the Architect/strategy), Fermand/Hermes
  (the Unbroken/endurance and synthesis), Anansi (the Spark/morale and agitation).
- `VB-020` / `VB-023` — one of the Voice Bible's five designated narrators: narrates the
  investigation chapters (alternating with Fermand). His register is Zafón Gothic/Noir atmosphere
  fused with Twain-Marx wit; never breaks character to explain the investigation to the reader.
- `VB-024` / `CC-034` — Fermand narrates all Ezio and Lauris POV chapters in his own clinical,
  contraction-free register — and reserves his only warmth in the entire Voice Bible for "My dear
  Ezio."

### Relationships
- `CC-029` / `MCD-021` / `CC-073` — his patron is Lady Nadea Thren, a defected SBD analyst
  operating independently (not T.D.K.'s champion, not "Glass Ordained" — her defection dissolved
  the Mirrored Chorus division, `MCD-284`). She is genuinely, secretly in love with him; Ezio
  figured out years ago that she is "the Viper" and stays anyway.
- `CC-031` / `MCD-032` / `MCD-194` — Lauris Letitia is his Attia (Sergeant-at-Arms), a former SBD
  external contractor he personally identified and recruited: he observed her Directorate career
  from a distance for roughly two decades, arranged the recruitment meeting through Aerelin's
  mediation, briefed her on Anu Un Ra's history via Sephtis's archives, and offered her the role.
  She accepted on three non-negotiable conditions (her independent Karesian-preservation agenda
  takes precedence when it conflicts with Lords of Cian operations; her relationship with Aerelin's
  network stays on her own terms, not central command's; her combat-deployment authority is
  absolute) — all still hold as of the present-day timeline.
- `MCD-194` — at that same recruitment meeting, Lauris's biological senses registered Ezio's body
  as inconsistent with his "non-combatant theorist" public identity; the two explicitly agreed
  never to discuss it, and the arrangement still holds — she has never raised it since.
- `CC-032` / `MCD-203` / `MCD-204` / `ARS-359` — roughly fourteen months after Lauris's
  recruitment, Ezio commissioned Kanja to forge Attia's Rite as the symbolic instrument of her
  Attia role; Kanja forged it in eleven days, and it was delivered privately to Lauris with Ezio
  present only as nominal commissioner. (`ARS-210`'s original listing of Attia's Rite as part of
  Ezio's own Concealed Arsenal is a superseded duplication error, corrected in favor of Lauris's
  ownership — see Abilities/gear below.)
- `MCD-205` — his present-day working relationship with Lauris runs through communication
  protocols compressed to a single word or gesture: he provides strategic direction, she provides
  survivable execution.
- `MCD-1626` — Fermand's reserved warmth ("My dear Ezio") is given narrative texture directly in
  Lauris Chronicle IX, "My Dear Ezio" — a stakes-free, non-combat evening between the two of them.
- `MCD-1564` / `MCD-1661` — in Lauris's own Chronicle series he functions as the party she reports
  operational debts back to (Chronicle IV, the Operation 38 facility) and as someone she
  deliberately does not brief when honoring a personal, off-the-books favor for Aerelin
  (Chronicle XLIV) — both consistent with `MCD-194`'s recruitment-condition carve-outs.
- `ARS-344` — Valen (already established as Ezio's cousin/combat mentor) is also locked as Kanja's
  own Master-at-Arms ("the White Lotus"), the one who ordered Kanja to document Mafesto's function
  starting at age 26 — a structural link between Ezio's own combat-tradition family and Kanja's
  crew infrastructure.

### Abilities / gear
- `CC-027` / `WC-016` / `ARS-405` — his classified combat profile: can kill a room in three seconds.
  Never dramatized directly on the page anywhere in the corpus to date — it stays a stated fact,
  not a shown one.
- `ARS-404` — the Archive-Key: twelve hair-thin Living Drakma filaments bio-tuned to his own
  resonance, housed in the hollow shaft of the Cipher Cane (a plain cane reading publicly as a
  theorist's affectation). Defeats locks/mechanisms by touch-reading their structure through
  micro-vibration feedback, and interfaces with Directorate Drakma data-plates to read sealed
  classified SBD records back to him the same way. The same cane performs Structural Interrogation
  (mapping a room's density/structure in two taps).
- `ARS-405` — the Socratic Trap: his signature interrogation method, not a weapon — oblique,
  apparently academic questions that lead a target down a logical path where only a truthful final
  answer avoids self-contradiction, closed with a deliberate silence. In-canon characterized as
  having extracted more intelligence than any blade in the crew's arsenal.
- `ARS-210` / `ARS-359` — superseded/corrected: Attia's Rite is not his own weapon. The original
  listing was a duplication error; it is Lauris's breaker, forged to mark his own promotion of her
  to Sergeant-at-Arms, not something he wields.
- `ARS-399` — his forensic accounting is locked as one of the two known real-world weaknesses of
  the SBD's Scrip-Tether system (alongside the Sovereign Umbrella's radius-nullification):
  publicly proving the debt's underlying math is fraudulent.

### Already-locked plot beats (book-level or Chronicle-level)
- `MCD-231` / `MCD-244` / `MCD-234` / `MCD-286` — the evidence-first, unarmed documentation method
  he is most associated with predates his own recruitment onto the page: Kanja's proof-not-violence
  doctrine begins at the Scrip-Forge Raid (age 18) and reaches its purest form at the Furnace
  District Strike (age 21), where Ezio (Kanja's own account puts him at ~16 here) compiles 4,000
  workers' testimony into a documented, deliberately unpayable debt structure.
- `MCD-070` — Book 1, "The Deposed King": Ezio and Fermand investigate the Fulfillment Ceremony's
  double regicide, hired by Ozmund. Three acts: Investigation → 10-Day Interregnum → Karkosa Heist.
- `CULT-044` / `CULT-053` / `CULT-071` / `CULT-075` / `CULT-080` / `CULT-081` / `MCD-1853` — the
  Book 1 investigation's actual texture: an eleven-minute death-certificate filing anomaly he
  finds first; a dead Fraction analyst's buried evidence of SBD leadership's advance knowledge; a
  Caucus senator's silent calculation that his investigation won't reach the relay (it does); a
  clearinghouse archive Keeper's theologically-motivated bureaucratic obstruction; and the SBD
  wet-work team's actual tradecraft (planted false-conspiracy evidence, a memory-suppressing
  compound) that misdirects his investigation for the first third of the book.
- `MCD-098` / `MCD-221` — Book 5 Gate Battle: Gate team is Orlok, Anansi, Ezio, Fermand, Legbara
  Kalunga. "Ezio's cover dies at the gate; the gate lives" — his cover identity, not necessarily
  Ezio himself.
- `MCD-279` — Book 2's climax: Bolo Troth's attempt to retrieve Archon Meridian collides with
  Ezio's own investigation; Book 2 ends with Ezio's discovery that the Crown-Scar is a root-access
  tether T.D.K. could reactivate to seize direct control of Ozmund's mind.
- `MCD-1864` — Callas Modrin (`CC-156`, a Batch-312 pre-Book-1 villain) is eventually exposed by
  Ezio personally, via the same evidence-first methodology, in a bureaucratic-judo defeat with no
  combat. The rule itself states plainly: **"No Chronicle prose has been drafted; this is a queued
  future beat for whenever Ezio's own Character Chronicle series launches"** — this is a
  ready-made, already-reserved Chronicle candidate.

### Reserved / unresolved threads
- His full classified combat capability (`WC-016`/`CC-027`) has never been shown on the page
  anywhere in the corpus — deliberately withheld across every appearance to date, including his 31
  Industrial Myth appearances, which are consistently unarmed/non-combat.
- Nadea Thren's secret love for him (`CC-073`) is locked as real and unresolved — not to be paid
  off or dramatized as reciprocated/rejected without Abad's direction.
- `MCD-1171` — Pell Ostra's private margin-notes (kept from Ezio) identify an unnamed recurring
  observer connecting two otherwise unrelated frauds; the observer's identity is deliberately left
  open — a live thread that could eventually intersect Ezio's own investigative arc.
- The entire Book 1 investigation (`CULT-044` etc.) and the Book 2 Crown-Scar discovery (`MCD-279`)
  are explicitly Book-1/Book-2-era plot material — reserved, not pre-Book-1 territory. Any launch
  wave for Ezio needs its own era constraint the way Ozmund's launch got one (strictly
  pre-Fulfillment-Ceremony); the natural equivalent boundary here is pre-Book-1 (before the double
  regicide), matching Ezio's own already-demonstrated corpus, which runs from his teens through his
  adult spymaster years without ever touching the investigation itself.
- His "cover dies at the gate" (`MCD-098`) in Book 5 is a live open question about what exactly his
  cover identity is and how it differs from Ezio himself — not defined anywhere yet, and not this
  track's to resolve.

### Existing Chronicle corpus
Unlike Ozmund or Kanja-version (both launched from near-zero), Ezio already has substantial
demonstrated characterization on the page — 31 Industrial Myth Alias Chronicles plus 4 Lauris
Character Chronicles, spanning from his teens through adulthood:

- **Origin appearance** (`MCD-373`, Industrial Myth III, "The Boy Who Kept the Numbers Honest"):
  ~age 16, already performing the method's real corrective function — cross-checking worker
  testimony against production records and quietly adjusting entries *upward* when a frightened
  worker under-claims, rather than taking testimony at face value.
- **Growth into an institution-builder**: dispersing decoy ledger copies to defeat a raid
  (`MCD-404`); articulating *why* the numbers-first method outlasts fear-based leverage (`MCD-439`);
  running fully epistolary campaigns against evasive administrators (`MCD-749`); keeping the method
  running without Kanja present (`MCD-761`); training a second-generation of independent district
  auditors (`MCD-896`, `MCD-931`, `MCD-1399`); training Kanja's own testimony-gathering successor
  alongside his own arithmetic-auditor track (`MCD-1443`).
- **Genuine friction with Kanja, not just partnership**: the method's first real disagreement
  (`MCD-925`, "What Ezio Refused to Enter") — Ezio wants to use unrelated personal scandal as
  leverage, Kanja refuses and draws a hard boundary, and Ezio stays genuinely unpersuaded.
- **His own tested integrity**: catches a testifier weaponizing the ledger to frame an innocent
  clerk (`MCD-924`); is offered and genuinely tempted by a bribe himself, and discloses both the
  offer and his own temptation before deciding (`MCD-1446`) — extending the crew's internal
  transparency discipline that Kanja himself models in `MCD-1152`.
- **His own vulnerability shown once**: injured off-page in `MCD-1156`, forcing Kanja to run the
  cross-referencing arithmetic alone for the first time — established as slower and less precise
  than Ezio's trained skill, the corpus's clearest statement of Ezio's own specific expertise.
- **Consistent traits across the full corpus**: methodical, exacting, initially reluctant to share
  or delegate his method (`MCD-766`) but grows past it; treats numbers as something that "don't
  flinch either way" (impartial even against a sympathetic claimant's own wishes, `MCD-1442`);
  capable of real moral nuance (reconciling two honestly conflicting testimonies rather than
  picking a winner, `MCD-1148`; inventing a new record category for grief that has no wage
  equivalent, `MCD-764`); consistently unarmed and non-combat in every one of his 31 appearances to
  date.
- **Lauris's own track** (`MCD-1564`, `MCD-1626`, `MCD-1661`, `MCD-1669`): confirms his role as the
  one she reports operational debts to, the one relationship allowed genuine on-page warmth via
  Fermand's narration, and `CC-134`'s explicit framing that among the crew's defining emotional
  burdens, "Ezio carries deception."

## 2. Psychological Profile

Built collaboratively with Abad, not handed to him finished. Draft proposals go here marked
**PROPOSED**, and are corrected in place (not appended-and-superseded) once discussed — this file
always reflects current understanding, not a batch-log history of how we got there.

- **Core wound / formative event: PROPOSED, genuinely open, flagged rather than invented.** The
  walkthrough has no locked rule stating why a ~16-year-old is already this disciplined, this
  protective of frightened workers' under-claimed dues, and already carrying a trained,
  three-second lethality he's chosen never to use publicly. Two anchored facts point toward
  candidates rather than settling one: (1) he's House Valcari, cousin to Valen, raised inside the
  "Sinister Bloodline" War-Side tradition (`CC-108`) — a family lineage whose expected currency is
  violence — and Ezio's entire adult life reads as a deliberate turn away from that currency
  toward an entirely different weapon (evidence, patience, paperwork), banking the trained
  lethality as a last resort instead; (2) his signature professional instinct is protecting people
  from their own self-erasure — correcting under-claimed testimony upward, correcting a veteran's
  pride-driven understatement against his own stated wishes (`MCD-1442`) — which reads as
  personal, not merely procedural, the kind of instinct someone develops from having once had
  their own true cost go uncounted, unclaimed, or disbelieved. Genuinely open for Abad: whether
  the wound is (a) the Sinister Bloodline itself — being raised to be a weapon and refusing the
  role while never being permitted to fully set it down, (b) something specific that happened to
  him or someone he protected before the Furnace District Strike that the corpus hasn't shown yet,
  or (c) something else entirely.
- **Defense mechanisms: PROPOSED.** Compartmentalization as an art form — he doesn't just keep
  secrets, he architects exactly who knows what and why, down to a five-person closed list for the
  single most basic fact about himself (`WC-016`/`CC-111`). Indirection as first resort: a
  document, a decoy, or a Socratic Trap before ever a blade — the three-second kill is the
  emergency measure, never the opening move, in every one of his 35 appearances to date.
  Compulsive verification past the stated boundary of any claim, including his own comfort with a
  case being "closed" (`MCD-1169`, `MCD-1033`) — he does not appear to trust a resolution simply
  because it looks resolved. Notably, this compartmentalization runs outward only: toward his own
  inner circle he over-discloses rather than under-discloses, self-reporting his own bribe
  temptation before deciding rather than after (`MCD-1446`) — the deception is reserved for the
  world, never (so far as shown) turned on the people who actually trust him.
- **Values — what they will not compromise: PROPOSED.** Evidence over violence, applied without
  exception across 35 shown appearances. A hard boundary against using someone's private,
  unrelated life as leverage — one he disagreed with when Kanja drew it (`MCD-925`) but has never
  shown violating. Radical internal honesty toward the people who trust him, even when it costs him
  standing (self-disclosing a genuine temptation, not just a clean refusal, `MCD-1446`). Protecting
  the vulnerable from their own fear or pride-driven self-erasure, even against their explicitly
  stated wishes (`MCD-1442`) — this one reads less like professional rigor and more like something
  he needs to be true.
- **How they hold contradiction (PROPOSED — the strongest, most load-bearing thread):** he is the
  single most transparent-seeming person in the crew — a public theorist who spends his entire
  professional life making other people's hidden truths undeniable and permanent — and
  simultaneously the single most hidden person in it. The master of finding other people's truth
  is himself the best-kept secret in the Lords of Cian. Someone trained from adolescence to end a
  room in three seconds has built an entire adult life's work around engineering situations where
  he never has to.
- **Relationship patterns: PROPOSED.** Selects people for years before acting — observed Lauris's
  career from a distance for roughly two decades before ever approaching her (`MCD-194`).
  Negotiates relationships as explicit, durable agreements rather than assumed loyalty — Lauris's
  three recruitment conditions have held, inviolate, for the full length of her tenure (`MCD-205`).
