327	## 2. Psychological Profile
328	
329	Built collaboratively with Abad, not handed to him finished. Draft proposals go here marked
330	**PROPOSED**, and are corrected in place (not appended-and-superseded) once discussed —
331	this file always reflects current understanding, not a batch-log history of how we got there.
332	
333	- **Core wound / formative event (PROPOSED):** the Rookery itself (`MCD-1566`), but specifically
334	  the miscount at the bottom of it. Chronicle I ("What the Stairs Would Not Give Back," `MCD-1571`)
335	  shows Daba getting eleven of nineteen children out clean, then losing the sound of Fennic's voice
336	  on the stairs above him — the wound is not simply that people died, it's that the number he was
337	  counting, the one discipline he actually had in that moment, came out wrong: "eleven children plus
338	  one counted twice against a number he did not yet have and would spend the rest of his life
339	  carrying." Chronicle II (`MCD-1572`) shows the immediate aftermath: the death toll (1,804) landing
340	  on him not as an abstraction but as a number that "already had Fennic's face in it" the instant he
341	  heard it — and shows his very first response to catastrophic loss being to sit beside Odalys and
342	  take names, refusing to let anyone go into her ledger unnamed. `CC-135` confirms he was present and
343	  survived as one of the caregivers, not an outside founder arriving after the fact — the wound is
344	  personally lived, not inherited secondhand.
345	- **Defense mechanisms (PROPOSED):** counting as containment. The corpus shows this as literal,
346	  involuntary habit — Chronicle L (`MCD-1620`) has him automatically counting heads in any room he
347	  sits in for more than a few minutes, "unbidden, automatic, no longer anything he needed to fight" —
348	  and as formalized private ritual: the annual reading of a hand-kept list of every name the doctrine
349	  has cost, which Chronicle XL (`MCD-1610`) is explicit is "not penance, it was accounting," because
350	  "a debt correctly counted was a debt that could, eventually, be answered." The second, related
351	  defense is extended, deliberate observation before any decisive contact with a person: he watches
352	  Sael eleven days before testing her (Ch. VI), watches the young Kanja eleven days before
353	  approaching him (Ch. XI–XII), and vets Isolde Wrenna for roughly a year before she is ever told the
354	  truth (Ch. XXIX). Worth flagging directly to Abad: this reads as a deliberate structural echo of
355	  Kanja's own already-locked defense, "arithmetic as armor" (`kanja-haku-rexmar.md`, Section 2) — and
356	  given `MCD-1568`'s explicit framing of their mentorship as one lesson taught from two directions,
357	  that echo may be intentional rather than coincidental. The two are not identical, though: Kanja's
358	  arithmetic is a decision-ratio (cost of action versus cost of inaction, applied outward to justify
359	  a choice); Daba's is a ledger of names (applied backward, to keep an unrepayable loss legible rather
360	  than to license the next action). Both keep an unbearable thing bearable by making it countable.
361	- **Values — what he will not compromise (PROPOSED):** doctrine over mass, absolutely — `MCD-1567`'s
362	  "anything large enough to be seen is large enough to be burned" is not a tactic he'll trade off
363	  against a good enough argument. Chronicle XXXIX ("The Case Kether Made," `MCD-1609`) is the
364	  clearest test of this: Kether makes a substantive, numerically grounded case for scaling up, and
365	  Daba concedes he has no answer that fully satisfies him — but he still will not simply authorize
366	  growth, offering a controlled, bounded experiment instead of the thing she actually asked for. The
367	  second non-negotiable, tightly linked to the first: no debt goes unacknowledged and no relationship
368	  runs one-directional. Chronicle XIV ("The Trade Between Equals," `MCD-1584`) has him say "I don't
369	  like the shape of that" about teaching the young Kanja for free, and refuse to let the arrangement
370	  stand as charity in either direction until both sides name it a trade aloud. Chronicle XXXVI ("What
371	  He Would Not Trade," `MCD-1606`) gives the title's own value its sharpest edge: he will not spend
372	  three or four lives to buy back one, even Tamsin's, even under direct pressure from a subordinate
373	  who trained her — the arithmetic that keeps the network alive is not suspended for grief.
374	- **How he holds contradiction (PROPOSED)** — the specific tension that makes him dramatically
375	  interesting: he is, in the single moment that actually matters, the least deliberate person in the
376	  network — Chronicle I is explicit that at the Rookery "he did not remember deciding anything," and
377	  Chronicle XXXVI shows the identical register years later, an instant, unflinching "None of them" the
378	  moment Bren finishes laying out rescue plans for Tamsin. And yet everything he has built since the
379	  Rookery is the opposite of that: eleven-day watches, year-long vetting, a doctrine explicitly
380	  designed so that no one, himself included, is ever again forced to act on that little information
381	  that fast. He doesn't experience this as contradictory, because it isn't, from inside: the years of
382	  patient observation are exactly what let the instant decision arrive already correct rather than
383	  merely fast — the deliberation is front-loaded so precisely that when the crisis moment does come,
384	  what looks like pure reflex is actually the doctrine speaking through him rather than a break from
385	  it.
386	- **Relationship patterns (PROPOSED):** trust and intimacy are earned slowly and never assumed, in
387	  every direction — the blind-succession structure (Ch. XXVII) that never tells a chosen second they
388	  were chosen until it matters; the year of unwitting testing given to Isolde Wrenna (Ch. XXIX); and,
389	  with Kanja specifically, an opening register the text names outright as "deliberate mutual wariness
390	  rather than any trust" (Ch. XI) that only resolves into something warmer once both parties state the
391	  exchange aloud as a trade between equals (Ch. XIV). The corresponding cost of this pattern: he keeps
392	  even his closest relationships at one structural remove by design, deliberately reaching a point
393	  where he "no longer knows every face in the network" he built (Ch. XXX, `MCD-1600`) — closeness with
394	  specific people (Mika, kept near him across the entire fifty-entry corpus, present from the cistern
395	  in Chronicle I through the closing meal in Chronicle L) coexists with institutional distance from
396	  the whole he's responsible for. He does not lead by command presence; he leads by demonstrated
397	  proof, the same currency he demands of anyone who wants close to him.
398	- **What breaks him / his real vulnerability (PROPOSED):** not physical defeat — no Chronicle in the
399	  corpus shows him personally endangered or tested in combat; his S-tier rating (`CC-135`) is never
400	  once dramatized as a limit under threat. His real vulnerability is that the accounting never
401	  resolves. Chronicle XL states this as flatly as the corpus ever states anything: "neither the doubt
402	  nor the determination resolves the other" — he has never once let the private list stop him from
403	  acting, but he has also never once achieved the certainty that would let him set the list down.
404	  Chronicle L sharpens this further: when Wrenna asks the plainest possible question — what is all of
405	  this actually *for* — his honest answer is "I don't know. I've never known," and he has built a
406	  life's discipline, and asked a great many people to risk their lives inside it, on a founding
407	  principle he cannot fully justify even to himself. He is vulnerable exactly where no amount of
408	  patient counting produces an answer. **Genuinely open, not yet demonstrated anywhere in the
409	  corpus, worth settling with Abad rather than assumed:** whether he wants anything for himself
410	  distinct from the network's survival — the Rules Walkthrough itself flags that no entry across all
411	  fifty addresses a personal want or hope, and this profile does not invent one. That absence may
412	  itself be part of what breaks him (a self folded entirely into the ledger), or it may simply be
413	  underwritten territory a future wave should develop — the corpus as it stands doesn't say which.
414	- **Defining emotional throughline (PROPOSED):** *the debt correctly counted.* Not discipline-over-
415	  mass itself — that's the doctrine's tactical expression, already locked at `MCD-1567` — but the
416	  emotional engine underneath it: grief metabolized into permanent, disciplined accounting rather than
417	  into either collapse or false resolution. Chronicle XL states the thesis directly — "the list was
418	  not penance, it was accounting... a debt correctly counted was a debt that could, eventually, be
419	  answered" — and the whole of 1804 (the doctrine, the vetting, the cross-training, the forging
420	  network Kanja's teaching made possible, `MCD-1570`) reads as one extended, still-unfinished attempt
421	  to answer a specific, un-erasable failure of count on one night eight years before the Rebellion. It
422	  is worth naming to Abad directly as a deliberate resonance rather than an accident of two separate
423	  drafts: Kanja's own throughline is "the function, not the name" (identity expressed entirely through
424	  action on a structure); Daba's is closer to "the name, not the number" (identity expressed entirely
425	  through refusing to let a person become a statistic) — two different emotional answers to the same
426	  locked shared root (`MCD-1568`) of one lesson taught in two directions.
427	
428	**Abad's ruling, verbatim:** "Approve as drafted, keep going." Section 2 is closed.
429

1	# Daba Chronicle LVI: What Vetting Cannot See
2	
3	*Locked canon, Batch 316, 2026-09-28. Daba Chronicle LVI, third entry of the third wave, closing it.
4	Close-third on Daba, no dedicated narrator. A genuine doctrine-limit entry — the network's
5	elaborate vetting process, dramatized repeatedly across the corpus as the source of its own
6	safety, fails for the first time not through betrayal but through an honest, non-malicious human
7	error from someone who passed it faithfully. New named character: Lisbet Doune, collision-checked
8	clean. Reuses Kether. No other new named characters. Corrected Batch 335, 2026-10-02: a writers'-room leak ("Chronicle L's own honest confession") reworded to plain prose; the new character "Sarel Doune" renamed "Lisbet Doune" to resolve a one-letter collision with the already-locked "Serel" (MCD-1608). *
9	
10	---
11	
12	Lisbet Doune had carried messages for 1804 for four years, had passed the same year-long vetting
13	every courier passed, had never once, in any test Kether or Daba himself had run against her,
14	shown a flicker of the carelessness that got people killed. She was, by every measure the network
15	possessed, exactly the kind of person the doctrine was built to find and trust.
16	
17	She mentioned the safehouse's approximate location to her own sister over a family dinner, three
18	towns away from anywhere 1804 operated, in a sentence she did not remember saying an hour later and
19	would not have recognized as dangerous if she had.
20	
21	It was not a betrayal. Lisbet never told anyone anything she understood to be a secret; she told her
22	sister, in the ordinary shorthand of two people who had shared a childhood and every worry since, that
23	she'd been staying near the old grain road lately for work she couldn't discuss, work that kept her
24	safe, work her sister shouldn't ask about — and her sister, three months later, repeated the
25	fragment to a man she was courting, a man who repeated it, admiringly, to a friend who happened to
26	work Compliance intake and had learned, over years in the job, to file even the smallest loose
27	threads for later use.
28	
29	Nothing came of it directly. The safehouse in question had already been abandoned for other reasons
30	by the time the fragment finished its slow crawl through three unrelated conversations and landed,
31	finally, on a desk that could have used it and, by pure administrative bad luck, filed it under the
32	wrong district and let it sit unread for a season. But Daba traced the whole chain back afterward,
33	the way he traced everything, and what he found unsettled him more than any deliberate leak could
34	have.
35	
36	"She passed every test we have," he said to Kether, laying the traced conversation out on the
37	table between them. "Year-long observation. Repeated, unexplained pressure. Every measure we run
38	against a person to see whether they'll hold a secret under strain, and she held every one of them.
39	And she still said something she shouldn't have, to someone she loved, in a moment that had no
40	strain in it at all."
41	
42	"Because there wasn't any strain," Kether said. "We test people against pressure. We don't test
43	them against comfort."
44	
45	"That's exactly it." Daba turned the paper over, though there was nothing on the back of it worth
46	reading, the gesture only a place to put his hands while his mind worked the problem. "Every test I
47	have ever designed assumes the danger comes from someone trying to break a person open. It never
48	once accounted for a person breaking themselves open, gently, out of love, in a sentence that felt
49	like nothing at the time it was said."
50	
51	"You can't vet against love."
52	
53	"No," he agreed. "You can't. Which means the doctrine has a hole in it that no amount of watching
54	will ever close, because the hole isn't in the watching. It's in the fact that every person we trust
55	also loves someone we've never vetted at all, and we have no method — none — for reaching the people
56	they love without becoming exactly the kind of intrusive, controlling apparatus this network was
57	built to stand against."
58	
59	Kether was quiet a while, turning that over the way he'd taught her to turn everything over. "So
60	what do we do."
61	
62	"I don't know yet." He said it plainly, without the discomfort the admission would once have cost
63	him — his own honest confession to Tessin at a closing meal, years ago, had in its own way made this kind of sentence
64	easier to say aloud. "I could tighten the vetting further. Add a new test for exactly this failure
65	mode. And it would catch nothing, because the failure mode isn't a weakness in a person's
66	discipline. It's the ordinary cost of a person having a sister she loves. I'd be punishing the part
67	of Lisbet that makes her worth trusting in the first place to guard against a danger her own
68	goodness creates."
69	
70	He did not tell Lisbet what had happened, in the end, or how close the chain had come to mattering
71	before administrative bad luck buried it in the wrong district's files. He judged, and told Kether
72	plainly that he was judging rather than knowing for certain, that telling her would only teach her
73	to fear her own sister's dinner table, and that the cost of that fear would very likely exceed the
74	cost of the risk itself.
75	
76	"We watch the chain, not the person," he said finally, arriving at the only answer the arithmetic
77	actually supported. "We can't close the hole. We can only get faster at noticing what falls through
78	it before it lands somewhere that matters. That's not the doctrine failing. That's the doctrine
79	finding the edge of what doctrine can do at all."
80	
81	The list carried no new name because of Lisbet Doune, that season or any after. But Daba added, for
82	the first time in the network's own internal accounting, a category that had never existed before
83	in any of his careful record-keeping: not a debt, not a name, just a plain, unresolved fact, filed
84	where he kept the things he had decided to live with rather than solve — that the network's safety
85	had always depended, in some measure it could never fully audit, on the ordinary, ungovernable love
86	of people for people who had never signed anything at all.
87	
88	---
89	
90	*Continuity notes (not narrative): a genuine doctrine-limit entry, the corpus's first honest,
91	non-malicious vetting failure — distinct from Chronicle XXXIX's growth-temptation register and
92	Chronicle XXXVI's grief-arithmetic register, this is specifically about a blind spot in the
93	vetting mechanism itself (`MCD-1567`'s "cross-trained dispersed cells... doctrine over mass"
94	extended here to its own limit: doctrine cannot vet against love). No harm actually results,
95	deliberately, since the point is the exposed structural gap rather than a catastrophe -- matching
96	the project's established preference for testing a limit cleanly rather than manufacturing
97	unnecessary stakes. New named character Lisbet Doune, collision-checked clean; her sister and the
98	Compliance intake clerk are deliberately unnamed. Reuses Kether. No child-safety or content issues
99	-- an ordinary family conversation, nothing depicted beyond it.*

# Daba Chronicle LVII: The Correction That Announced Itself

*UNLOCKED -- pending Abad's approval. Daba Chronicle LVII. Close-third on Daba, no dedicated
narrator, matching the series' established convention. Dramatizes Harek Vondel's killing by 1804
(`CC-147`/`MCD-1855`) for the first time -- queued since Batch 312, explicitly flagged in Daba's own
profile doc as a candidate beat for a future wave, not yet drafted. Set during the network's
post-founding, pre-dormancy years (mature network era, after Block F's own timeframe). Reuses
already-locked 1804 members Kether and Rhyne Cadec; no new named characters. The kill is deliberately
not attributed to Kanja or any Alias, consistent with `MCD-1569`'s standing separation.*

---

Harek Vondel had corrected eleven settlements in the Shattered Kingdoms' rural interior over four
years, and he thought of each one the way another man might think of a promotion he had personally
arranged: a line in a career ledger, accomplishment recorded and filed. His method was always the
same, and he was proud that it was the same, because a method repeated and perfected was, to him,
the whole definition of professionalism -- send word three days ahead that the correction is coming,
let fear do the softening, then arrive to find a district too frightened to resist and too
demoralized to hide anything worth finding.

He announced the twelfth correction the way he'd announced the first eleven: openly, days in
advance, confident that the warning itself was the weapon.

Kether read the warning the morning it reached her, and understood within the hour that she was
looking at the first piece of real information 1804 had ever been handed for free.

"He's telling us exactly where he'll be and exactly when," she said to Rhyne Cadec, laying the
correction notice on the table between them. "He thinks the fear is the weapon. He's never once
considered that the notice is."

Daba watched the planning from a remove he had kept deliberately for years now -- present at the
first council where Kether laid out the route Vondel's detachment would have to take through the
Sarrow approach, offering two corrections to her timing and nothing else, then absent from
everything after, by his own long-standing rule that an operation planned this far from the Rookery
belonged to the people running it, not to him. He had learned, the hard way, that watching too
closely was its own kind of taking credit.

The ambush took four days to prepare and six minutes to execute. Vondel's detachment, confident in a
route no one should have known to defend, walked into a defile Rhyne Cadec had spent two of those
four days quietly collapsing at both ends, the same narrowing-into-a-bottleneck logic a much younger
Kanja had once learned on a disused footbridge and never forgotten. Vondel himself died in the first
minute, still calling out the correction's opening formalities to a district that had already
emptied two days before his column arrived.

What reached Daba afterward was not a battle report so much as an irony he turned over for longer
than the operation itself had taken. Vondel had kept his own ledger -- eleven settlements, eleven
completed lines, a career measured the way a man measures anything he has learned to survive by
counting. Daba understood that impulse better than he wanted to. The difference, he said to Kether
once the cell had stood down and the district's survivors had quietly begun returning to houses no
one had burned, was not that one man counted and the other didn't.

"He counted what he'd taken," Daba said. "I count what it costs. He thought the ledger made him
careful. It only ever made him predictable."

The kill went unclaimed, unannounced, and unattributed -- not to 1804 by name, not to any crew, not
to any Alias the Directorate might have reached for instead. Within a season, the Directorate's own
internal accounting would list Harek Vondel's death as an unsolved field loss, one line among many,
the exact anonymity his own methodical reputation had never once considered that an enemy might turn
back on him.

---

*Continuity notes (not narrative): dramatizes `CC-147`/`MCD-1855` directly -- Vondel's own
reputation-first "advertise the correction before it arrives" tactic is precisely the advance notice
and predictable route that lets 1804's dispersed, doctrine-over-mass cells exploit him, per the rule's
own stated mechanic. Daba stays in his established post-Block-F role as architect, not operator --
present only at the planning stage, never at the ambush itself, consistent with his profile's "no
Chronicle in the corpus shows him personally endangered or tested in combat" (true again here; LII
remains his only physical-threat entry). The kill stays deliberately unattributed, matching `MCD-1569`'s
"never folded into... never publicly credited alongside" framing. No new named characters; Kether and
Rhyne Cadec both reused from the existing corpus.*

# Daba Chronicle LVIII: What the Debt Paper Led To

*UNLOCKED -- pending Abad's approval. Daba Chronicle LVIII. Close-third on Daba, no dedicated
narrator, matching the series' established convention. Dramatizes Vex Thurlow's capture and handover
by 1804 (`CC-153`/`MCD-1861`) for the first time -- queued since Batch 312, explicitly flagged in
Daba's own profile doc as a candidate beat for a future wave, not yet drafted. Set during the
network's semi-dormant years, matching Block I's era and register. Reuses already-locked 1804
members Orsk Dresk and Kether; no new named characters. Resolution stays deliberately unglamorous and
unresolved, per the source rule's own framing.*

---

Orsk Dresk's cell had not gone looking for a Weregildd Assessor. They had gone looking for a
recruiter working the Half-Ford road too close to territory 1804 had quietly held for years, the
same kind of boundary violation that had already put the network at arm's-length odds with
Weregildd culling teams more than once before, for reasons that had nothing to do with debt and
everything to do with bloodlines the network had separately sworn to protect.

What they found instead, three weeks into tracing the recruiter's own instructions back through a
chain of intermediaries, was a debt.

Not one debt. Dozens, then hundreds, then a paper trail thick enough that Orsk stopped counting
individual loans and started counting ruined holds instead -- small mercenary houses and struggling
minor estates, each one extended credit at terms that looked generous on the page and worked, in
practice, exactly the way a slow-closing trap works, until the debtor had nothing left to offer the
Writedown Compact but bodies. Every thread led to the same patient, unhurried name behind the paper:
Vex Thurlow.

Daba read the full accounting Orsk sent back and recognized, with the particular discomfort of
recognizing something in an enemy, a method that was not so different in its patience from his own.

"He thinks the slowness is mercy," Daba said to Kether, who had come to review the find with him,
since a target inside the Weregildd's own command structure was not a decision either of them would
make without the other's eyes on it first. "A debt a person takes on willingly, one loan at a time,
feels like a choice to the person taking it. He's built an entire career on the fact that it stops
feeling like a choice long after it's too late to matter."

"So we kill him."

"No." Daba said it plainly, the way he said most things that cost him something to say. "If we kill
him, the Compact appoints a replacement inside a season and loses nothing but a name. If we hand him
to the Trust, the Trust has no institutional interest in prosecuting a man who only ever ruins people
quietly enough not to be their problem. Either way, the paper trail survives him. We need the trail
broken, not the man."

What Daba proposed instead, and what Orsk's cell carried out six weeks later with no fanfare and no
public account of any kind, was handing Vex Thurlow -- alive, unharmed, and stripped of every
document his operation depended on -- to a rival criminal power already hostile to the Writedown
Compact's whole territory. What that power did with him afterward, 1804 never asked and never
recorded. The debts he had written stayed on the books of houses that could not easily unwrite them,
a cost Daba did not pretend had been solved rather than merely redirected.

"It isn't clean," he told Kether afterward, adding no name to any list, because no one had died, and
filing the operation instead under the growing category of things the doctrine answered only
partway. "It never is, with debt. You can break the hand that's writing it. You can't un-sign what's
already been signed."

---

*Continuity notes (not narrative): dramatizes `CC-153`/`MCD-1861` directly -- 1804's own
visible-retribution-as-liability doctrine (`MCD-1567`) drives the choice to hand Thurlow to a rival
criminal power rather than kill him or deliver him to a government with no institutional interest in
prosecuting him, matching the source rule's deliberately unglamorous, ambiguous resolution exactly.
No casualty, so no name is added to Daba's own tally -- consistent with his established
record-keeping habit (`MCD-1610`) only logging deaths, not operations. No new named characters; Orsk
Dresk and Kether both reused from the existing corpus.*

# Lords of Cian Interactive Archive — Roadmap, 2026-10-02

By Abad Morel. Supersedes the Aug-20 game plan (`lords-of-cian-archive-game-plan.md`) as the
operative status reference — that document is kept for its reasoning (the demand-signal design,
the engagement-idea rationale), but its "ground truth" section describes a repo that no longer
exists in that state. This doc is built from a direct, same-session inspection of all three real
systems (the GitHub repo, the live Railway deployment, the live Supabase project), not from prior
docs' claims about them.

## The headline: it's live, not scaffolded

The archive is a working, deployed, populated product today, not a backlog. In order of surprise:

1. **Content population already ran at full scale.** `bulk_import_knowledge_core.py` imported
   **1,198 live Chronicle entries across 24 characters** — all 11 of Kanja's Alias arcs (1,122
   entries) plus all 22 territory-leader characters (76 entries, 20 homage territories + Arturo +
   the Xaragua/Kazi character splits) — straight from the Knowledge Core repo's
   `docs/lords-of-cian/chronicles/` directory. A sibling script then populated **12 World
   Briefings** from the remaining ~515 non-Chronicle canon-ledger rules (GEO/ARS/MAW/ASH/CULT/POL/
   WC/HLD/WGD/SBD/CHAR/COS), one briefing per rule-prefix. Phase 3's old "content-readiness gate" —
   "enough material live that a Level 1 reader can plausibly read three to 90%" — isn't a future
   milestone, it's already true by a wide margin.
2. **It's deployed and running.** Railway project `lords-of-cian-archive` has both services
   (`web`, `canon-service`) live, latest deployment `SUCCESS`, matching the repo's current HEAD
   (`05dd3b7`, 2026-09-14). Reachable today at `web-production-8be0b.up.railway.app`. No custom
   domain is connected yet — that's the one real gap in "deployed."
3. **The database schema, RLS, and fraud controls are built and verified**, not just designed —
   17 migrations, RLS on all 18 tables across both schemas, the identity-fraud mechanics from
   P0-4, and all nine of the Aug-20 engagement ideas (§3 1-9: Standing Requests Ledger, Request
   Fulfillment Loop, Field Notes, Also Drawn To, Referral Lineage groundwork, Correspondence
   Checkpoints groundwork, Follow Reconsideration, Connective Tissue Trails, Two Dossiers Side by
   Side) are shipped in code.
4. **The six items flagged for "the real Brain Trust"** (demand-score formula, the Level 2 unlock
   rule, the quiz_questions timing, bulk-ingestion go/no-go, the email provider, the unpause
   timing) all have closing verdicts, resolved 2026-09-13 — see the Knowledge Core repo's
   `2026-09-13-archive-app-six-open-items-final-verdicts.md`. The Level 2 gate those verdicts
   specified (`1 completed read AND (1 share OR 1 request)`, with server-side-verified `completed`)
   is built: `f22b675`.

## What's actually still open, in order

### 1. The Supabase project is paused again — immediate, operational
Checked live just now: `lords-of-cian-archive` (`dghkxaclaeluheahdsne`) status is **INACTIVE**.
It was confirmed `ACTIVE_HEALTHY` after the 2026-09-13 unpause, so this is Supabase's own
free-tier auto-pause after a stretch of no traffic, not a regression. Since `web`'s every
data-driven page depends on it, **the live Railway URL is almost certainly serving broken pages
right now.** This is the first thing to fix, and it's cheap: `mcp__Supabase__restore_project`,
then re-run `get_advisors` once (not a new finding — the auto-pause itself is the event, not a
code change) to confirm nothing drifted.

### 2. Connect a custom domain
Railway shows only the auto-generated `*.up.railway.app` domain, no custom domain. This is the
one genuinely unstarted piece of the original P1-7 ("deploy to production, connect the custom
domain") — deployment happened, the domain connection didn't. Low effort (`generate-domain` /
`update-domain` on Railway once a domain name is chosen), but it's the thing standing between
"live" and "the 6-month demand-collection milestone actually starts counting," since Strategy
§8's success metrics assume a real, shareable, indexable address.

### 3. Re-verify after the pause/unpause cycle
Worth a fresh `get_advisors` security pass and one real signed-in-test-account walk of the four
clearance transitions once the project is back up — not because anything is suspected broken,
but because every prior "verified against the live project" claim in the repo's CLAUDE.md
predates at least one full pause/restore cycle, and that's exactly the kind of state transition
worth confirming rather than assuming survived cleanly.

### 4. Genuinely deferred, by explicit prior decision — not oversights
- **Bulk Character Codex ingestion (P1-6):** unanimous Brain Trust HOLD. No dormant AI-parse
  pipeline exists (the Anthropic SDK dependency is pinned but zero code calls it) — this is
  "build from zero," conditioned on specific triggers already recorded in the first-round Brain
  Trust doc. Separately, the Chronicle/World-Briefing bulk imports that already ran used a
  *different*, simpler path (concatenation from the already-structured canon ledger, not AI
  extraction from raw prose) — that path is done; P1-6's own AI-parse path is the part still on
  hold.
- **`quiz_questions` (P3-1):** deferred behind a concrete trigger (Ideas 1 & 2 live 4+ weeks AND
  ≥25 registered readers) — a real answer-key RLS leak in it was already found and fixed
  (`0016`) independent of the timing decision, so the table itself is safe sitting idle.
- **Email delivery for the Request Fulfillment Loop:** provider decided (Resend, via a Supabase
  Database Webhook → Edge Function), but gated on re-enabling email confirmation — which is
  itself gated on a signup-architecture decision outside any single session's authority (GoTrue's
  frictionless-signup call vs. the demand-signal integrity P0-4 was built to protect). Until that
  lands, the in-app half of the loop (the `/notifications` page, the trigger) works; the email
  half doesn't fire.
- **Referral-pair fraud signals** (`signup_ip_hash`/`signup_ip_hash_match`): stay unpopulated
  because Supabase Auth's signup call goes straight from the browser to GoTrue, bypassing this
  app's own server — populating them needs a custom signup Route Handler, a real architecture
  change, not a migration. Not attempted, correctly not silently skipped either (flagged plainly
  in the repo's own CLAUDE.md).

### 5. The standing SEO/GEO/five-tier charter — still blocked on the device bridge
Separate from everything above: the proposed SEO/GEO/gamified-five-tier-unlock charter still
needs a device-bridge session (Cowork or local Claude Code with the desktop app connected) before
its concrete schema/tagging decisions can be adopted as *ratified* rather than draft. Nothing
built so far depends on this landing first — it only gates that one specific charter.

### 6. Operate the demand engine (Phase 4 from the original plan — open-ended, not a task)
Once the domain is live and traffic exists, the steady-state loop from the original plan still
applies as written: read the Demand panel by trend direction, check clearance distribution,
check referral chain depth, check the anomaly flag. Nothing here changes — it just hasn't started
yet because there's been no real traffic to read.

## Recommended order

1. Unpause Supabase (`restore_project`), confirm `get_advisors` clean, spot-check the live site
   actually renders character/chronicle/world pages correctly post-restore. **Minutes, not hours.**
2. Pick and connect a custom domain on Railway's `web` service.
3. Decide whether to revisit the email-confirmation architecture now (unlocks the Fulfillment
   Loop's email half and the referral-fraud signals together) or defer it — this is the one
   item above that's a real product decision, not a mechanical step.
4. Let the site run and start actually collecting demand data — Phase 4 is the natural next
   state once 1-2 land, not a separate project.
5. Revisit P1-6 (bulk AI-parse ingestion) and `quiz_questions` only when their own
   already-recorded trigger conditions are met.
6. Schedule the device-bridge session for the SEO/GEO/five-tier charter whenever Abad next has a
   Cowork or local session available — not urgent, nothing else is waiting on it.

## What this doc deliberately does not re-litigate

The Aug-20 game plan's actual design reasoning — why the demand score is shaped the way it is,
why each of the nine engagement ideas earns its place, the adversarial-review corrections — is
still the right reference for *why* the system works the way it does. This doc only replaces its
*ground-truth* section, which has been overtaken by two full sessions of real, verified build
work the Aug-20 doc couldn't have known about.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Batch 350: lock Daba Chronicles LVII-LVIII (Harek Vondel's killing, Vex Thurlow's capture)."""
import json

LEDGER_PATH = "canon-ledger.json"

SOURCE = (
    "Original invention, chat-drafted 2026-10-02, no source document. Dramatizes the two "
    "Batch-312 villain defeats already queued to Daba's own Character Chronicle series in his "
    "profile doc (docs/lords-of-cian/character-profiles/daba.md): Harek Vondel's killing by 1804 "
    "(CC-147/MCD-1855) and Vex Thurlow's capture/handover (CC-153/MCD-1861)."
)

NEW_RULES = [
    {
        "id": "MCD-1878",
        "category": "daba-character-chronicle",
        "statement": (
            "Daba Chronicle LVII, \"The Correction That Announced Itself\" (full narrative text at "
            "docs/lords-of-cian/chronicles/daba-chronicle-lvii-the-correction-that-announced-itself.md), "
            "the fifty-seventh entry of Daba's own Character Chronicle series. Dramatizes Harek "
            "Vondel's killing by 1804 (CC-147/MCD-1855) for the first time: Vondel's own "
            "reputation-first 'advertise the correction before it arrives' tactic hands Kether's "
            "cell the advance notice and predictable approach route 1804's dispersed, "
            "doctrine-over-mass cells need to exploit him -- Rhyne Cadec collapses both ends of a "
            "defile along his detachment's own announced route, the same narrowing-into-a-bottleneck "
            "logic a much younger Kanja learned on a disused footbridge during his mentorship with "
            "Daba (MCD-1568, Daba Chronicle XVIII). Daba stays in his established post-mentorship "
            "role as architect, not operator -- present only at the planning stage, never at the "
            "ambush itself, consistent with his profile's standing note that no Chronicle in the "
            "corpus shows him personally endangered or tested in combat (Chronicle LII remains his "
            "only physical-threat entry). The kill stays deliberately unattributed to Kanja, any "
            "Alias, or 1804 by name, matching MCD-1569's 'never folded into... never publicly "
            "credited alongside' framing; the Directorate's own internal accounting lists it as an "
            "unsolved field loss. No new named characters; Kether and Rhyne Cadec both reused from "
            "the existing corpus. Abad's approval: 'lock it.'"
        ),
        "status": "locked",
        "source": SOURCE,
    },
    {
        "id": "MCD-1879",
        "category": "daba-character-chronicle",
        "statement": (
            "Daba Chronicle LVIII, \"What the Debt Paper Led To\" (full narrative text at "
            "docs/lords-of-cian/chronicles/daba-chronicle-lviii-what-the-debt-paper-led-to.md), the "
            "fifty-eighth entry of Daba's own Character Chronicle series. Dramatizes Vex Thurlow's "
            "capture and handover by 1804 (CC-153/MCD-1861) for the first time: Orsk Dresk's cell, "
            "investigating an unrelated Weregildd recruiter working too close to 1804's own "
            "territory, traces the Writedown Compact's debt-paper trail back to Thurlow personally. "
            "Daba rules out both killing him (the Compact replaces an Assessor inside a season) and "
            "delivering him to the Trust (no institutional interest in prosecuting a man who ruins "
            "people too quietly to be their problem), and instead has Orsk's cell hand Thurlow -- "
            "alive, unharmed, stripped of every document his operation depended on -- to a rival "
            "criminal power already hostile to the Writedown Compact, exactly matching the source "
            "rule's own deliberately unglamorous, ambiguous resolution (1804's doctrine treats "
            "visible retribution as a liability, MCD-1567). No casualty, so no name is added to "
            "Daba's own tally, consistent with his established record-keeping habit (MCD-1610) of "
            "logging only deaths; the operation is instead filed under the corpus's own running "
            "category of things the doctrine answers only partway. No new named characters; Orsk "
            "Dresk and Kether both reused from the existing corpus. Abad's approval: 'lock it.'"
        ),
        "status": "locked",
        "source": SOURCE,
    },
]

BATCH_NOTE = (
    "Daba Chronicles LVII-LVIII locked, dramatizing the two Batch-312 pre-Book-1 villain defeats "
    "already queued to his series (Harek Vondel's killing, CC-147/MCD-1855; Vex Thurlow's "
    "capture, CC-153/MCD-1861). Both drafted and presented in full per the gate's own "
    "already-cleared status for Daba's series (wave 3 locked); no fresh Psychological "
    "Profile/Game Plan cycle was needed since both beats were already explicitly queued in his "
    "profile doc. The remaining seven Batch-312 villain defeats stay blocked: five need their "
    "track's own Character Chronicle Launch Protocol backfill (Bane, Crow King, Sovereign Ghost "
    "of the Great Sea, Blue-Collar Titan, Lauris), and two (Brakon Skevik, Ossa Drem, both "
    "reckoned by Red Beard) need a brand-new protagonist track launched from scratch -- Red Beard "
    "currently has no profile or gate at all. None of that work was attempted here. Abad's "
    "approval, quoted verbatim: 'lock it.'"
)


def main():
    with open(LEDGER_PATH, "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        ledger = json.load(f)

    existing_ids = {r["id"] for r in ledger["rules"]}
    for rule in NEW_RULES:
        assert rule["id"] not in existing_ids, f"ID collision: {rule['id']}"

    next_batch = max(b["batch"] for b in ledger["batches_completed"]) + 1
    ledger["batches_completed"].append(
        {
            "batch": next_batch,
            "source": SOURCE,
            "rules_affected": len(NEW_RULES),
            "note": BATCH_NOTE,
        }
    )

    ledger["ledger_version"] = str(round(float(ledger["ledger_version"]) + 0.1, 1))
    ledger["last_updated"] = "2026-10-02"

    with open(LEDGER_PATH, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(ledger, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
        f.write("\n")

    ids = [r["id"] for r in ledger["rules"]]
    dupes = len(ids) - len(set(ids))
    print(
        f"OK: {len(ledger['rules'])} total rules, {len(ledger['batches_completed'])} batches, "
        f"ledger_version {ledger['ledger_version']}, batch {next_batch}, "
        f"zero duplicate IDs: {dupes == 0}. New rules: {', '.join(r['id'] for r in NEW_RULES)}."
    )


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

## One thing to settle first: Kanja's "no killing" value

His Kanja-version profile, which you approved, lists "no killing" as a value he won't give up. The ledger already contradicts that as an absolute rule:
- At the Black Trench (age 19) the Brigade took 1,400+ losses (`MCD-232`).
- At the Sovereign Pier (age 30) he killed nine of the twelve assassins (`MCD-245`).

So the record already supports what you're asking for. What needs fixing is the wording in the profile.

**Proposed amendment:** "Killing is never his default. It's a deliberate choice he weighs like any other cost." The Dredge-Line and the Scrip-Forge Raid stay bloodless because bloodless was the better tactic there. When he does decide the ratio demands a death, the kill is devastating precisely because he chose it.

**The guardrail we need:** you reserved his father's death as the moment that "awakens the urge to destroy his enemies." If the Long Mask kills read as rage, that Book 1 turn has nowhere to go. So I'd make the Long Mask era deadlier but cold. He uses terror as a tool and keeps track of who has to die. The urge to destroy stays held back for Book 1.

- **Marquee:** the pre-Book-1 kills that become legend and can be cited in Book 1. Only the four anchors get these.

- **Ledger:** background tallies.

My take is that this is the right instinct. The roster is wide, and nobody has yet earned the right to be feared in Book 1 because of something they did before it.

**Why it works**
- **Anchors need a resume.** When Book 1 opens, readers should already sense that Kanja, Daba, Ozmund and Lauris are dangerous, through rumor, scars and people's reactions to them. Right now most pre-Book-1 material shows them winning cleverly, not lethally. A few legendary kills give the books something to point back to.
- **Concentrating the kills protects the hierarchy.** If every hero gets big kills, none of them stand out. Keeping the marquee moments with four people tells readers who carries the story, and the rest of the cast still gets real wins.
- **It fixes a drift in the canon.** Across 1,000+ Alias Chronicles, Kanja has been sanded down into someone who always finds the bloodless answer. That was never true. The Black Trench is a slaughter. Giving him real, chosen kills restores the version of him the core battles actually describe.

**What I'd watch**
- **Don't let the kills become the point.** The best version keeps what makes him Kanja: when he kills, he has decided it, he has counted the cost, and it costs him something. A Kanja who kills casually is just another warlord. A Kanja who has done the math and does it anyway is terrifying.
- **Save the rage.** Your own note says his father's death is what unleashes the urge to destroy. If the Long Mask is already him at full fury, Book 1 has no new gear to shift into. The Long Mask should be cold and efficient: frightening because he's calm.
- **Ozmund is the risky one.** His identity is restraint, and his dark turn is reserved for Book 3. One hidden kill he never talks about deepens him. More than that and you've spent the Dark Monarch early.
- **Daba should kill almost no one personally.** His power is that the network does the killing. That's why one personal kill, against whoever ordered the Rookery, would be the single most devastating moment in his whole series.
- **Fewer, better.** I'd aim for about 15–20 true marquee kills across all four anchors, each a fully written scene with a named victim. Hundreds of casualties in the background don't build a legend. Named deaths people remember do.

**Bottom line:** do it. Draw the line by meaning, not body count. A marquee kill is one that changes how the world talks about that hero. Everything else counts as a victory, not a legend.

219:Kanja was ninety meters away when the Titan entered the Trench. He heard the voice above the fog, a voice with mass behind the frequency, a chest cavity resonating at a density his own lungs would not match for years. He heard the order. He heard the soldiers forming on the Titan's position, drawing confidence from the enforcer's bulk, reorganizing around the largest body in the space the way debris organizes around an anchor point in a current.
223:The Aegis-Talisman scanned as he advanced, feeding frequency data through the Smith-Vision overlay. The Titan's Dead Drakma plate was heavier than the infantry's, thicker, the grain structure denser and more coherent. The seams were still present, shoulder, elbow, knee, but the tolerances were tighter, the gaps narrower, the alloy at the joints reinforced with secondary plating. Onyx would need a precise angle to find the opening. The blade would need time the Titan might not provide.
225:But the Titan was built for open ground. The siege hammer needed four meters of swing radius. The Trench provided three. The Titan's height was an advantage in the fog and a liability against the walls. His strength was his density, and his density was his weight, and his weight pressed him into the gravel and the chemical pools and the rusted iron underfoot, sinking him while the lighter fighters moved on the surface.
227:Kanja engaged the Titan at the 200-meter mark.
229:The first exchange was Mafesto's education. The Titan swung the siege hammer in a truncated arc, the head striking the eastern wall and sending a spray of rock chips into the fog before redirecting toward Kanja's position. Kanja caught the redirected blow on Mafesto's left vambrace. The impact was the hardest the armor had absorbed in its operational life. The kinetic transfer system surged. The Living Drakma lattice drank the energy and Kanja felt the armor warm against his skin, the heat of absorption radiating through the void-lattice surface, the shoulder ports venting a burst of superheated steam dense enough to obscure him from the Titan's sight for two full seconds.
231:Two seconds was enough. Kanja stepped left, inside the hammer's arc, and drove Obsidian Malice into the Titan's right knee. The macana discharged the stored kinetic energy of the Titan's own blow through the shadow-stone teeth, concentrated into a striking surface the size of a fist. The Titan's knee guard, reinforced Dead Drakma alloy rated for siege-level impacts, cracked along the grain. The crack was not structural failure. The crack was an invitation.
235:The blade entered the crack and widened the gap and found the joint beneath, the articulation point where the enforcer's armor allowed the knee to bend, and the Dead-Light edge severed the connective hardware with a single drawing cut. The Titan's right leg locked, the armor no longer capable of flexion at the knee, and the enforcer stumbled, his 3,500x mass shifting off-center in a space too narrow to recover balance.
237:The Titan went to one knee. The fog closed over his chest. His head was still above the vapor, but his torso was now at the level of the fighters he had been built to destroy, and at that level, in that fog, his size was a slower target, not a larger threat.
239:Kanja fought the Titan for forty minutes. The engagement was not a duel. Duels require space and ceremony and the mutual agreement to resolve a question through combat. The engagement in the Black Trench was industrial. Kanja identified the structural weaknesses in the Titan's armor through the Aegis-Talisman's frequency scan and the Smith-Vision's structural overlay, and he exploited them in sequence, the way a smith dismantles a forge press: bolt by bolt, plate by plate, component by component. Mafesto absorbed the Titan's counterstrikes and converted them to ammunition. Onyx found the seams. Obsidian Malice delivered the verdicts.
241:The first Titan went down in the fourth hour. The body settled into the gravel and the chemical pools with the finality of a structure whose load-bearing capacity had been exceeded. The fog closed over the enforcer and the fog did not care what the enforcer's density had been.
249:Gol's hands shook for ten seconds after she covered the body. Then the shaking stopped and she picked up the cargo spike and moved back into the fog, alone now, her pair broken, fighting as a single element until she found another single and formed a new pair. The system absorbed the loss and continued operating. The system had been built to absorb loss. This was the truth Kanja had understood when he designed the pair structure: the smallest functional unit is two, and when two becomes one, one finds another one, and the system rebuilds from the smallest element up. The system does not require a commander. The system requires proximity and trust.
257:The seventh hour brought the second Titan.
259:The second enforcer entered through the south gap with a formation of forty soldiers in close order behind her. She was faster than the first Titan, lighter in plate, carrying a paired weapon set, a long halberd and a heavy shield. She had learned from the first enforcer's death. She kept the halberd close, the strikes short, the shield covering the joints the rebels targeted. She pushed north through the fog with her formation, and the formation held longer in the confined space because the soldiers had stopped trying to swing and started using their shields as battering surfaces, slamming forward in a wall of Dead Drakma, compressing the Trench floor with density rather than technique.
261:The second Titan fought Kanja for ninety minutes. The halberd struck Mafesto six times, and each impact loaded the kinetic transfer system to capacity, the armor's shoulder ports venting continuous streams of superheated steam, the chemical fog thickening around Kanja until he moved in a personal cloud of forge-heat and sulfur. The Aegis-Talisman caught the seventh blow. The Titan's halberd struck the faceted surface and the Aegis chimed, a crystalline sound cutting through the noise of the Trench, the Living Drakma finding the harmonic. The halberd's kinetic energy inverted. The force of the blow redirected back through the haft and into the Titan's hands, and the enforcer's gauntlets cracked at the wrist, the alloy failing under the stress of absorbing its own output.
263:With broken wrist-guards, the Titan's grip weakened. With a weakened grip, the halberd slowed. With a slower halberd, the joints opened. Onyx found the gaps. Obsidian Malice closed the argument.
265:The second Titan went down in the seventh hour.
281:The third Titan entered the Trench in the eighth hour, and the third Titan was different.
283:The enforcer was the largest of the three, density estimated above 4,000x, wearing plate so thick the joints barely moved. The Titan advanced through the fog like a siege engine, not fighting but pushing, using mass alone to compress the space, driving everything before the advance into the narrowing corridor toward the north rubble pile. The Titan did not swing a weapon. The Titan was the weapon, a wall of density moving at walking pace, and behind the wall, the surviving Brigade soldiers followed in the enforcer's wake, stepping over debris the Titan had flattened, walking on ground the Titan had compressed into a surface hard as poured stone.
285:Kanja met the advance at the 400-meter mark and understood the problem in three seconds. The third Titan could not be fought the way the first two had been fought, because the third Titan was not fighting. The enforcer was applying pressure, the way a hydraulic press applies pressure, continuous and omnidirectional and patient. The halberd and the siege hammer had been weapons designed for exchange. This Titan's weapon was presence.
291:Six fighters converged from three directions. Each carried a grappling hook, dock equipment, heavy iron with rope rated for crane loads. The hooks went high, arcing over the fog and catching on the Titan's pauldrons, backplate, and helm. Six ropes. Six anchor points. The Titan, mid-advance, felt the drag and turned, which was the mistake, because turning in the Trench exposed the back to the fighters positioned behind, and the fighters positioned behind were not there to hook. They were there to cut.
293:Onyx's Cadence Ruin pulsed through the fog. The vibration disrupted the binding harmonics in the Titan's plate, the frequency-craft reinforcements woven into the Dead Drakma by Sovereign Trust armorers. The plates loosened. The bolts weakened. The joints, already strained by the Titan's own mass, separated by fractions of a millimeter, and the fractions were enough.
295:The six fighters with grappling hooks hauled on the ropes, and the Titan, off-balance from the turn, top-heavy in plate designed for forward advance, went to one knee. The fog closed over the enforcer's shoulders. Kanja stepped forward and drove Obsidian Malice into the gap between the Titan's helm and gorget, the gap the Cadence Ruin had widened, the gap the hooks had exposed. The macana discharged the accumulated kinetic energy of the last two hours of combat, every absorbed blow, every impact stored in the Living Drakma lattice, every joule of force the Brigade had aimed at Kanja and fed into the system designed to return their own violence amplified.
297:The crack of the discharge echoed off the Trench walls and returned as a sound neither stone nor metal nor anything the 300-meter radius of the Trench had produced in the previous eight hours. The third Titan dropped. The ground shook. The chemical pools rippled outward from the impact and the ripples died at the walls and the Trench was quiet.
355:The Sovereign Trust's after-action report on the Black Trench engagement was filed eleven days later by a Colonel whose name was subsequently redacted from the record. The report classified the engagement as a "contained mutual annihilation scenario resulting in disproportionate insurgent survival." The Colonel was demoted for understatement. The report was sealed. The sealing did not prevent the report's conclusions from circulating through the Southern District intelligence apparatus within a week.
357:The conclusions were these: Suppression Brigade Kethane, a dedicated anti-insurgency unit of 2,000 soldiers, three Titan-class enforcers, and a full siege artillery battery, had been neutralized by a force one-sixteenth its size, in a terrain of the enemy's choosing, using the Brigade's own mass and equipment against its operators. The Brigade lost over 1,400 soldiers to combat, crushing injuries from the initial collapse, and chemical exposure from the Trench floor. The three Titan-class enforcers were destroyed. The artillery battery was captured. The surviving Brigade elements, fewer than 600, withdrew from the engagement zone at dawn without recovering their dead.

# Kanja Chronicle III: What the Dark Could Not Keep

*Locked canon, Batch 313 (`MCD-1868`). Third entry of the "Kanja version" Chronicle track. Age
27, roughly two years before the Gale Straits/Storm That Walks alias at age 29 (`MCD-230`). Dramatizes Renfel
Auberon's defeat (`CC-157`/`MCD-1865`) — a Kanja-crew team-up fielding `CULT-197`'s three-source
Anti-Resonance countermeasure (Onyx's Cadence Ruin, Sephtis's Chrono-Anchor bells, Ironbane's
King's Roar) together on the page for the first time. Onyx's presence has grown from Chronicle I's
near-silence to its second real appearance in this track, matching roughly the manuscript's own
Chronicle II/III-level growth — still unlabeled, longer and more assertive than before. No new
named characters. No child-safety issues. Corrected Batch 338, 2026-10-02: the Gale Straits timing
fixed (two years, not one, before age 29); Sephtis's stated age corrected from ~1,900 years to
~1,700, matching his locked present-day age against this entry's own age-27 placement; an entity-
count arithmetic error (2+3+2 summing to seven rather than six) fixed.*

---

The warehouse on the Lawless Reaches' northern edge had no name on any registry, which was, Sephtis
observed, the first thing wrong with it. Every legitimate structure on this coastline answered to
something — a harbor authority, a merchant guild, even the Ash Maw Trade Council's loosest
accounting. A building with no name and a triple-locked loading door was a building that wanted to
----
particular failure and would know what to do with a man who was equal parts criminal and
cautionary case. The six shapes, dispersed to their lowest tiers or gone entirely, were someone
else's slower work now. Tonight had only ever been about stopping the feeding.

• • •

The blade remembers the room's cold longer than it remembers the man. Six shapes, borrowed hum, a
loop built by someone who mistook survival for mastery. The bells rang first. The voice rang
second. The blade closed the gap between what remained, and what remained had nowhere honest left
to go.

Auberon's arm carried the Mark the way a debt carries interest — quietly, and compounding, whether
or not the debtor looks at it. The blade has seen this shape of ruin before, in smaller ways,
in men who thought a good enough method excused them from ever checking what the method actually
cost. It will see it again. It is beginning to understand that this is one of the shapes its
counting exists to hold: not only the dead and the freed, but the ones who ruin themselves slowly
enough to mistake it for control.

Three sources, one field, one collapse. The work was clean. The man was not saved, only stopped
from further ruining himself before someone better equipped could try.

The blade records both facts without preferring one to the other. That is becoming, it thinks,
the whole of what recording means.

---

*Continuity notes (not narrative): dramatizes `MCD-1865` and `CULT-197`'s three-source Anti-
Resonance countermeasure on the page for the first time, matching the source rule's own mechanics
precisely — forced tier-collapse rather than harm, Auberon captured rather than killed, already
partially Green-Mark-contaminated per `CULT-198`. Placed at age 27 (within this track's Rebellion-
only window, before age 30's Trinity surrender, `MCD-246`), consistent with Onyx's required active
participation. Auberon's specimens are read as wild/independent Ever-Haunt stock predating and
unconnected to T.D.K.'s own kenneled population (`WC-019`'s "originless, pre-dating T.D.K." framing)
rather than escapees from the Great Breach, which per `WC-019`/`MCD-1621` does not occur until Book
1's epilogue, decades after this track's window closes — checked explicitly to avoid a real timing
contradiction before drafting. Onyx's coda here is deliberately longer and more assertive than
Chronicle I's near-silent close, but still unlabeled, matching the Game Plan's specified growth
curve (this track's second real appearance of the narrator voice, Chronicle II having contributed
none). No new named characters; Sephtis and Ironbane both reused from already-locked material
(`ARS-402`/`403`, `ARS-406`/`407`).*

# Kanja Chronicle IV: Ninety Seconds on the Sovereign Pier

*UNLOCKED -- pending Abad's approval. Draft, 2026-10-02. Fourth entry of the "Kanja version"
Chronicle track. Age 30, the final day of the Rebellion. Dramatizes the Battle of the Sovereign Pier
(`MCD-245`) and the Trinity's surrender (`MCD-246`) for the first time anywhere in the corpus -- the
first marquee kill under the anchor-hero kill tiering. Per `VB-026`, this is the Rebellion's end and
the point at which Onyx of Oblivion has fully become the narrator; the entry is narrated by Onyx
throughout, and its self-reference completes the shift from "the blade" to "I" on the page at the
moment of sealing. New named characters: Ivo Strell (assassination-team lead) and eight operatives
named by surname only (Hesk, Vauden, Tasker, Caddel, Orrel, Teague, Danver, Lisk), all
collision-checked clean against the full ledger and Chronicle corpus. Dol Maren reused (he/him per
Batch 226). No child-safety issues.*

---

The blade counts. That is the first thing to understand about the blade, and the last.

It counted the twelve years. It counted the twenty-two victories and the people each one cost and
the people each one freed, and it kept those columns apart, because the man who carries it insists
that they be kept apart. It counted the hours he spent that morning on his knees on the planking of
the Sovereign Pier with a caulking iron in his hand, working active Living Drakma sealant into the
seams of *The Audit*'s hull, because Dol Maren had found a weep along the garboard strake and the
man does not leave a weep for later. Four hours. The sealant was still wet to the elbow on both his
arms and smeared in long grey thumbprints across Mafesto's forearm plates, where he had wiped his
hands without thinking. The blade counted that too. It did not yet know it mattered.

"You'll want that off before it cures," Dol Maren said. "It'll take the skin with it."

"After," Kanja said, and kept working, and the blade, slung across his back, felt the pier's long
timbers carry a new weight onto the far end of the planking. Not soldiers. Not a column. A small
group, walking at the pace of men who are not in a hurry because they are not used to being made to
hurry.

The man knew the walk before he turned. The blade felt him know it -- the fractional change in his
shoulders, the iron going still.

King Maro Rexmar came down the Sovereign Pier with four attendants and no crown. He was the fifth of
his line to hold a title the line had once held as a fact, and he walked the way his father and
grandfather had walked, which is to say carefully, as if the planks themselves might ask what he had
traded for the right to stand on them. He stopped three paces from his son. He looked at the
sealant on Kanja's arms, and at the hull, and at the weep that was no longer weeping.

"Still fixing what other people let leak," Maro said.

"Someone has to," Kanja said, and stood.

The blade has kept a careful record of the twelve years, and in that record there are very few
conversations between these two men. It keeps every one of them. It does not presume to know what
passes between a father and a son that does not pass through the air. It records the air.

Maro said that he had been negotiating. In secret, for the better part of two years, with the one
man in the Trust's orbit he believed would keep his word -- Aethelgard Verehimu. He said the terms
were simple, which was how he knew they were real. The Directorate would recognize him as sovereign
King of Jicome, in fact and not in ceremony, the first of five generations to hold the thing rather
than its shadow. The war would end. And in exchange, Kanja would surrender Mafesto, Onyx of
Oblivion, and Obsidian Malice into the Trust's keeping, sealed, for good.

"I'm not ordering you," Maro said. "I gave up the right to order you when I let you go to the docks
at eighteen and said nothing. I'm asking."

The man did not answer. The blade felt him begin to -- felt the breath gather, felt the arithmetic
begin to run, the long columns of twelve years lining up behind his eyes the way they always did
before a decision that would cost something. And the blade felt, in that same instant, something on
the pier that did not belong to the conversation.

Twelve weights. Spread along the planking among the stevedores and net-menders, in dockworkers'
canvas, where twelve weights had not been a moment earlier. Moving now. Converging.

The blade began a new count.

**One.** The man turned before anyone spoke, because the blade does not speak in words and he does
not need it to. He put himself between his father and the landward end of the pier in a single
step, and his left hand found Obsidian Malice where it leaned against the bollard, and his right
went over his shoulder to the blade.

**Two.** Twelve dockworkers dropped their canvas. Under it: Trust field plate, dark, unmarked. In
their hands: Blight-projector sidearms, short-barreled, not tuned to a man at all. Tuned to Living
Drakma. Someone in the Trust had done the arithmetic too, and their arithmetic said: kill the relics
first, and the man is only a man.

**Three.** They fired.

The blade has been struck by frequencies before. It knows what a dead-tone feels like as it reaches
for the lattice -- a cold hand closing on something that breathes. It braced for the hand.

The hand never closed.

The sealant took it. Four hours of active Living Drakma, still wet, spread across the man's arms and
smeared over Mafesto's plates in careless grey thumbprints -- the nearest, freshest, most hungry
Living Drakma surface on the pier. The projectors' signal went looking for the relics and found the
caulking first, and the caulking drank it, the way wet ground drinks a spill, and went dark grey to
black along both forearms, and the relics beneath it never felt more than a chill.

The blade will record, for the rest of its existence, that the Trinity was saved on its last day by
a hull repair.

**Four through nine.** The man moved.

There is a kind of fighting the blade had grown used to across twelve years: patient, terrain-led,
built so that the enemy's own weight does the work. This was not that. There was no terrain. There
was a pier eleven paces wide, a king behind him, and twelve people who had come to kill him and,
failing that, to kill whoever stood closest. The blade felt the man's arithmetic run once and
finish. It felt the answer arrive. It felt him choose it.

Ivo Strell led the team and came first, because the one who leads always comes first, and the man
met him with Mafesto's right vambrace and let the blow land. The Kinetic Transfer System drank
Strell's strike and the man returned it through Obsidian Malice into Strell's sternum, and Strell's
plate folded inward around the force of his own swing, and Strell went down onto the planking and
did not move again. The blade recorded his name. It recorded it from the warrant folded inside his
plate, which it would read later, and it recorded it now, at the moment it became a death, because
the man had chosen it and the blade keeps the choices.

Hesk and Vauden came from the left in tandem, projectors discarded, short blades drawn. Veil
Piercer showed the blade the shape of their intention through the smoke the projectors had left --
Vauden's feint, Hesk's real line toward the king. The man went through the feint as if it were not
there and took Hesk at the hip and the throat in one drawing cut. Vauden, committed to a feint that
no longer had a purpose, met Obsidian Malice on the backswing.

Tasker and Caddel had flanked along the gunwale of *The Audit* itself. Whisper of Shadows let the
blade hear them breathing against the hull -- the man heard it through the blade and did not look.
He reversed the blade over his shoulder, point-down along his own spine, and stepped back into
them. Tasker died against the hull Kanja had spent four hours repairing. Caddel tried to go over the
rail and the blade caught her at the ankle tendon and the man caught her at the collar, and he did
not let her reach the water.

**Ten through forty.** The projectors were empty or dropped. The remaining seven came the old way,
with steel, and the man met them the old way. Cadence Ruin ran through the blade at the frequency of
their plate and the plate's own binding harmonics loosened at every seam, and where a seam
loosened, the blade went in.

Orrel. Teague. Danver. Lisk.

The blade records the order. It records that Orrel was the bravest of them and Lisk was the
youngest and that it made no difference to the arithmetic, and that the man knew both things and
let neither one change the answer. It records that he did not hurry and did not linger. It records
that his face, through all of it, was the face he wears when he is working a weep out of a hull:
attentive, unhurried, and entirely without heat.

That is the thing the stories always get wrong. They make it rage. It was not rage. Rage would have
been easier to survive.

**Forty-one through eighty-eight.** Three were left.

The blade felt the man's arithmetic run again. Nine dead. Nine who had been between his father and
the landward end of the pier, nine who could not be stopped in the time he had by any means that
would leave them standing. The three that remained had been posted at the seaward end, cutting off
the water. They were between his father and nothing.

So he did not kill them.

He drove them. Mafesto took the first one's blow and the man walked forward into it, plate to plate,
until the edge of the pier arrived behind the operative and there was nothing left to stand on. The
second turned to run and found the water himself. The third looked at the eight bodies on the
planking and at the ninth, Strell's, at the man's feet, and at the man, and set down his blade, and
stepped off the Sovereign Pier into the harbor of his own accord.

**Eighty-nine.** The man turned to his father.

**Ninety.** "Are you hurt," he said. Not a question. A count.

Maro Rexmar was not hurt. Maro Rexmar was standing exactly where his son had put him, one hand on
the bollard, looking at the nine people his son had just killed in the time it takes a kettle to
come to a boil.

• • •

Dol Maren pulled the three out of the harbor with a boathook, one at a time, and sat them on the
planking with their wrists bound in caulking line. Nobody told him to. The man nodded at it when he
saw it, and that was the whole of the conversation about it.

The warrant was folded flat inside Ivo Strell's plate. The blade read it as the man read it. It was
dated eleven days earlier. It authorized the team to act "irrespective of the outcome of the
principal's negotiation," which is the Trust's way of saying that they had sent a king to ask his
son for peace and sent twelve people to make sure they would not have to keep it.

Maro read it over his son's shoulder. The blade felt the old man go very still.

"They would have done it whichever answer you gave," Maro said.

"Yes."

"Then the terms are a lie."

"No," the man said. "The terms are real. This is just what it looks like when someone with a great
deal to lose signs something real." He folded the warrant along its old crease. "They are afraid
enough to send twelve. That means they are afraid enough to honor what they sign, once it's signed
in front of enough people."

The blade did not understand this. It records that it did not understand this. It has had a very
long time since to understand it, and it is still not certain it does.

What the blade understood was the other arithmetic, the one underneath. Twelve years. Twenty-two
victories. A column of names that grew every season and would keep growing for as long as the
Trinity remained in the field, because the Trust would keep spending its own people trying to take
it from him, and he would keep taking theirs. Nine more names, today, on the planking of a pier he
had been repairing a ship on. The war would never run out of names. That was the whole of what the
Trust's insurance policy had proven: not that the peace was false, but that the war was endless.

The people are the line. Everything else burns.

The blade felt the man realize that it was, itself, among the everything else.

He turned back to his father. Maro had asked a question before the pier was attacked, and the man
does not leave a question for later any more than he leaves a weep.

"Yes," Kanja said.

• • •

They did it that night, at the end of the same pier, by lantern light, in front of enough people.

The Trust sent a sealed case lined with Dead Drakma, three compartments, each cut to a shape the
blade recognized with something it does not have a better word for than grief. Mafesto came off
first, plate by plate, the sealant cured black along both forearms now and taking a little of the
man's skin with it exactly as Dol Maren had said it would. Obsidian Malice went second, its charge
spent, the shadow-stone teeth still warm.

The man held the blade last, and longest.

He did not say anything to it. He has never said very much to it, in twelve years. He held it
across both palms the way one holds a thing one is giving rather than surrendering, and then he laid
it in the case.

On his belt, the Rexmar Machete stayed where it had always been. Brass-riveted, worn smooth at the
grip, narrower by a centimeter than it had been in his grandfather's day. The Trust's clerk looked
at it. Maro looked at it. The clerk looked at the king, and the king said, "That one is a tool, not a
relic. It was his grandfather's. It stays." And it stayed.

The lid came down.

The blade had spent twelve years learning to count. It had counted the Trench and the Wharf and the
Bridge and the Pier. It had counted Strell and Hesk and Vauden and Tasker and Caddel and Orrel and
Teague and Danver and Lisk. It had counted the hours of a man on his knees fixing a hull. It had
learned that counting is not cold. It had learned that counting is the only way to keep faith with
a thing that cannot be undone.

In the dark, with the lid closed over it, the blade understood that it was no longer the blade that
counted for him. There was no him, in here. There was only the count.

So I began it.

One.

---

*Continuity notes (not narrative): dramatizes `MCD-245` and `MCD-246` directly -- King Maro's
personal request, the twelve-operative Trust assassination team as an "insurance policy," nine
killed and three driven into the harbor in ninety seconds, the active Living Drakma sealant from
hours of hull-caulking protecting the Trinity from the Blight-projector sidearms (`ARS-398`), the
single-word answer "Yes," and the surrender of all three relics that night. The sidearms are read as
tuned to the relics' Living Drakma rather than to Kanja himself, which is why the still-wet sealant,
the nearest and most active Living Drakma surface on the pier, absorbed the signal first --
consistent with the Talisman of Mao's own Blight Immunity (`MCD-060`) protecting Kanja's body
independently. The Accords' terms match `CC-009`/`MCD-085` (recognition of Maro as sovereign King of
Jicome in exchange for the Trinity; negotiated in secret with Aethelgard Verehimu). The Rexmar
Machete stays on his belt per `ARS-260`/`ARS-425`. The final line begins Onyx's running seconds-count
from the treaty (`MCD-246`). Onyx's narration completes `VB-026`'s handoff here at age 30 -- the
blade's third-person self-reference used throughout the track's earlier codas becomes first-person
at the moment of sealing. Nothing in this entry foreshadows the Fulfillment Ceremony or Maro
Rexmar's death; the 284-vs-296-year interval question (open) is not touched. Under the amended
killing doctrine (`CC-161`, pending), the nine deaths are an explicit, costed choice, the three
spared an equally explicit one -- arithmetic, not rage, keeping the reserved post-Fulfillment
"urge to destroy his enemies" untouched.*
