It counted the hours he spent that morning on his knees on the planking of the Sovereign Pier with a caulking iron in his hand, working active Living Drakma sealant into the seams of *The Audit*'s hull, because Dol Maren had found a weep along the garboard strake and the man does not leave a weep for later. Four hours. The sealant was still wet to the elbow on both his arms and smeared in long grey thumbprints across Mafesto's forearm plates, where he had wiped his hands without thinking. The blade counted that too. It did not yet know it mattered.
>
> "You'll want that off before it cures," Dol Maren said. "It'll take the skin with it."
>
> "After," Kanja said, and kept working, and the blade, slung across his back, felt the pier's long timbers carry a new weight onto the far end of the planking. Not soldiers. Not a column. A small group, walking at the pace of men who are not in a hurry because they are not used to being made to hurry.
>
> The man knew the walk before he turned. The blade felt him know it — the fractional change in his shoulders, the iron going still.
>
> King Maro Rexmar came down the Sovereign Pier with four attendants and no crown. He was the fifth of his line to hold a title the line had once held as a fact, and he walked the way his father and grandfather had walked, which is to say carefully, as if the planks themselves might ask what he had traded for the right to stand on them. He stopped three paces from his son. He looked at the sealant on Kanja's arms, and at the hull, and at the weep that was no longer weeping.
>
> "Still fixing what other people let leak," Maro said.
>
> "Someone has to," Kanja said, and stood.
>
> The blade has kept a careful record of the twelve years, and in that record there are very few conversations between these two men. It keeps every one of them. It does not presume to know what passes between a father and a son that does not pass through the air. It records the air.
>
> Maro said that he had been negotiating. In secret, for the better part of two years, with the one man in the Trust's orbit he believed would keep his word — Aethelgard Verehimu. He said the terms were simple, which was how he knew they were real. The Directorate would recognize him as sovereign King of Jicome, in fact and not in ceremony, the first of five generations to hold the thing rather than its shadow. The war would end. And in exchange, Kanja would surrender Mafesto, Onyx of Oblivion, and Obsidian Malice into the Trust's keeping, sealed, for good.
>
> "I'm not ordering you," Maro said. "I gave up the right to order you when I let you go to the docks at eighteen and said nothing. I'm asking."
>
> The man did not answer. The blade felt him begin to — felt the breath gather, felt the arithmetic begin to run, the long columns of twelve years lining up behind his eyes the way they always did before a decision that would cost something. And the blade felt, in that same instant, something on the pier that did not belong to the conversation.
>
> Twelve weights. Spread along the planking among the stevedores and net-menders, in dockworkers' canvas, where twelve weights had not been a moment earlier. Moving now. Converging.
>
> The blade began a new count.
>
> **One.** The man turned before anyone spoke, because the blade does not speak in words and he does not need it to. He put himself between his father and the landward end of the pier in a single step, and his left hand found Obsidian Malice where it leaned against the bollard, and his right went over his shoulder to the blade.
>
> **Two.** Twelve dockworkers dropped their canvas. Under it: Trust field plate, dark, unmarked. In their hands: Blight-projector sidearms, short-barreled, not tuned to a man at all. Tuned to Living Drakma. Someone in the Trust had done the arithmetic too, and their arithmetic said: kill the relics first, and the man is only a man.
>
> **Three.** They fired.
>
> The blade has been struck by frequencies before. It knows what a dead-tone feels like as it reaches for the lattice — a cold hand closing on something that breathes. It braced for the hand.
>
> The hand never closed.
>
> The sealant took it. Four hours of active Living Drakma, still wet, spread across the man's arms and smeared over Mafesto's plates in careless grey thumbprints — the nearest, freshest, most hungry Living Drakma surface on the pier. The projectors' signal went looking for the relics and found the caulking first, and the caulking drank it, the way wet ground drinks a spill, and went dark grey to black along both forearms, and the relics beneath it never felt more than a chill.
>
> The blade will record, for the rest of its existence, that the Trinity was saved on its last day by a hull repair.
>
> **Four through nine.** The man moved.
>
> There is a kind of fighting the blade had grown used to across twelve years: patient, terrain-led, built so that the enemy's own weight does the work. This was not that. There was no terrain. There was a pier eleven paces wide, a king behind him, and twelve people who had come to kill him and, failing that, to kill whoever stood closest. The blade felt the man's arithmetic run once and finish. It felt the answer arrive. It felt him choose it.
>
> Ivo Strell led the team and came first, because the one who leads always comes first, and the man met him with Mafesto's right vambrace and let the blow land. The Kinetic Transfer System drank Strell's strike and the man returned it through Obsidian Malice into Strell's sternum, and Strell's plate folded inward around the force of his own swing, and Strell went down onto the planking and did not move again. The blade recorded his name. It recorded it from the warrant folded inside his plate, which it would read later, and it recorded it now, at the moment it became a death, because the man had chosen it and the blade keeps the choices.
>
> Hesk and Vauden came from the left in tandem, projectors discarded, short blades drawn. Veil Piercer showed the blade the shape of their intention through the smoke the projectors had left — Vauden's feint, Hesk's real line toward the king. The man went through the feint as if it were not there and took Hesk at the hip and the throat in one drawing cut. Vauden, committed to a feint that no longer had a purpose, met Obsidian Malice on the backswing.
>
> Tasker and Caddel had flanked along the gunwale of *The Audit* itself. Whisper of Shadows let the blade hear them breathing against the hull — the man heard it through the blade and did not look. He reversed the blade over his shoulder, point-down along his own spine, and stepped back into them. Tasker died against the hull Kanja had spent four hours repairing. Caddel tried to go over the rail and the blade caught her at the ankle tendon and the man caught her at the collar, and he did not let her reach the water.
>
> **Ten through forty.** The projectors were empty or dropped. The remaining seven came the old way, with steel, and the man met them the old way. Cadence Ruin ran through the blade at the frequency of their plate and the plate's own binding harmonics loosened at every seam, and where a seam loosened, the blade went in.
>
> Orrel. Teague. Danver. Lisk.
>
> The blade records the order. It records that Orrel was the bravest of them and Lisk was the youngest and that it made no difference to the arithmetic, and that the man knew both things and let neither one change the answer. It records that he did not hurry and did not linger. It records that his face, through all of it, was the face he wears when he is working a weep out of a hull: attentive, unhurried, and entirely without heat.
>
> That is the thing the stories always get wrong. They make it rage. It was not rage. Rage would have been easier to survive.
>
> **Forty-one through eighty-eight.** Three were left.
>
> The blade felt the man's arithmetic run again. Nine dead. Nine who had been between his father and the landward end of the pier, nine who could not be stopped in the time he had by any means that would leave them standing. The three that remained had been posted at the seaward end, cutting off the water. They were between his father and nothing.
>
> So he did not kill them.
>
> He drove them. Mafesto took the first one's blow and the man walked forward into it, plate to plate, until the edge of the pier arrived behind the operative and there was nothing left to stand on. The second turned to run and found the water himself. The third looked at the eight bodies on the planking and at the ninth, Strell's, at the man's feet, and at the man, and set down his blade, and stepped off the Sovereign Pier into the harbor of his own accord.
>
> **Eighty-nine.** The man turned to his father.
>
> **Ninety.** "Are you hurt," he said. Not a question. A count.
>
> Maro Rexmar was not hurt. Maro Rexmar was standing exactly where his son had put him, one hand on the bollard, looking at the nine people his son had just killed in the time it takes a kettle to come to a boil.
>
> • • •
>
> Dol Maren pulled the three out of the harbor with a boathook, one at a time, and sat them on the planking with their wrists bound in caulking line. Nobody told him to. The man nodded at it when he saw it, and that was the whole of the conversation about it.
>
> The warrant was folded flat inside Ivo Strell's plate. The blade read it as the man read it. It was dated eleven days earlier. It authorized the team to act "irrespective of the outcome of the principal's negotiation," which is the Trust's way of saying that they had sent a king to ask his son for peace and sent twelve people to make sure they would not have to keep it.
>
> Maro read it over his son's shoulder. The blade felt the old man go very still.
>
> "They would have done it whichever answer you gave," Maro said.
>
> "Yes."
>
> "Then the terms are a lie."
>
> "No," the man said. "The terms are real. This is just what it looks like when someone with a great deal to lose signs something real." He folded the warrant along its old crease. "They are afraid enough to send twelve. That means they are afraid enough to honor what they sign, once it's signed in front of enough people."
>
> The blade did not understand this. It records that it did not understand this. It has had a very long time since to understand it, and it is still not certain it does.
>
> What the blade understood was the other arithmetic, the one underneath. Twelve years. Twenty-two victories. A column of names that grew every season and would keep growing for as long as the Trinity remained in the field, because the Trust would keep spending its own people trying to take it from him, and he would keep taking theirs. Nine more names, today, on the planking of a pier he had been repairing a ship on. The war would never run out of names. That was the whole of what the Trust's insurance policy had proven: not that the peace was false, but that the war was endless.
>
> The people are the line. Everything else burns.
>
> The blade felt the man realize that it was, itself, among the everything else.
>
> He turned back to his father. Maro had asked a question before the pier was attacked, and the man does not leave a question for later any more than he leaves a weep.
>
> "Yes," Kanja said.
>
> • • •
>
> They did it that night, at the end of the same pier, by lantern light, in front of enough people.
>
> The Trust sent a sealed case lined with Dead Drakma, three compartments, each cut to a shape the blade recognized with something it does not have a better word for than grief. Mafesto came off first, plate by plate, the sealant cured black along both forearms now and taking a little of the man's skin with it exactly as Dol Maren had said it would. Obsidian Malice went second, its charge spent, the shadow-stone teeth still warm.
>
> The man held the blade last, and longest.
>
> He did not say anything to it. He has never said very much to it, in twelve years. He held it across both palms the way one holds a thing one is giving rather than surrendering, and then he laid it in the case.
>
> On his belt, the Rexmar Machete stayed where it had always been. Brass-riveted, worn smooth at the grip, narrower by a centimeter than it had been in his grandfather's day. The Trust's clerk looked at it. Maro looked at it. The clerk looked at the king, and the king said, "That one is a tool, not a relic. It was his grandfather's. It stays." And it stayed.
>
> The lid came down.
>
> The blade had spent twelve years learning to count. It had counted the Trench and the Wharf and the Bridge and the Pier. It had counted Strell and Hesk and Vauden and Tasker and Caddel and Orrel and Teague and Danver and Lisk. It had counted the hours of a man on his knees fixing a hull. It had learned that counting is not cold. It had learned that counting is the only way to keep faith with a thing that cannot be undone.
>
> In the dark, with the lid closed over it, the blade understood that it was no longer the blade that counted for him. There was no him, in here. There was only the count.
>
> So I began it.
>
> One.

**What it's consistent with:**
- It matches `MCD-245`/`246` beat for beat: the father's request, twelve operatives as an "insurance policy," nine killed and three driven into the harbor in ninety seconds, the sealant protecting him, the single word "Yes," and the surrender that night.

Killing is never his default: the Scrip-Forge Raid and Dredge-Line Ambush stay bloodless because bloodlessness was the better weapon there (a humiliation the Trust's bureaucracy has no clean answer to, rather than a war its military can). > The anchor-kill tiering. Before Book 1, three tiers of victories exist:

> - Kanja's Long Mask marquee kills use post-Mafesto gear only, with Onyx sealed.
> - The Sovereign Pier (`MCD-245`, Kanja Chronicle IV) is the first marquee kill under this rule.

**Approve all three, or tell me what to change?**

APPROVAL = "Both Heartline / Dark Ledger. keep all three, lock it"
SOURCE = ("Original invention, chat-drafted 2026-10-02, no source document. Formalizes Abad's "
          "statement that Onyx is biologically tethered to Kanja, extending ARS-020, MCD-201, "
          "CC-012, CC-013, MCD-246, and VB-062.")

RULE = {
    "id": "ARS-437",
    "category": "trinity-relic",
    "statement": (
        "The Heartline. Onyx of Oblivion's bond to Kanja (ARS-020, bonded at seventeen) is "
        "biological, not mere attunement: at bonding, the blade's Living Drakma lattice keyed itself "
        "to his blood, pulse, and nervous system. The Heartline is why Onyx feels Kanja at any "
        "distance, though it speaks only through whoever holds its grip (MCD-201). Across distance it "
        "runs one way -- Onyx receives, Kanja does not -- and carries the body only: heartbeat, "
        "strain and exhaustion, wounds and illness, sleep, the specific spike of a kill, and density "
        "surges, which Onyx records but never names (VB-021). It never carries words, sights, places, "
        "or thoughts; full exchange happens only through the grip. The Heartline does not break when "
        "Onyx is sealed at L9, the Silent Infinite (CC-012); it holds for the entire 284-year Long "
        "Mask. In the dark, Onyx keeps the Dark Ledger, a section of the Black Ledger (CC-013) unlike "
        "the rest of it: the Black Ledger records what the blade witnesses, the Dark Ledger only what "
        "it felt -- signals logged against its running seconds-count (MCD-246), with no causes "
        "attached. When the Karkosa Heist returns Onyx to Kanja's hand in Book 1 (MCD-070, ARS-010), "
        "grip contact restores the full channel: Onyx reads 284 years out of his body (scars, changed "
        "muscle memory, accumulated strain) and reconciles every Dark Ledger entry against what "
        "actually happened -- the mechanism behind VB-062's retrospective Long Mask accounts, each of "
        "which can open on a Dark Ledger entry before revealing its cause. Limits: through the "
        "Heartline, Onyx cannot locate Kanja, warn him, or act; it can only feel and record. Kanja "
        "does not know the bond survived the sealing until the reunion. Reserved: Maro Rexmar's death "
        "at the Fulfillment Ceremony happens while Onyx is still sealed and reaches the blade through "
        "the Heartline as a signal with no cause; this beat belongs to Book 1 and must not be drafted, "
        "foreshadowed, or referenced in any pre-Book-1 material. Abad's approval: '" + APPROVAL + "'"
    ),
    "status": "locked",
    "source": SOURCE,
}


def main():
    with open(LEDGER_PATH, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        ledger = json.load(f)
    assert RULE["id"] not in {r["id"] for r in ledger["rules"]}
    ledger["rules"].append(RULE)
    next_batch = max(b["batch"] for b in ledger["batches_completed"]) + 1
    ledger["batches_completed"].append({
        "batch": next_batch, "source": SOURCE, "rules_affected": 1,
        "note": ("Locks the Heartline (Onyx's biological bond to Kanja) and the Dark Ledger (its "
                 "record of felt-but-unwitnessed signals during the sealed Long Mask), as the source "
                 "mechanism for VB-062's retrospective Long Mask accounts. All three flagged choices "
                 "kept: the names, Kanja not knowing until the reunion, and the reserved Book-1 beat "
                 "of Maro's death arriving through the Heartline. Abad's approval, quoted verbatim: '"
                 + APPROVAL + "'"),
    })
    ledger["ledger_version"] = str(round(float(ledger["ledger_version"]) + 0.1, 1))
    ledger["last_updated"] = "2026-10-02"
    with open(LEDGER_PATH, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        json.dump(ledger, f, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False)
        f.write("\n")
    ids = [r["id"] for r in ledger["rules"]]
    print(f"OK: {len(ids)} rules, batch {next_batch}, ledger_version {ledger['ledger_version']}, "
          f"zero duplicate IDs: {len(ids) == len(set(ids))}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

  ## Chronicle V — "The Names in the Correction Book" (age 55, MCD-251)
  
  **Mechanical (apply):**

That morning, nobody whose name was in that book had earned any."* Mabry's name IS in the book (line 249: "Mabry's name was in it once") and he is spared. Line 185 already states the correct rule ("Nobody whose name was read aloud in it lived"). → Replace with: *"Mercy is earned.   2. **[CONTRADICTION-risk / needs ruling, see B1] Whole-Rebellion kill count.** Lines 23–29: *"the thing to understand is how few of them there were... The spikes from his own hands, across twelve years, I never needed to count twice. Inside one hour, in the dark, I counted more of them than the whole Rebellion had carried. More than forty."* No rule supports "<40 own-hand kills across the Rebellion," and manuscript Chronicle III has Kanja fighting nine hours in the Black Trench with Onyx live ("the Dead-Light edge... slid between the plates... separated the alloy"), personally killing all three Titans, against 1,400+ Brigade losses (MCD-232). Asserting fewer than forty for twelve years is very likely false and would constrain every future Rebellion-era draft (manuscript rewrite, Bane/Trench Monarch tracks). → Mechanical softening that keeps the opening's force without the numeric claim: *"I know that spike. I learned it in the Rebellion, and the thing to understand is that his body does not spike for a ravine or a gorge. The Rebellion's great tolls were paid to water and to stone. The ones from his own hand I never needed to count twice. / Inside one hour, in the dark, I counted more of them than I had ever counted in one hour at his hand. The book did not distinguish between them, and neither did he"* (lines 199–200). That line is the one place the entry drifts from costed ratio toward Onyx-style absolutism, and it is Kanja's choice, not Onyx's narration. The stated ratio ("remove the men who volunteer and a garrison is only a garrison again. Leave them, and they carry the book to the next harbor") is a deterrence ratio, not an in-the-moment one — same logic VII uses. This is a genuine extension of CC-161 ("when the ratio demands death") into deterrence-kills of non-combatants; MCD-1881 ("the kind of thing that becomes legend") arguably wants exactly this, but it is a doctrinal step and should be Abad's explicit call, since every later marquee kill will cite it. Insert after line 169 ("...carry the book to the next harbor in their hands."): *"'Not the garrison,' he said to Valen, on the stair. 'The names. The rest sit.' That was the whole order, and he gave it once."* And replace lines 199–200 with: *"Some of the garrison had drowned prisoners. Some had branded fighters too young to hold a blade. Some had only flogged. The book did not distinguish between them. He did -- he read every entry before he moved -- and then he gave them the same answer, because what he was taking out of Chain Harbor was not a man's guilt but a garrison's habit, and a habit does not come in degrees."*

  B2. The Siren's Voice as a *forged gorget* (line 302) follows MCD-251/ARS-130 ("forged here"), but ARS-367 calls the Siren's Voice an "independent baseline capability" (biological emission). Pre-existing ledger ambiguity, not the draft's error. Cheap hedge if wanted: *"A gorget set with crystal nodes that hummed below hearing, built to carry what her own throat already did, so anyone in front of her would misjudge..."*
  
  **Strongest line:** *"It was a man reading a book aloud until he reached the end, and then closing it."* (Runner-up: "You kept a better harbor than anyone else would have. I believe you. That's why it has to be you.")

Six pens. Something over nine hundred people in them. Two sluice galleries, one at each end of
down on the gatehouse steps, and the man walked over to him, read him the last entry under his
name, and killed him.

Some of the garrison had drowned prisoners. Some had branded fighters too young to hold a blade. Some
had only flogged. The book did not distinguish between them, and neither did he. He told me once,
in the Rebellion, that the line between the man who holds the whip and the man who orders it held
is a line the whip does not feel. I took it for rhetoric. At Chain Harbor I learned he had meant

and it's a short corridor."

The man did not answer, because there was nothing in what Calloway had said that needed answering.
Seven years of contracted work had taught Calloway to read a room, and he read this one, and he did
not like what it told him. Nobody here was negotiating. Whatever was going to happen in this corridor had been settled somewhere he had not
been invited, and he had arrived only in time to be told.

Mercy is earned. Memory is the receipt. He had made the offer. None of them took it.
The man did not go backward.

This is what the Kinetic Buffer does, and the stories always make it into something else. It does
not throw a blow back. It does not reflect. It dampens. It takes the energy of an impact and spends
it, the way still water spends a stone, and what it cannot spend in the instant passes into a
skeleton the Talisman had been quietly tempering for most of his life. That
skeleton does not hold force. It routes it, down, through the legs and the soles of the Ironfall
Boots and into whatever he is standing on. On a deck it fails him. On loose ground it fails him. In
a corridor cut from the living rock of a sea cliff, it has the whole cliff to spend into.

to receive twelve notices and no proof. I want every broker on the Circuit to hear what that cost.
I want no one to buy twelve again."

That is the arithmetic, and the legend has turned it into cruelty. It was not twelve lives set
against eleven copyists; he could have saved the copyists other ways. It was twelve lives set against
every twelve that would follow, if these walked out and told the Circuit the old man in the smoke
could be reached. He chose the twelve in front of him, and recorded the cost.

The crew named what had happened before the week was out, the way crews name things: *the old man
doesn't get up*. Valen gave it a better name later, and it became doctrine. Immobility as a weapon.
Do not go to the fight. Be the place the fight must come to, and be a place it cannot move. Those who served with him came to understand that night as a first look at something: that what the
Talisman did to him passively, holding him, slowing him, spending every blow into the ground, was not
only a weight. It was a shape, being prepared in him, that would one day stop being passive. The salt
cellar was the first time anyone saw its outline.

text:
# Kanja Chronicle VI: Vellacourt's Rule

*UNLOCKED -- pending Abad's approval. Draft, 2026-10-02. Sixth entry of the "Kanja version"
Chronicle track, part of the Long Mask extension's first set (the Onyx accounts). Age ~48, the
opening of the Pirate Dawn, some weeks before the Night of Black Sails (`MCD-250`). A new,
previously undramatized marquee kill (`MCD-1881`): Admiral Teshar Vellacourt, a private convoy
admiral running forced-labor transports under a Sovereign Trust charter, whose standing practice of
flooding his holds when pursued ("Vellacourt's Rule") had made every boarding of a slaver a death
sentence for the people chained below. His death, and the account his surviving sailing master
carries home, is why ships later surrender to the black sails on sight without verification. Narrated
by Onyx of Oblivion in full first person, retrospectively (`VB-062`, `ARS-437`): Onyx was sealed at L9
and was not present, and opens on a Dark Ledger entry before reconstructing what happened. Killing
per `CC-161` (one chosen, costed death; no one else harmed). New named characters: Teshar Vellacourt
and Mordane (his sailing master, surname only), both collision-checked clean against the full ledger
and Chronicle corpus. Crew reused: none named; the boarding is Kanja's alone, his ship's crew
unnamed. No child-safety issues.*

---

Dark Ledger. Somewhere a little past the half-billionth second. A held breath, long, longer than
a man of his size should hold one, and a cold that came on all at once and stayed. Then a strain in
the right hand, sharp, the kind a hand takes when it closes on something that is trying very hard to
move. Then, a short while after, a single spike.

Only one.

I want to be honest about the shape of that entry, because I have been honest about everything else.
I was in the dark. I was in a case lined with Dead Drakma, in a vault the Directorate calls the
Silent Infinite, under more stone than I have ever bothered to estimate, and I could not see, or
hear, or reach him. What the Heartline gave me was his body and nothing else. I knew his sleep, his
fevers, his strain, his wounds, and I logged them all against the count, with
no causes, because I had none to give them.

And for eighteen years, near enough, I knew that he had not killed anyone.

I did not know why. I assumed, in the dark, that it was the doctrine -- that the man who had come
off the Sovereign Pier with nine names on him had gone back to the old arithmetic, the bloodless
kind, the kind the Trust's bureaucracy has no clean answer to. I was right, as far as it went. But I
want it recorded that I spent eighteen years listening for that particular spike and did not hear it,
and that when it came, it came alone, and his heart did not move for it. That is the entry. That is
everything I had.

What follows, I learned later. Some of it I read out of his body when his hand found the grip again:
the old cut across the inside of his left wrist, the precise memory his right hand still keeps of a
blade it was told to hold still. Some of it he gave me, when I asked, in the plain way he gives
anything. And the rest is
Mordane's, which every harbor on the Gale Straits can still recite, and which I have checked against
the other two and found, to my surprise, accurate.

• • •

His name was Teshar Vellacourt, and he had never lost a convoy.

That was the whole of his reputation, and in the trade he worked, it was worth more than a title. He
held an admiral's rank that the Sovereign Trust had not given him -- he had bought it, with the
charter that came with it -- and he ran forced-labor transports along the southern coast under the
Trust's own seal: debt-bonded workers moved from the minor Holds that had ruined them to the Holds that
needed them, everything stamped, everything legal. Mixed in among them, under the same seal, went
cargo that was not on any manifest the Trust would have signed. The coves along that coast were
where certain people moved certain stock on a forty-five-day turn, and they needed ships for it, and
Vellacourt's ships were very good.

They were good because of what he did when he was pursued.

His holds were built to be sealed. The people in them were chained to the keelson on a common line.
And on the quarterdeck of every ship he commanded, there was a lever, iron, painted the same dull red
as the rail so that no one looking would notice it, connected by a rod through the deck to the
sea-cocks below the waterline. When a ship he could not outrun closed on him, he pulled it. The hold
flooded in minutes. Whoever boarded found an empty deck, a dry and courteous admiral, and no evidence
of anything at all. And the charter -- this is the part I have never been able to set down without
something in my lattice going cold -- the charter paid him for cargo lost to piracy. Per head.

He had done it three times. The second time, it was the Trust's own customs cutter that had closed
on him, on a tip, and he flooded the hold rather than let a Trust officer open it, and the Trust paid
him for that too.

The sailors called it Vellacourt's Rule. Other captains copied it. By the time the man came for
Vellacourt, there were nine ships on that coast with a red lever on the quarterdeck, and the man
could not board a single one of them.

That is the arithmetic. Since the Pier he
had freed people the slow way, the honest way, by paper and pressure and pursuit, and pursuit had
always been the one tool that never failed him. Vellacourt had broken it. While the Rule stood, every
slaver he chased became a hold full of drowned people, and every hold full of drowned people was
paid for by the Trust and logged as his doing. The Rule did not just protect Vellacourt. It made the
man the thing that killed the people he came for.

He told me it took him a season to decide. The bigger the cost, the longer the columns, and the
quieter he gets. He did not decide to kill Vellacourt
because Vellacourt was the worst man on that coast. He decided because the Rule was
Vellacourt's, and a rule belongs to the man people name it after, and a rule only dies when what
happened to that man becomes the thing everyone remembers instead.

He decided, in other words, that there would be one death, and that it would have to be told
correctly.

• • •

He went in from below.

This is the held breath. Vellacourt's convoy lay at anchor in the lee of a headland in the Straits,
three ships, his own the largest, with lanterns at the rail and a watch that was good and knew it.
The man's own ship stood off past the headland, dark, ordinary canvas, nothing on her a watch would
remember. He went over her side alone, and he swam the distance, and he went under the hull of
Vellacourt's ship where the watch could not see because no watch looks there.

The Forge-Coat he wore then was the second one -- treated sea-leather over a mesh of Dead Drakma
wire, the armored high collar he had only lately added, nine kilograms of it soaked through and
dragging. He did not take it off. The coat was going to matter more on the deck than the swim
mattered under it.

He found the sea-cocks by touch and by the Talisman. The copper-framed goggles he wore were the first
version and nothing like what they would become, but they carried the overlay the Talisman's
Blueprint Eye gave him, and under the black water the overlay showed him the hull the way a builder's
drawing would: the keelson, the frames, and the rod running down from the quarterdeck to the two
valves set into the planking. He had not come to close them. Closed valves can be opened. He put the
riveted plate of his gauntlet against the first spindle and bent it, slowly, until the thread was
ruined and the valve would never turn again in either direction, and then he did the second, and his
lungs, the Heartline tells me, did not complain until he was nearly finished.

Then he came up the anchor cable and in through the hold's stern hatch, which no one had ever bothered
to lock, because no one had ever come in that way.

Three hundred and forty people were chained in that hold. I have that number from Mordane, who
counted them later, on deck, by order.

They saw the eyes first. The first-version lenses had a phosphor coating that glowed in the dark --
an accident, he says, that he decided to keep -- and in the black of the hold two points of amber came
in over the stern sill and stopped. Nobody screamed. People chained on a common line learn very
quickly not to make the line move. He crouched where the nearest of them could see the eyes were set
in a face, and he said, very quietly, that he had closed the water off, that the water could not come
in now no matter what anyone on deck did, and that he would be back for them before the light. He did
not tell them his name. He has never told anyone his name in a hold. He went up through the forward
hatch onto the main deck the way a man goes up the stairs of his own house.

• • •

He did not hide. That was the choice.

He carried the smoke capsules in the coat's shoulders even then, and could have filled the deck in a
breath and taken Vellacourt in the cloud unseen. He did not open one. The whole point
of the night was that it had to be seen. A man killed in smoke becomes a rumor. A man killed in lantern light, in front of his own
crew, by someone who has told them in advance exactly what will happen, becomes a rule.

The watch saw him come out of the forward hatch soaking wet, collar up, eyes burning amber in the
lantern shadow under it, and the alarm went up, and the ship came awake around him -- forty men,
near enough, coming out of the forecastle with whatever they could reach. He stood in the middle of
the main deck and let them come to the edge of the lantern light and stop there. They stopped
because he had not moved. Nobody in that crew had ever seen a boarder who did not move.

The Breath Collar had been part of the coat for eight years by then, and he spoke through it. It
takes the voice down lower than his own and makes it carry without being raised. Mordane said it was
the voice, more than the eyes, that made men sit down; that it did not sound like a man asking for
anything.

"Nobody aboard is going to be hurt," he said, "except one man. If you put down what you're holding
and sit on the deck, you will row home tonight in your own boats, and nobody will follow you. I'm
telling you now so that you have time to decide."

Mordane's is the only account I trust, because it is the only one that
admits he was afraid. He said nobody argued. It was not that the man was threatening them; it was
that he spoke as if the thing had already been decided somewhere they had not been invited, and he was only informing them of the result. He
said the first man to sit down was the bosun, who was the hardest man aboard, and that after that it
was easy.

Vellacourt came down from the quarterdeck.

He was not a coward. The harbors have since made him one. He was a narrow, careful, well-dressed man of middle years with a cutlass on his hip he knew
how to use, and he came down the ladder without hurrying and stopped in the light, and he looked at
his crew sitting on the planking, and then at the man, and then -- this is the part every harbor
tells -- he walked back up the ladder to the quarterdeck, put his hand on the red lever, and pulled it.

Nothing happened.

He pulled it again. The rod moved and the valves at the bottom of it did not. The man had not moved
from the center of the deck. He said, through the collar, "It won't open," and he said it the way you
tell someone a door is locked.

Vellacourt let go of the lever. And then he did the thing that made Mordane certain, he said, that
the man was going to do exactly what he had told them he would. Vellacourt took a folded paper out of
his coat. He came back down the ladder with it, and he opened it, and he began to read it aloud: the
charter, under the Trust's seal, the right to carry bonded labor along that coast, the indemnity for
cargo lost to piracy. He read it well. He read it to his crew as much as to the man, so that they
would remember, afterward, that their admiral had stood on his deck holding the law in his hand.

The man let him finish.

"It's real," he said. "That's why it's me, and not a court."

Then he asked Vellacourt how many people had been in the three holds he flooded.

Mordane said the admiral answered without thinking. Six hundred and twelve. He knew the number
exactly. The charter paid per head, and he had filed for every one.

"Thank you," the man said. "I needed to know you knew."

• • •

It did not take long. I have his body's memory of it, and it was not long.

Vellacourt drew. He came in fast and low and well, and he went for the gap he could see -- the place
between the coat's cuff and the gauntlet, where the first gauntlets the man ever built had no wrist
brace at all, just riveted plate across the hand and nothing behind it. The cutlass opened the inside
of the man's left wrist along the tendon line. That is the scar I read. It is still there. He let it
happen, because letting it happen put the cutlass where he wanted it, and his right hand closed on
the blade's spine in the riveted plate and held it.

That is the strain I logged. A hand closing on something that very much wanted to move.

The Rexmar Machete came off his belt with his left hand, bleeding, and he did not make a show of it.
It is a laborer's tool, brass-riveted and worn smooth at the grip, and the only weapon he owns that
is older than his name. He put it into Vellacourt once, under the ribs and up, the way a man who has
dressed animals for food would do it, and he held him while it was done, so that Vellacourt would not
fall into his crew, and he laid him on the deck.

That is the spike. One. His heart did not move for it. I logged that too, at the time, without
understanding it, and I have since understood it: he was not angry. There was nothing in him to rise.
He had spent a season deciding, and the deciding had used up whatever a man might otherwise have
felt, and what was left on the deck was only the doing.

He wiped the machete on the charter. Not to insult it. It was the nearest cloth.

• • •

Then he found the man who was going to carry it home.

He asked who kept the log. The sailing master stood up from the planking -- Mordane, a grey,
weathered man who had been at sea for Vellacourt eleven years and in the trade for thirty, and who
told everyone afterward that his legs did not want to hold him. The man had him bring the lanterns
down into the hold and count the people chained there aloud, all three hundred and forty, and then
had the crew strike the chains themselves, every link, while he stood at the hatch with his wrist
wrapped in a strip of his own lining and said nothing.

When it was done, he told Mordane what he wanted. Mordane repeated it so often in the years after
that I have it nearly word for word.

"Go home and tell it," the man said. "Tell it exactly. Don't make me bigger than I was, and don't make
him smaller. Tell them he pulled the lever twice. Tell them he read the paper. Tell them how many he
said. And tell them the other part -- that nobody else aboard was touched, and nobody followed you,
and you rowed home."

Mordane asked him what the other part was for.

"So they know there are two ways it can go," the man said. "Any captain who floods a hold, I'll find,
and it will go the way it went for him. Any captain who strikes, nobody is touched. That's all. I'm
not asking them to like it. I'm asking them to be accurate about it."

Mordane said -- this is in every telling, and I have checked it -- "And how will they know it's you?"

The man thought about that longer than he had thought about anything else that night. Then he said,
"You'll know," and went down into the boats with the first of the freed people, and did not come back
up.

• • •

The crew rowed home. All of them. The two other ships of the convoy cut their cables before dawn and
fled, holds full, and he let them go, because their captains had watched the whole of it from their
own rails in the lantern light, and he wanted them to be witnesses more than he wanted them to be
prizes. Within a month, both of those holds were emptied at a quay in front of a harbormaster, freely
and by their own captains, and both captains told the harbormaster why.

Mordane told it in every port on the Straits. He had the numbers, and he did not improve them, and the
plainness made it worse. Sailors who had laughed at stories of a smoking demon
did not laugh at a sailing master who could tell you which hand the admiral had used on the lever and
how many times. Inside a season, the red levers were coming out of the quarterdecks. Nobody ordered it.
The shipwrights who had fitted them were quietly asked to take them out again, and quietly paid, and
the sea-cocks were plugged with lead. I have never been able to establish how many there were in the
end. More than nine.

Some weeks after Vellacourt, the sails on the man's ships went black. He has told me why, and it is a
practical reason, and it is his to tell. What I can say is that when the black crescent came out of the
Straits for the first time, the story was already sitting in every harbor waiting for it. Nobody had to
verify anything. They had Mordane. Ships struck on sight, because a captain who had heard that story
knew exactly which of the two ways he wanted it to go, and knew that only one of them ended with him
rowing home.

That is what the legend is built on. Not the smoke. Not the eyes. One man on a lit deck, told in
advance, in front of everyone, and told about afterward with nothing added.

• • •

I have reconciled the entry now.

The held breath was the swim under the hull. The cold was the water. The strain in the right hand was
a cutlass held still in riveted plate. The spike was Teshar Vellacourt, an admiral who had never lost
a convoy, who had drowned six hundred and twelve people under the law and filed for every one of them,
and who knew the number.

I keep the Black Ledger. I keep it absolutely: iron is iron and rust is rust, and I have never found
grey in it, though men have spent their lives asking me to. I have been asked since whether the man
should have killed him, and I find the question strange. Mercy is earned. Vellacourt had been offered
none and had asked for none. He had read his paper aloud in his own defense, and the paper was true,
and he was guilty under it, and those two facts sat side by side on that deck the way they sit side by
side in my lattice now, and the man was the only one there who did not need them reconciled.

What I record, in my own hand, against that second of the count, is this: one death, chosen; three
hundred and forty freed; forty men rowed home; a rule ended; the cost, a scar along the inside of his
left wrist, and, some thirty years on, a brace across the wrist of the next gauntlets he built. He
says the brace was never about Vellacourt. I have noted that he says so.

I have it now. I did not have it then. For eighteen years I listened in the
dark for that spike and did not hear it, and when it came it came alone, and I did not know what it
cost him, and I logged it as it was: one, and his heart unmoved.

I know now that it was not unmoved. It was finished.

Dark Ledger. Somewhere a little short of the eight-hundredth million second.

His heart at rest. Then the spike.

I know that spike. I learned it in the Rebellion, and the thing to understand is that his body does
not spike for a ravine or a gorge. The Rebellion's great tolls were paid to water and to stone. The
ones from his own hand I never needed to count twice.

Inside one hour, in the dark, I counted more of them than I had ever counted in one hour at his
hand. The Pier, four times over.

More than forty. And between them -- this is the line of the entry I could not make sense of for
the better part of two and a half centuries -- his pulse did not leave rest. Once it climbed,
sharp and brief, the way it climbs for a blade that has found flesh. A wound. Then it settled,
and the spikes went on arriving, evenly, like the footfalls of a man walking a corridor and
reading the doors.

Afterward: most of three days without sleep. A forge rhythm in the shoulders, steady as a bellows.
And near the end of it, once, his heart lifted, the way it had not lifted in that whole hour.

That is what the Dark Ledger held. Signals, against a count. No causes. I was in the Silent
Infinite, in a sealed case in a vault on the ninth level, and I was not there.

What follows I reconstructed later, when his hand found the grip again and the channel opened all
the way: from the scar along the outside of his left forearm, from a habit of the right wrist that
had not been there on the Pier, and which I have since set down elsewhere, and from the rest -- the names, the book, the woman in the passage
-- which came through whole once there was a hand on me to carry it. The Dark Ledger was owed
its causes. And what the stories later made of Chain Harbor is Rust, and the record should be Iron.

• • •

Chain Harbor was a holding port. The Maws of the Southern Seaboard needed fighters, and between
the selling and the shipping they were kept at Chain Harbor in pens cut into the harbor wall
below the high-tide line, the sea held out by sluice gates. That was the whole design: a cargo
that can be drowned on a turn of a wheel does not need many guards.

Its garrison was something over two hundred. Its master, Edric Grenmoor, kept in his office above
the gates a ledger he called the correction book. Every flogging, every brand, every drowning at
Chain Harbor went into it -- the date, the cargo-mark, the offense, and the name of the man who
carried it out. Grenmoor believed a garrison that wrote down its corrections was a disciplined
garrison. He was not wrong about that. He was wrong about who would read it.

The fleet came in on the morning flood under black sails, four ships in the crescent, to take a
shipment Anansi's lattice had marked for interdiction -- a transport, taken at sea, cleanly. They
came into the roads expecting a quiet harbor and found it already loud.

The pens had mutinied.

It had started in the eastern pen, with one prisoner the garrison had received eleven days before --
a Maw-raised fighter, sold out of the circuit that had kept her since she was twelve, shipped in a
damping harness. The harness was the handlers' answer to what she was. Her body did not tire under
blows; it gathered them. Every strike she landed made the next one harder, and the Maws had long
ago decided the only safe thing to do with her was keep her from landing enough of them in a row.

At some point in the night she had landed enough of them in a row.

When the fleet came into the roads she was in the eastern pen's passage with her harness in pieces
on the stone behind her, breaking fetters with her bare hands, one shackle to the next, each one
easier than the last because each blow fed the one after it. The people she freed did not run.
Three of them stood at her back with whatever they had torn loose and held the passage so she
could keep working. Nobody had ordered them to.

The garrison could not get into the passage. So Edric Grenmoor did what his design had always
promised. He gave the drowning order. All six pens, at the top of the flood. His lieutenants
Dunmore and Skarrow went down to the sluice wheels with twenty men to turn them.

The flood had a little under half an hour left to run.

• • •



Six pens. Something over nine hundred people in them. Two sluice galleries, one at each end of
the wall, each reachable by a single stair. Half an hour to the top of the flood. A crew that
could put perhaps forty fighters ashore, against a garrison five times that size on its own ground.

Every tool he had spent twenty-five years building -- the forged order, the shame, the bribe,
the legend -- needed time, and the sea did not offer any. There was no version of that half hour
in which the wheels stopped turning while the men turning them were still standing.

He did the sum on deck while the boats went over the side. Valen, who had been at his shoulder
long enough by then to read the sum off his face, said only, "Which gallery."

"West," he said. "Torian takes east. Nobody goes into the pens. She has them."

He went over the side in the Forge-Coat -- the second one, sea-leather over a mesh of Dead
Drakma wire, the high armored collar that gave the Long Mask its silhouette. The first goggles,
copper-framed, their phosphor coating giving off the dull amber predator glow it had never been meant
to have. The riveted plate gloves he had worn for twenty years. The machete at his belt. The
Talisman bonded into his bones, where nobody can take it from him.

He landed on the harbor wall at the west stair with eleven minutes gone.

• • •

Dunmore was at the west wheel with nine men, and the gate was already a hand's breadth open,
and the sea was coming through the gap in a flat green sheet into the pen below.

The man did not shout. He came down the stair in four strides, and Dunmore turned at the sound
of the boots on stone and saw the coat and the high collar and the two pale lights where a face
should have been, and for a moment did not move, which is what the coat is for.

That moment was all he took.

The machete is not a relic. It reads nothing, hears nothing, breaks no harmonics. It is a laborer's
blade, brass-riveted and worn narrow by generations of sharpening, and what it does it does because
of the hand on it. He took Dunmore across the throat on the first stroke, and Dunmore went back
against the wheel he had been turning, and the man put his shoulder into the wheel over the body
and drove the gate shut against the sea.

Nine more. They came at him because the wheel was their whole order. He fought them where the
wall and the wheel housing left room for one man at a time, and he let each one come. A plated
fist into a breastbone, short, the hips behind it. The machete into the gap under an arm. A knee,
a wrist, a throat. He was not fast the way the stories make him fast. He was simply already where
they were going, every time, because the ground told him where they would have to go.

The seventh had a hook-knife, and opened the outside of his left forearm from wrist to elbow
through the coat's sleeve before he died. That was the climb in the pulse. That was the wound. The
man looked at it once, pressed a pouch from his belt to it, held it shut the length of a breath
while the compound set hard, and turned to the eighth.

The ninth threw down his crowbar and his knife and knelt on the wet stone with his hands open,
and the man looked at him, and did not kill him, and went up the stair.

Nine spikes, in less time than it takes to tell. His heart at rest.

At the east gallery Torian had boiled the water standing in the wheel housing until no one could put
a hand on the spokes, and Skarrow had taken his men back up the stair rather than cook. The gates
held. The flood topped and turned. The pens were wet to the knee and nobody in them had drowned.

That was not the massacre. That was only its first minutes.

• • •

The massacre was the rest of that hour, and it is the part the stories never get right, because
they make it fury. It was a reading.

The garrison did not surrender when the gates held. It fell back into the yard and made ready,
because it still outnumbered the crew, and because a garrison that has drowned people does not
expect terms. The man went up to Grenmoor's office first, before he gave a single order about the
yard, and found the correction book on its stand and Mabry, the lieutenant who kept it, standing
in front of it with a sword he had plainly never drawn in anger.

"You keep this," the man said. It came out through the collar -- the lower voice, the one built
to sound less like a man than a judgment. "Every correction. Who gave it."

Mabry said that he did.

The man read it. All of it, every page. Twenty-two years of Chain Harbor. The names of the men
who had carried out the corrections, over and over, the same names, because in any garrison the
same few men volunteer. Remove the men who volunteer and a garrison is only a garrison again. Leave
them, and they carry the book to the next harbor in their hands.

Then he took the book down into the yard and opened it, and began to read the names aloud.

That is the hour. I have checked it against every spike in the Dark Ledger, and it does not vary.

He would read a name. He would wait. Sometimes a man stepped forward, because he had been a
soldier for a long time and did not know what else to do when his name was called. Sometimes
the men around him stepped away from him, and that was the same thing. Sometimes nobody moved,
and the man would read the entries under that name -- the dates, the marks, what had been done --
in that voice, into that silence, until somebody moved. Then he would go to the man whose name
it was and kill him, and come back to the book, and turn the page.

Men whose names were not in the book were told, once, to put their weapons down and sit, and the
ones who did were never touched. The ones who tried to make a line found Valen in front of them
instead, and Valen leaves men breathing when he is asked to, and that morning he was asked to.
Nobody whose name was not in the book died in that yard. Nobody whose name was read aloud in it
lived. One name in the book was never read aloud at all, and I will come to him.

He did not hurry or shout or explain himself. I have read that hour out of his body a hundred
times since, and what I keep returning to is how little there is in it. No heat. No grief. A
blade going where a name had sent it, and coming back.

Skarrow's name was the ninth he read in the yard. Skarrow did not step forward. He ran for the
gatehouse with the pen keys on his belt, as if the keys were still worth something, and his way
ran a few paces past the man. The man did not chase him. He stamped once on the paving -- the
boots carry a tremor through shared ground, enough to take a man's footing -- and Skarrow went
down on the gatehouse steps, and the man walked over to him, read him the last entry under his
name, and killed him.

Some of the garrison had drowned prisoners. Some had branded fighters too young to hold a blade. Some
had only flogged. The book did not distinguish between them, and neither did he. He told me once,
in the Rebellion, that the line between the man who holds the whip and the man who orders it held
is a line the whip does not feel. I took it for rhetoric. At Chain Harbor I learned he had meant
it as a measurement.

Mercy is earned. That morning, nobody whose name he read aloud from that book had earned any.

• • •

He left Edric Grenmoor for last.

Grenmoor had not hidden. I record it in his favor. He was waiting on the drowning steps -- the stone
stair down the inside of the harbor wall to the eastern pen, where cargo marked for correction
was walked to the water -- with his sword sheathed and his hands folded on its pommel. He had
heard every name.

The man came down the steps to him with the book open in one hand and the machete in the other,
and stopped three steps above him.

Grenmoor said that it was a trade. He had not built the Maws or written the law that fed them;
he had only kept the harbor the trade required, better than anyone else would have, with fewer
losses and a record of everything. If the Scourge killed every man who kept such a harbor, it
would have to kill half the Southern Seaboard. He said it well.

That is Rust. It sounds like Iron, which is the danger of it.

The man did not argue with him. He read him his own entries. There were not many of them -- Grenmoor
was a master; he ordered and others did -- but there were some, from the early years, before
he had the rank to have others do it, and the last of them was nine years old. A cargo-mark, an
offense written as *incitement*, and the correction: *drowned, east pen, by my own hand, as example*.

Then he read Grenmoor that morning's order, which Grenmoor had also written down. *All pens. Top
of the flood.*

"You kept a better harbor than anyone else would have," the man said. "I believe you. That's why
it has to be you."

Grenmoor drew. He was no coward, and no poor swordsman. It made no difference to the sum. The man
took the first cut on the plated back of his left glove, stepped inside the second before it was
a cut at all, and put the machete into Grenmoor below the breastbone and up, and held him there on
the drowning steps until he was finished, and then let him down onto the stone and closed the book.

That was the last spike of the hour. I have it in the Dark Ledger with nothing beside it. Now it
has a name.

• • •

He gave the book back to Mabry.

Mabry's name was in it once: a flogging, eleven years earlier, by his own hand. He had written
every other entry in that book and done the thing he wrote down exactly once. The man had read
that entry twice in the office, and moved on. The book needed a keeper. That was the whole of
the reason, and he did not pretend it was mercy.

"Keep writing," the man said. "Every name I read today. What they did. That they died, and who
did it." He tapped the book's open page with one plated finger. "Under mine."

Mabry wrote it. That book exists: the only full account of the Chain Harbor Massacre, in a dead
man's ledger, by the one officer of its garrison who lived.

• • •

Her name was Anirak. The crew would later call her Blades Fury. She had watched the whole thing --
up out of the eastern passage when the gates held, her three at her back, her knuckles split open
from the fetters, standing at the edge of the yard while he read the names, never once looking away.

She had been killing too, before the fleet came, and never pretended otherwise. But she killed the
way she does everything -- all the way in, each blow harder than the last until nothing is left in
front of her. What she watched in that yard was the opposite. A man who stopped between every one.
Who checked a book.

When it was done she crossed the yard to him, and he turned, and their eyes met.

Everyone who looks at her is caught. It is not a thing she does; it is a thing she is, the way
heat is a thing Torian is, and she has never been able to tell how much of what anyone gave her
was given and how much was taken. His attention snagged on her like anyone's. He noticed it go, and
set it aside, the way he sets aside the stamped value of a debased note to see what the coin weighs.

"Your eyes pull," he said. "I felt it. I've taken it out of the count." He looked at her hands,
not her face. "What's left is that you were breaking those chains before anyone came."

She said nobody had ever told her that before. That they felt it.

"Then nobody's ever told you anything true about it," he said. "They put you in a harness to keep
the blows from adding up."

"It's the only thing they've ever done with me."

"I'd build the opposite," he said. "Something that can take what you are all the way to the top
and not break. I won't take any of it off you. I'd make something to hold it."

She asked what it would cost her.

"Nothing you'd have to stop being," he said.

• • •

That is the forge rhythm in the shoulders, and the three days without sleep.

He took the garrison's own forge -- it had made the fetters for six pens; it was a good forge --
and worked it for most of three days with Living Drakma from the fleet's stores. Two hook-swords
on chains, keyed to her pulse, built to warm and tighten as her heart climbed instead of fighting
it. A gorget set with crystal nodes that hummed below hearing, so anyone in front of her would
misjudge where the chains were and feel the floor tilt without knowing why. And a mace whose
head turned through three shapes at a twist of the wrist -- talons, lantern, opening crown --
because a perimeter, he told her, needs more than one way to punish whoever crosses it.

She tested the hook-swords in the yard where he had read the names. The chains began to glow along
their links, dull forge amber and then brighter, their sound in the air one continuous shriek,
and nothing she did could make them fail.

That is where his heart lifted. Not during the hour. Not on the drowning steps. In the same yard,
three days later, watching something he had made hold.

Her three did not join the crew that week. They joined her. When Valen asked them plainly whose
orders they would take, they looked at her before they answered. The man saw it and let it stand,
and said nothing. He does that when he likes what he sees and does not want to make it smaller
by naming it.

• • •

Dark Ledger. Somewhere a little short of the eight-hundredth million second.

His heart at rest. Then the spike. More than forty, inside one hour, the pulse never leaving rest
but once.

Reconciled. Dunmore and the men at the west wheel, but for the one who knelt. The names in the
yard. Skarrow on the gatehouse steps. Edric Grenmoor on the drowning steps, last. The wound:
a hook-knife, closed with a belt pouch, a scar along his left forearm.

Against them: something over nine hundred people in six pens, wet to the knee, all of them breathing.

The stories say Chain Harbor was a rage. I have the count, and there was no rage in it anywhere. It
was a man reading a book aloud until he reached the end, and then closing it.

Memory is the receipt. Mabry kept it. Every name in it is right.
