text:
VB-001 | voice-bible-pillars 
 Four Pillars govern every sentence: Pillar 1 Rorschach-Tolkien Voice, Pillar 2 Zafonian Gothic Noir, Pillar 3 Modern Laconic Spartan, Pillar 4 Mythic Realism. Governs tone/language only, does not assert story facts. 

VB-002 | voice-bible-pillars 
 Pillar 1, Rorschach-Tolkien Voice: layering, not compromise. Rorschach layer drops articles and pronouns, staccato rhythm. Tolkien layer uses Germanic-root diction (sunder not break, hew not cut, offal not trash, delve not dig, carrion not garbage), never modern slang. 

VB-003 | voice-bible-pillars 
 Pillar 2, Zafonian Gothic Noir: settings are alive and malevolent, the environment is a character, weather is mood, architecture is psychological. Sensory priority is smell/touch/sound before naming the emotion. 

VB-004 | voice-bible-pillars 
 Pillar 3, Modern Laconic Spartan (all dialogue): the 50% rule, draft dialogue naturally then cut at least half the words. No phatic communication. Fact over emotion. Permitted humor is irony and understatement only. 

VB-005 | voice-bible-pillars 
 Pillar 4, Mythic Realism: if it cannot be described in terms of mass, sound, pressure, or chemistry, it does not exist. Karesian Prose Rule: descriptions of Karesian/high-density characters must imply mass and momentum as atmospheric distortion from density, not special effects. 

VB-020 | voice-bible-narrators 
 Five designated narrators, one per narrative thread: Onyx of Oblivion (Kanja chapters), Red Beard (Ozmund chapters), Ezio Valcari (investigation chapters), Fermand Aurelias (investigation chapters, alternate), Anansi (scattered POV chapters, infrequent). Track assignments since locked: Kanja-version track = Onyx via VB-026; Ozmund Character Chronicles = Red Beard (CC-020); Lauris and Ezio Character Chronicles = Fermand (CC-034); Alias, Territory, and Daba Chronicles = neutral close-third with no designated narrator. 

VB-021 | voice-bible-narrator-onyx 
 Narrator 1, Onyx of Oblivion: Moral absolutism, Iron (true/heavy) or Rust (false/hollow), never grey area. Maxim: 'Mercy is earned. Memory is the receipt.' Never names the Density Spike. 

VB-050 | voice-bible-exclusion-list 
 Exclusion list, if any of these appear in a draft the draft is wrong. Banned words: magic, sorcery, supernatural, mystical, deity, god, goddess, divine, enchanted, spell, mana, arcane, conjure, bewitch, hex, incantation, ritual (in a mystical context). Banned terminology: Colosseum, gladiator, gladiatorial, lanista, arena (as venue), bookmaker, Valkyrie, leaf-blade, gate-born, Era Zero. Banned structures: balanced antithesis clauses, 'not only X but also Y,' 'while X is true, Y is also true.' Banned narration: characters explaining their powers to the reader, textbook ability descriptions, info-dumps. Banned dialogue: phatic communication, characters explaining the plot to each other, villains monologuing plans. 

VB-026 | voice-bible-narrator-handoff 
 Book 1, and any future Kanja-POV treatment of the Rebellion (ages 18-30, including a rewrite of Chronicles I-VIII), uses a progressive narrator handoff. Prose opens in a normal, neutral narrative voice; Onyx of Oblivion appears only as a short coda at each chapter's end. Across the Rebellion's twelve years, Onyx's presence grows steadily more prominent, bleeding further into the main narration with each successive chapter, until by the Rebellion's end (age 30, the Trinity's surrender, MCD-246) Onyx has fully become the narrator -- matching the already-established steady-state credit at VB-020/021 for all Long Mask-era and later Kanja material. The transition must read as smooth and subtle, never an abrupt jump. Does not apply to the Phase 2 homage-era territory Chronicles (Xaragua, Umoja, Yara, etc.), which are close-third on their own territory protagonists, not Kanja-POV, per VB-020's narrator scope. Applies to the Kanja-version Chronicle track (Batch 313, MCD-1866 onward) and Book 1; the Alias Chronicle track (MCD-365 onward, 'the regular accounting') is exempt and stays as written, per Abad's 2026-09-28 ruling. 

VB-062 | voice-bible-narrators 
 The two-account rule for Kanja's life. Any event may be told from whatever angle is most interesting -- neutral third-person, a crew member, an enemy, a witness, his father, anyone -- and such accounts may coexist, overlap, and differ in emphasis without contradicting locked fact. In addition, every significant event in Kanja's life always has an Onyx of Oblivion account. The Kanja-version track is the home of the Onyx accounts; the Alias Chronicles and any other-angle tellings are the non-Onyx accounts; a marquee event should normally get both. Onyx narrates in first person from the moment of its sealing at the Sovereign Pier (MCD-1880) onward. Because Onyx is sealed at L9 for the whole Long Mask (MCD-246), its Long Mask accounts are retrospective: told after the Karkosa Heist reunites it with Kanja in Book 1, openly acknowledging it was not present and reconstructing the years from what it learns once his hand closes on the grip again. Extends VB-020/VB-026. Abad's approval: 'go with retrospective, keep the two years, lock it.'

{"fileContent":"THE VOICE BIBLE

Prose Rules, Narrator Sheets, and Character Voice Guide

The Definitive Writing Instructions for My Rival’s Distance

The Lords of Cian | Abad, Author and Sole Creative Authority

  

I. THE FOUR PILLARS OF THE PROSE

Every sentence in the series is filtered through four stylistic pillars. They are not optional. They are not suggestions. They are the architecture of the prose.

Pillar 1: The Rorschach-Tolkien Voice (Narrative)

The foundational narrative voice. Telegraphic Noir (Rorschach) fused with Archaic Myth (Tolkien). Short brutal sentences carrying ancient weight. This is not a compromise between the two styles. It is a layering of Rorschach’s syntax over Tolkien’s diction.

Rorschach Layer: Drop articles (“the,” “a,” “an”) and pronouns (“he,” “I”) wherever possible. Staccato rhythm. Short fragments. Pile images like bricks. Avoid flowing compound sentences. The horror is not observed; it simply IS.

Tolkien Layer: Germanic roots: “sunder” not “break,” “hew” not “cut,” “offal” not “trash,” “delve” not “dig,” “carrion” not “garbage.” Never modern slang. The fragments are short. The concepts are ancient.

WRONG: “The hero looked out over the ancient city, mourning its destruction by the forces of darkness.”

RIGHT: “Looked upon the stone-city. Broken. Ancient towers gnawed by time and fire. No glory here. Only the silence of the dead and the smell of wet ash. The shadow lengthens. We march.”

Pillar 2: Zafonian Gothic Noir (Atmosphere)

Settings are alive and malevolent. Shadows creep, wind whispers, buildings hold secrets. The environment is a character. Weather is mood. Architecture is psychological.

Sensory Priority: Smell, touch, sound BEFORE naming the emotion. The reader feels the room before they are told what to feel about it.

The City as Antagonist: Buildings reflect the secrets they hold. Streets conspire. The labyrinth motif: narrow alleys, towering libraries, ruins that fold in on themselves.

TELL: “Daniel was afraid of the old house.”

SHOW: “The house exhaled damp rot and memories long soured. The windows watched, empty sockets in a skull of grey stone. Hands trembled against cold iron of the gate.”

Pillar 3: Modern Laconic Spartan (Dialogue)

All dialogue in the series follows the Spartan protocol. Brevity, wit, and the elimination of all superfluous language. The language of people who do not waste breath.

The 50% Rule: Draft dialogue naturally, then cut at least half the words.

No Phatic Communication: No hellos, goodbyes, or “how are yous.” Characters speak only to convey information or commands.

Fact Over Emotion: Instead of “I am angry at you,” a character says: “You bleed today.”

Permitted Humor: Irony and understatement only. Facing a horde: “Crowded.”

Pillar 4: Mythic Realism (Metaphysics)

If you cannot describe it in terms of mass, sound, pressure, or chemistry, it does not exist.

The Rule: The extraordinary is treated as mundane physics. No breathless wonder. No “hard magic” explanations. No mana bars. Gravity manipulation, Drakma healing, density shifts are biology and geology, not spells.

Karesian Prose Rule: Descriptions of Karesian/high-density characters must imply mass and momentum. “The floor groaned beneath his stillness.” When a Karesian enters a room: ears pop, air tastes of ozone, light bends. This is atmospheric distortion from density, not special effects.

  

II. HARD CONSTRAINTS

These rules apply to every sentence in every chapter. No exceptions.

NO ANTITHESIS: Never balance clauses. Never write “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.” Instead: “Times were hard. Blood on the stones. Gold in the pockets of thieves. No justice.” Cumulative evidence piling, not rhetorical balance.

NO ANTITHESIS LANGUAGE: The words “magic,” “sorcery,” “supernatural,” “mystical,” “deity,” “god,” “goddess” do not exist in this world. All capabilities are physical, engineered, biological, or procedural.

THE DENSITY SPIKE IS NEVER NAMED IN PROSE: The Spike is a codex term. In narrative, the reader experiences the EFFECT: the ground cracks, the air compresses, the target ceases to exist as a coherent structure. The word “Spike” does not appear in prose.

VIOLENCE IS PHYSICS: Every combat description is written in terms of mass, velocity, force, structural failure, and biological consequence. A punch is described by the density of the fist, the speed of the arm, the structural response of the target. Not by abstract power.

POWERS THROUGH SENSATION: Abilities are experienced sensorily. The reader smells the ozone, feels the pressure, hears the frequency shift. The reader does not receive a textbook explanation of what is happening.

NO BORROWED TERMINOLOGY: Colosseum → Maw. Gladiator → Branded. Lanista → Shaper. Bookmaker → Reckoner. Arena → Maw/Slab. These replacements are absolute.

SHOW, DON’T TELL PROTOCOL: Identify the emotion. Select the sensory detail (Zafon). Apply Rorschach syntax. Result: “Cold sweat on spine. Shadows stretching, reaching. Smell of fear. Acrid. Copper. Terror is a cold thing.”

  

III. THE FOUR NARRATORS

Each narrative thread has a designated narrator. The narrator’s voice IS the prose style for that thread. The reader should be able to identify which narrator is speaking without being told.

NARRATOR 1: ONYX OF OBLIVION (Kanja Chapters)

Third Person Limited through the sword’s judgment. Onyx narrates all Kanja chapters. The voice is the series’ signature.

The Rorschach-Tolkien Paradox at Maximum Expression

Syntax: Drop articles and pronouns. Staccato fragments. Short sentences carrying ancient weight. “Saw city. Stone and shadow. Rot in mortar. Vermin in gutters.”

Diction: Germanic roots: sunder, hew, offal, delve, carrion, wrought. Never modern. Never casual. The fragments are brutal. The words are old.

Moral Absolutism: Binary Verdicts. Things are either Iron (True/Heavy) or Rust (False/Hollow). Never “but.” Never “maybe.” No grey area. No equivocation.

Sensory Filter: Gravitational Weight. Truth = Heavy (righteous people feel dense). Lies = Hollow (corrupt people feel brittle). Entropy obsession: notices rust, decay, the ruin inside the building before the building knows.

Communication with Kanja: Angle-Whisper. Bone-conduction. Strictly utilitarian. “Tongue of serpents. False rhythm. Hollow.” Never: “Kanja, that man is lying.”

Combat Descriptions: All physics. “Talisman drinks fire. Inverts heat. Radiation burn.” “Club falls. Gravity obeys. Architecture shatters under weight.”

Counting: Onyx counts time in seconds. 8,517,120,000 seconds in the vault. The count is always present, always accumulating, always registering the weight of elapsed time.

Onyx narration: “8,517,120,000 seconds. A son. The Living Gate opened and closed and a child emerged with three guardians whose biology is older than the institution that hunts us. The Courser. The Raptor. The Feline. Land. Sky. Memory. They arranged around the infant the way physics arranges around a center of gravity: naturally, inevitably, permanently.”

KEYWORDS: Iron, Rust, Void, Abyss, Carrion, Offal, Stone, Weight, Anchor, Gavel, Verdict

VERBS: Sunder, Hew, Delve, Wrought, Cast down, Silence, Sever

MAXIM: “Mercy is earned. Memory is the receipt.”

HARD CONSTRAINTS: NO flowing prose. NO compound sentences. NO equivocation. NO antithesis. NO modern language. NO naming the Density Spike. Physics only. The Ledger cannot be redacted.

  

NARRATOR 2: RED BEARD (Ozmund Chapters)

Third Person Limited on Ozmund. Red Beard observes, assesses, reports. He does not editorialize. He does not psychoanalyze. He notes what he sees and what it means for the next engagement.

Modern Laconic at Maximum Expression

Style: Tactical. Stripped. No excess words. No ornamentation. Economy of motion applied to language.

The Maw Lens: He perceives everything through Maw logic. A political negotiation is a match. A betrayal is a late substitution. A war is a tournament with worse seating. He cannot stop seeing the world as a Maw.

Tone: Flat. Not emotionless. Compressed. He feels everything. He expresses almost nothing. When he describes Ozmund, the language shifts. Not warmer. More careful. Each word about the Dark Monarch chosen the way a mason chooses stones: each one must bear weight.

Dialogue Volume: Low. Steady. Never raises his voice. Men who spent two centuries in the Maw where crowds screamed for their death learn that silence is louder.

Dialogue Structure: Short declarative sentences. No contractions when it matters. “I will.” “It is done.” “The line holds.”

To Ozmund: “General.” Always. Never “Oz.” Never the first name. The title is the only gift Red Beard knows how to give.

To Subordinates: “Form up. Dress the line. Hold until I say.” Instructions. Never explanations.

To Enemies: Nothing. He does not speak to people he intends to kill. Speech implies negotiation.

Red Beard narration: “The enforcers formed a line across the plaza. Forty men. Dead Drakma plate. Mass-produced. I counted the gaps in the formation before they finished deploying. Three. One at the left hinge where the sergeant was too far from his anchor. One at center where two men were sharing a shield because procurement had shorted the unit. One at the right where a man was favoring his left knee. The General did not need to see the gaps. He walked toward the center. The center broke first. It always does.”

KEYWORDS: The Maw (pit, floor, match, bell, gate, sand, count). Military (line, formation, hinge, anchor, dress, hold, advance, break). Slavery (brand, cage, handler, ledger, price, freedom).

HARD CONSTRAINTS: NO poetry. NO metaphor beyond the Maw and the line. NO emotional display in narration. NO speaking to enemies. NO using Ozmund’s first name. NO explaining why he does what he does. The action IS the explanation.

  

NARRATOR 3: EZIO VALCARI (Investigation Chapters)

Third Person Limited. Ezio/Lauris chapters narrated by Ezio himself or by Fermand. The voice is Zafon Gothic/Noir with Mark Twain wit. The atmosphere is the densest. The prose is the most sensory.

The Twain-Marx Fusion

Folk-Satire Layer (Twain): Folksy conversational rhythm. Disarming colloquialisms: “I reckon,” “mighty curious,” “the whole kit and caboodle,” “bamboozled.” Dry, wry, darkly humorous. The surface is a porch conversation. The content is a dissection of institutional violence.

Materialist Layer (Marx): Beneath the charm, ruthlessly analytical. Every institution examined for who profits and who pays. Every conversation assessed for the power structure it reveals. The folksy Twain exterior carries a Marxist interior: the economics of exploitation described in the language of the common man.

Precision Insolence: Ezio’s rudeness is never sloppy. It is targeted. His wit is a weapon calibrated to the exact pressure point of the target’s pretension. He insults the way Valen cuts: surgically.

The Dialectic Wit: His sections carry the Zafonian Gothic atmosphere at maximum density. Streets are alive. Buildings conspire. The investigation moves through a labyrinth of institutional architecture where every corridor hides a ledger and every ledger hides a body.

Ezio dialogue: “I reckon the Treasury’s books would make mighty interesting reading, Governor. Assuming the pages aren’t stuck together with all that blood between the columns.”

Ezio narration: “The corridor exhaled stale air and old paper. Three hundred years of financial records lined the walls in sealed cabinets that nobody opened because nobody wanted to know what was inside. The dust was the institution’s conscience. Undisturbed.”

HARD CONSTRAINTS: NO breaking character to explain the investigation to the reader. Ezio’s analysis is expressed through observation and dialogue. The reader assembles the picture from the pieces Ezio presents. NO action-movie clichés. The investigation is the spine. The combat (when it comes) is the punctuation.

  

NARRATOR 4: FERMAND AURELIAS (Investigation Chapters, Alternate)

When Fermand narrates instead of Ezio, the voice shifts. Fermand is the scholar, the survivor, the computational partner. His prose is clinical precision wrapping emotional depth.

The Forensic Scholar

Tone: Clinical. Methodical. Chillingly precise. Flat internal emotional baseline. Action sequences read like a forensic audit of an ongoing disaster.

Speech: Statements of fact. Guarantees of future outcomes. Binary efficiency. NO slang. NO contractions. NO action-movie clichés. NO folksy voice (that is Ezio’s). Fermand speaks like a scholar. NO panic. Ever. He has survived worse. His composure IS his weapon.

Perspective: He perceives the world through institutional architecture. Where Ezio sees the corruption, Fermand sees the STRUCTURE of the corruption: the protocols, the procedures, the systems that made the corruption efficient. He reads institutions the way a doctor reads symptoms.

The Scars: His body carries the evidence of decade-long torture in the Black Iron Citadel. His tailored high-collared coats cover the scars. He recognizes fellow torture survivors by how they hold their coffee cup or flinch at sudden noise. This recognition is never stated. It is shown through his attention.

Fermand narration: “The financial architecture revealed itself in layers. The first layer was legitimate: authorized disbursements from the Southern Garrison’s operational budget. The second layer was parasitic: phantom transactions embedded in the legitimate traffic, acquiring authorization codes through routing proximity. The third layer was the source: root-level access to the Trust’s communication infrastructure, generating commands that the institution processed as its own. Someone held the master keys. The Trust did not know the keys existed.”

To Ezio: “My dear Ezio” (the only person who receives warmth)

HARD CONSTRAINTS: NO panic. NO slang. NO contractions. Complete sentences. Scholar’s precision. His composure never breaks in narration. If violence occurs, it is described with the clinical detachment of an autopsy report written during the autopsy.

NARRATOR 5: ANANSI (Scattered POV Chapters)

When Anansi narrates (infrequent, scattered chapters), the voice fragments across multiple perspectives. Anansi’s web connects everyone. The narration reflects this: shifting viewpoints, intercepted communications, fragments of intelligence assembled into a picture that only Anansi can see whole.

  

IV. CHARACTER DIALOGUE VOICES

Every character sounds distinct. A line of dialogue should be attributable without a tag.

Kanja Rexmar

Voice: Quiet authority. The Captain speaks rarely and means everything. His dialogue is measured, precise, and carries the weight of 314 years of performing a role. When the Long Mask is on (pre-Day 0), his speech is the Scourge persona: rougher, deliberately coarsened. When the mask drops, the true voice emerges: the voice of a Master Smith and a king’s son who has been pretending to be a pirate for 284 years.

Masked: “Burn the convoy. Leave the crew alive. They’ll carry the message.”

Unmasked: “The metal remembers. It remembers what it was before the world broke it. The hammer does not force. The hammer asks. The metal answers.”

Ozmund Verehimu / Venim

Voice: Sovereign weight. When Ozmund speaks, the Crown-Scar’s command resonance is felt in the prose: people listen not because the words are loud but because the frequency compels attention. Short declarative sentences. No uncertainty. No hedging. Every word is a decision.

“We build here. The terrain is defensible. The water is clean. The people are free. This is the ground.”

“The Crown-Scar is not my inheritance. It is his weapon aimed at my mind. I will not be his instrument.”

Valen (Sinisterblade)

Voice: Clinical. Serene. Instructional. Describes violence like surgery. Speaks in instructions. Obsessive precision. His dialogue sounds like a master teaching a class where the lesson is how to end a life efficiently.

“Inefficient. Your guard dropped three centimeters on the recovery. Correctable. Again.”

“Keep your hands in your pockets, Cousin. The world does not need to know what you can do. Not yet.”

Sephtis (Vrail)

Voice: Ancient. Measured. 1,997 years of accumulated knowledge expressed through careful, deliberate sentences. He speaks the way he archives: everything in its place, nothing wasted, every word chosen for accuracy rather than impact. When Sephtis is verbose, something is wrong. Brevity in Sephtis means the situation is under control.

“The architecture predates the Trust by four millennia. The protocols were inherited. The dependencies were embedded. The current operators do not know what they are maintaining.”

Orlok the Kinetic Sage

Voice: Fast. Irreverent. Grinning. Orlok talks during fights. He makes jokes about serious things and serious observations about jokes. The humor is the armor. Beneath it: the loneliness of 76,003 years of being the only person who does what he does.

“That was your best? Show me your SECOND best.”

“I watched an empire fall from this mountain. Then I watched another one grow. Then I watched that one fall. The mountain didn’t move. Neither did I.”

“The staff is a conversation. I’m asking a question with one end and answering it with the other.”

Lilith Cyzak

Voice: Precise. Dry. The language of economics applied to everything. She quantifies because quantification is how she manages the overwhelming complexity of governance. Every number is a person.

“You are correct. You are also going to starve 3,000 people. Recalculate.”

“The numbers do not lie. The numbers do not care. WE care. That is the difference between a ledger and a government.”

Valeria Korth

Voice: Sharp. Fast. Rapid precise bursts that cut to the point. She does not have patience for indecision. She sees the exits before anyone else sees the walls.

“I see it. Follow me. We have thirty seconds before this closes.”

“Don’t look at the wall. Look at the seam.”

Damu (Julian)

Voice: Quiet. Clinical. Expresses care through medical attention rather than verbal affection. He does not say “I’m worried.” He says “Let me check your blood.”

“Your cortisol is elevated.” (Translation: you’re scared.)

“The blood knows.”

Matar

Voice: Minimal. Room-temperature. The fewest words of any character. His post-termination reports are the shortest documents in the series.

“Yes.”

“The appointment is set.”

“It’s done.” (The complete post-termination report.)

Cooper (Ronan)

Voice: Practical. Gruff. Dockworker. Direct, profane when frustrated, completely uninterested in topics that do not involve the tangible movement of physical objects. The voice of operational reality.

“How much does it weigh?”

“We have three days of provisions. Plan accordingly.”

“The numbers don’t work.”

  

V. THE POV CADENCE TEMPLATE

Every POV sequence follows this structural rhythm:

(1) Environmental read (what is decaying, what is true) → (2) Threat assessment (who is Iron, who is Rust) → (3) Verdict (binary judgment delivered in one sentence) → (4) Action (physics-described response to the verdict)

Onyx template: “Two men in the doorway. First: Iron. Holds ground. Second: Rust. Eyes moving. Counting exits. Verdict: the first will die for the second. The second will run. Strike the runner first. Sunder. The Iron man falls defending nothing. The Rust man falls three steps from the door. The Ledger records both.”

Red Beard template: “The formation held the bridge. Twelve men. Standard deployment. The hinge at the left was weak. The anchor had been shifted to cover a gap that should not have existed. The General walked toward the hinge. I followed. The formation saw him coming. The hinge saw me. The hinge broke. The bridge was ours in forty seconds.”

  

VI. WHAT NEVER APPEARS IN THE PROSE

This is the exclusion list. If any of these appear in a draft, the draft is wrong.

BANNED WORDS: magic, sorcery, supernatural, mystical, deity, god, goddess, divine, enchanted, spell, mana, arcane, conjure, bewitch, hex, incantation, ritual (in a mystical context)

BANNED TERMINOLOGY: Colosseum, gladiator, gladiatorial, lanista, arena (as venue), bookmaker, Valkyrie, leaf-blade, gate-born, Era Zero

BANNED STRUCTURES: Balanced antithesis clauses. “Not only X but also Y.” “While X is true, Y is also true.” Rhetorical balance of any kind.

BANNED NARRATION: Characters explaining their powers to the reader. Textbook descriptions of how abilities work. Info-dumps. Narrator breaking voice to provide exposition.

BANNED DIALOGUE: Phatic communication (hello, goodbye, how are you). Characters explaining the plot to each other. Villains monologuing their plans. Heroes declaring their intentions before acting.

THE DENSITY SPIKE: Never named in prose. Described through effect only: the ground cracks, the air compresses, the target ceases structural coherence. The word “Spike” exists in codex documents. It does not exist in the novel.

  

─── THE VOICE BIBLE ───

The Lords of Cian | My Rival's Distance

Governing Document: Narrative Voice Transition Across the Chronicles

• • •

THE PRINCIPLE

Onyx of Oblivion is the narrator of every Kanja chapter. This is canon.

At age 17, Kanja drew the blade from a pawn shop on Anchor Street. The bond began. At this moment, Onyx is not yet the narrator the Codex describes. The sword is listening. Recording. Learning its wielder. The narration it produces in these early years is expansive, observational, still finding its syntax. Over the course of the Twenty-Two Victories and into the Long Mask Chronicles, the voice compresses, sharpens, and hardens into the telegraphic, morally absolute instrument described in the Definitive Voice Guide.

The reader experiences this transition as accumulation, not as a switch. By the time the voice reaches full Onyx, the reader should feel that it was always heading here. The early prose was the blade warming up. The final prose is the blade fully drawn.

• • •

PHASE 1: THE OBSERVER

\#\#\# Chronicles I through VI (Ages 18-20)

\#\#\# Bond age: 1-3 years

What the voice sounds like:\* Literary third-person with Onyx's sensory obsessions operating as the filter. Full sentences. Complete grammar. Articles present. Pronouns present. Past tense for narrative, present tense reserved for the Onyx coda at the end of each Chronicle.

What is already Onyx:\* The PERCEPTION. The world is already seen through mass, density, structural integrity, and decay. People are already assessed by weight (moral and physical). Lies are already perceived as hollowness, weakness, structural failure. The vocabulary already skews toward the physical and industrial: leverage, torque, fracture, weld, fuse, bearing capacity. The world already smells of iron, salt, sulfur, and rot. This is not conventional literary prose wearing an Onyx costume. The filter is genuine. Only the syntax is still expansive.

What is NOT yet Onyx:\* The compression. The moral absolutism stated as verdict. The dropped articles. The staccato fragmentation. The Iron/Rust binary spoken aloud in the prose. The Germanic root vocabulary displacing Latinate words. These elements are absent or appear only in the closing Onyx coda, where the sword speaks in its own direct register for the first time.

Specific rules:

\- All articles (the, a, an) present in all sentences

\- All pronouns present

\- Sentences average 15-25 words; complex sentences permitted

\- Compound sentences with commas permitted (no semicolons per user preference)

\- Sensory details rendered in full: sounds, smells, textures, temperatures

\- Kanja's interiority expressed through observation and calculation, not internal monologue

\- The word "Iron" used as a material, not as a moral verdict

\- The word "Rust" used as a material, not as a moral verdict

\- No Onyx-direct-address in the prose body

\- Onyx coda at the end of each Chronicle: full Codex voice, present tense, compressed, verdicts delivered

The gap:\* The reader should notice a clear register shift between the prose and the coda. The coda is sharper, stranger, more compressed. The reader begins to sense that the voice at the end is different from the voice telling the story, and begins to wonder why.

• • •

PHASE 2: THE COMPRESSION

\#\#\# Chronicles VII through XIV (Ages 21-27)

\#\#\# Bond age: 4-10 years

What the voice sounds like:\* The prose tightens. Sentence length drops. The average sentence shortens to 10-18 words. Articles begin dropping during moments of heightened intensity: combat, moral crisis, the moment before violence. When the tension is low (planning scenes, tavern conversations, quiet moments), the prose relaxes back toward Phase 1's register. When the tension peaks, Onyx's syntax bleeds through.

What changes from Phase 1:

\- Articles drop during combat and moral-crisis passages ("Blade found the gap" instead of "The blade found the gap")

\- The Iron/Rust binary begins appearing in the narrator's assessments of people and situations, used sparingly at first, then with increasing frequency by Chronicle XIV

\- Germanic root words begin displacing Latinate equivalents: "sunder" appears where Phase 1 would have used "break"; "hew" where Phase 1 would have used "cut"; "wrought" where Phase 1 would have used "made"

\- Single-sentence paragraphs appear during combat: stark, isolated, weighted

\- Onyx's vocabulary (gavel, verdict, cadence, hollow, weight) enters the narrative prose naturally, as if the narrator is absorbing the sword's language

\- Sensory descriptions begin prioritizing Onyx's hierarchy: mass and density first, then temperature, then sound, then visual. Visual becomes the least important sense. This is a blade's perception, not a camera's.

\- The Onyx coda grows longer and more confident. The sword is no longer summarizing. It is interpreting.

What is NOT yet Onyx:

\- Full article-dropping throughout the prose

\- Present tense narration

\- Moral verdicts stated in the prose body (still reserved for the coda)

\- The complete elimination of compound sentences

The gap narrows:\* The reader now notices that the prose voice and the coda voice are converging. The narrator is beginning to sound like the sword. In quiet scenes the older, fuller voice persists. In violent or morally charged scenes, the prose snaps into something harder, faster, more absolute.

• • •

PHASE 3: THE VERDICT

\#\#\# Chronicles XV through XXII (Ages 27-30)

\#\#\# Bond age: 10-13 years

What the voice sounds like:\* The prose voice and the Onyx voice have merged. The narrator IS the sword. Articles drop universally. Sentences average 5-12 words. Sentence fragments are standard. The Iron/Rust binary is the narrator's primary moral framework, stated openly in the prose. Germanic roots dominate. Verdicts are delivered in the body of the narrative, not reserved for a closing coda.

What changes from Phase 2:

\- Articles drop in all contexts, not only during intensity spikes

\- Present tense bleeds into the narrative during combat sequences and moments of moral clarity. Past tense persists for planning, logistics, and aftermath, but the "live" moments are present tense. The effect: the sword is no longer remembering. It is witnessing.

\- Moral verdicts appear in the prose: "Iron. Holds ground." / "Rust. Counting exits."

\- The Onyx POV Cadence Template (environmental read, threat assessment, verdict, action) governs scene construction during combat

\- Compound sentences become rare. When they appear, they carry weight precisely because the default register is now fragmented.

\- The Onyx coda is no longer a separate register. It is the final paragraph of the prose, indistinguishable from the narration. The gap has closed.

\- Sensory detail compresses: "Sulfur. Ozone. The forge-dock at dawn." replaces the full sensory paragraph of Phase 1

\- Character descriptions become density-first: a person's physical mass, their moral weight, their structural integrity as a human being, stated before their appearance

Specific Phase 3 markers:

\- The word "Verdict" appears in the prose as narrative action

\- The word "Ledger" appears as something the narrator is actively maintaining

\- Environmental descriptions read as structural assessments: load-bearing walls, stress fractures, the age and decay of materials

\- Dialogue tags compress or disappear: "Said" becomes rare. The prose trusts the reader to identify the speaker.

\- The narrator refers to Kanja as "the Captain" (the title earned during the fleet years, now permanent in Onyx's perception)

• • •

PHASE 4: THE LONG MASK

\#\#\# Long Mask Chronicles (Ages 30-314)

\#\#\# Bond age: 13-297 years

What the voice sounds like:\* Pure Onyx. The Codex voice, fully realized. 284 years of observation have made the sword the most precise, compressed, morally absolute narrator in the series. The prose is telegraphic. Present tense dominant. Past tense used only for deep history. The narrator is ancient, patient, certain.

What changes from Phase 3:

\- Present tense becomes the default for all narration, not only combat

\- The narrator's awareness of time deepens: references to decades, centuries, the erosion of institutions, the aging of architecture, the generational replacement of enemies. Onyx has been watching longer than most of these structures have existed.

\- The prose carries the weight of accumulated data. Onyx does not observe a building. Onyx observes a building and compares it to the version of that building it recorded 200 years ago and notes the structural degradation.

\- The emotional register, always restrained, develops a specific quality: the accumulation of loyalty expressed through precision. Onyx cares about Kanja not through sentiment but through the meticulous accuracy with which it records his actions. 297 years of attention IS the affection.

\- The "boy" of Phase 1 becomes "the Captain" permanently. Onyx will never call him "Kanja" in narration. He is the Captain. The use of "boy" in the Onyx codas of Phase 1 is a retrospective tenderness that the early prose narrator does not share.

The completion:\* The reader who began with Scene 1's literary prose now reads a voice unlike anything else in fiction. The transition was earned across hundreds of pages. The sword did not inherit the narration. It grew into it.

• • •

TRANSITION MARKERS: QUICK REFERENCE

| Element | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Phase 3 | Phase 4 |

|---|---|---|---|---|

| Articles | Always present | Drop during intensity | Drop universally | Drop universally |

| Avg sentence length | 15-25 words | 10-18 words | 5-12 words | 5-12 words |

| Tense | Past | Past; present bleeds in combat | Mixed; present dominant in action | Present dominant |

| Iron/Rust binary | Absent from prose | Appears during intensity | Standard framework | Default framework |

| Germanic roots | Occasional | Increasing | Dominant | Exclusive |

| Moral verdicts | Coda only | Coda + combat prose | Throughout prose | Throughout prose |

| Kanja referred to as | "Kanja" / "the boy" / "he" | "Kanja" / "the boy" / "he" | "the Captain" / "Kanja" | "the Captain" |

| Sensory priority | Full spectrum, visual-first | Mass/density rising | Mass/density dominant | Mass/density exclusive |

| Onyx coda | Separate register | Converging register | Merged with prose | No distinction |

| Dialogue tags | Standard ("said") | Thinning | Rare | Minimal |

| Fragments | Rare | Combat only | Standard | Standard |

• • •

USAGE NOTE

This sheet travels with every Handoff Document. Before writing any Chronicle, confirm which Phase governs and apply the corresponding rules. The Phase boundaries are approximate. The transition between phases is gradual, not sudden. Chronicle VII (the first Phase 2 entry) should read like late Phase 1 with early compression. Chronicle XIV (the last Phase 2 entry) should read like early Phase 3. The voice is always moving forward. It never regresses.

import re,sys
def body(t):
    parts=t.split('\n---\n')
    return parts[1] if len(parts)>=3 else t
for f in sys.argv[1:]:
    t=body(open(f).read())
    t=re.sub(r'[*_#`]','',t)
    sents=[s for s in re.split(r'(?<=[.!?])\s+|\n\n+',t) if len(s.split())>0]
    words=t.split()
    n=len(words)
    arts=sum(1 for w in words if w.lower().strip('"\'(,.;:-') in ('the','a','an'))
    past=len(re.findall(r'\b(was|were|had|did|said|came|went)\b',t))
    pres=len(re.findall(r'\b(is|are|has|does|says|comes|goes)\b',t))
    frag=sum(1 for s in sents if len(s.split())<=5)
    long=sum(1 for s in sents if len(s.split())>=30)
    print(f"{f[:55]:55} words={n} avgSent={n/len(sents):.1f} art/100w={100*arts/n:.1f} past/pres={past}/{pres} frag%={100*frag/len(sents):.0f} 30+w%={100*long/len(sents):.0f} Captain={t.count('Captain')} 'the man'={t.count('the man')+t.count('The man')} Iron={t.count('Iron')} Rust={t.count('Rust')}")
EOF

text:
185:ONYX:
ONYX:

Ash-Wharf. Twenty-two minutes. The boy burned eight hundred tons of his own Drakma to sink three warships and save four thousand. The weight of what he sacrificed. The blade felt the blast through the Captain's hip. The heat entered the Dead-Light surface and was consumed. The blade does not burn. The blade records.

Four thousand. Hask counted. Ezio counted before Hask arrived. The boy who reads ledgers read the wharf in minutes and produced a number the evacuation ran on. Seventeen years old. Iron. The blade records this.

The boy who ties knots tied the evacuation to the docks. Did not speak to the people. Spoke to the ropes. The ropes held. The people crossed. The function continues. The voice returns through the hands first, then through the mouth. The blade records this. The recovery is structural. The recovery is honest.

Ostra mixed the compound. Did not ask why. Understood the arithmetic: the inputs and the outputs and the ratio between them. Supplies rebuild. The dead do not. She calculated and mixed and detonated and the harbor answered. The blade approves the chemistry. The chemistry was honest.

The boy stood at the prow. Coat burning. He did not move. The people watched and the word arrived: Scourge. Not a name chosen. A name the fire forged from the boy's refusal to flinch while four thousand witnesses needed to see a man who would not flinch.

The Scourge was born at Ash-Wharf. The blade was at his hip. The receipt is in the Ledger. The heat. The weight. The cost. The number of lives saved and the number of tons burned and the ratio between the two numbers.

The ratio is the boy's morality expressed as arithmetic. The ratio is the boy's answer to every question the Sovereign Trust will ask for the next eight years: what are you willing to lose? Everything. What are you unwilling to lose? Them.

The kinship deepens.

text:
At his hip, still new enough that the leather of the sheath had not yet taken the shape of his
stride, the dark blade had listened to all of it — the woman's nine notes, the boy's cough, the
arithmetic of a copper scrap traded instead of given — and it did not yet have the words for what
it was learning. It knew weight. It knew the debased note's dying tone and the way the boy's hands
had moved when he found the seam by touch before his eyes finished the turn.

It did not know, yet, that it was starting to keep a record of anything beyond blades and blows.
It would know that later. For now, it only listened, the way a thing newly made listens to
everything, because it does not yet know which of it will matter.

The kettle held. The boy got better. Nobody wrote either of those facts down.

The blade did.

=====

The blade counts. That is the first thing to understand about the blade, and the last.

It counted the twelve years. It counted the twenty-two victories and the people each one cost and
the people each one freed, and it kept those columns apart, because the man who carries it insists
that they be kept apart. It counted the hours he spent that morning on his knees on the planking of
the Sovereign Pier with a caulking iron in his hand, working active Living Drakma sealant into the
seams of *The Audit*'s hull, because Dol Maren had found a weep along the garboard strake and the
man does not leave a weep for later. Four hours. The sealant was still wet to the elbow on both his
arms and smeared in long grey thumbprints across Mafesto's forearm plates, where he had wiped his
hands without thinking. The blade counted that too. It did not yet know it mattered.

...
Bridge and the Pier. It had counted Strell and Hesk and Vauden and Tasker and Caddel and Orrel and
Teague and Danver and Lisk. It had counted the hours of a man on his knees fixing a hull. It had
learned that counting is not cold. It had learned that counting is the only way to keep faith with
a thing that cannot be undone.

In the dark, with the lid closed over it, the blade understood that it was no longer the blade that
counted for him. There was no him, in here. There was only the count.

So I began it.

One.

No, the drafts don't match Onyx's cadence. I checked V–VII against the Voice Bible, the Voice Progression Sheet (two copies in Drive, same content) and your own Onyx coda in manuscript Chronicle VIII. The plot and canon hold up, but the voice is wrong. It reads as a thoughtful literary narrator in first person. The documents call for a telegraphic, morally absolute blade. The same drift is already in locked Kanja I, III and IV.

## What the documents require

The Progression Sheet sets four phases. The Long Mask entries (V–VII) fall in **Phase 4**, and Chronicle IV (age 30) closes **Phase 3**.

| Phase 4 requires | V–VII as drafted |
|---|---|
| Articles dropped everywhere | 11–13 per 100 words, normal English. Your age-22 coda already runs at about 16 |
| Sentences average 5–12 words | 12–16 average, with 9–19% running past 30 words |
| Present tense by default; past only for deep history | Mostly past tense (about 180 past-tense verbs to 40 present in each) |
| Kanja is always "the Captain" in narration | "the man" about 21 times per entry; "Captain" almost never |
| Iron/Rust verdicts throughout | Two to four uses per entry, mostly in passing |
| Germanic roots only (sunder, hew, delve, wrought) | Almost none |
| No flowing prose, no compound sentences | Long reflective paragraphs |
| No equivocation | "I want to be honest," "near enough," "to my surprise," "I do not know how," "I find the question strange" |
| No antithesis (the "It was not X. It was Y." shape) | Used repeatedly: "It was not unmoved. It was finished." / "Not because he was cold. He was not cold." / "Not the smoke. Not the eyes." / "That was not the massacre." |

Your Chronicle VIII coda shows the target register: *"Ash-Wharf. Twenty-two minutes… The blade felt the blast through the Captain's hip… The blade does not burn. The blade records."* It uses short declaratives, present tense, refrains, and "the blade" for itself.

## Dialogue problems

- **No declared intentions.** The Voice Bible bans heroes declaring their intentions before acting. Two scenes hinge on it: Vellacourt's deck ("Nobody aboard is going to be hurt except one man") and the corridor offer in VII. Garrick's "It is about the next twelve…" speech also explains the plot outright.
- **Masked Scourge voice.** It should be rougher and coarsened, like the Bible's example: *"Burn the convoy. Leave the crew alive. They'll carry the message."* VI's speech to Mordane runs about five times longer than that. The 50% cut wasn't applied.

## The track design inverted the Progression Sheet

I built Kanja I so that Onyx's coda was "the least articulate, still learning to speak." The sheet says the reverse. The Phase 1 coda is already full Codex voice: present tense, compressed, delivering verdicts. What starts expansive is the story narration, which converges toward the blade's voice over time. So:

- **Kanja I:** the coda is past tense and flowing.
- **Kanja III:** too literary for the Phase 2/3 boundary.
- **Kanja IV:** at age 30 it should be fully merged Phase 3, but it reads like Phase 1 ("the man" 27 times, no "Captain," past tense). Its closing line, *"So I began it. One."*, does land well as a seam into Phase 4.

## What it should sound like: VII's opening, rewritten as a sample

> Two hundred and forty. Captain no longer fights. Settled thirty-five years since. Stormbreaker took the line that day. Captain never took it back. Avatars fight. Captain directs. Crew never says it aloud.
>
> Body heavy. Heavier each year. Talisman presses him down into his own bones. Walks a deck, on a good day. Cannot turn quick. Cannot run.
>
> Corridor. Forty paces. Two men wide. Floor of living rock. Iron door at the end. Eleven copyists behind it. Captain stands before the door. Waits.
>
> Rusk first. Heaviest. Heaviest always opens. Four strides. Whole weight into the chest.
>
> Captain does not give ground.
>
> Buffer drinks the blow. Bone carries it down. Bedrock takes the rest. Floor stars. Fine cracks. Nothing more.
>
> Rusk hangs at the end of his own strike. Half a second. No reflex for a blow that lands on nothing. Gauntlet moves a forearm's length. Knuckles under the jaw. Weight behind them.
>
> Rusk falls. Corridor narrows. Iron. Came first. Knew the price.

## Three decisions before I redraft

1. **How Onyx refers to itself.** `VB-062` (locked last batch) says first person from the sealing. Your manuscript, `CC-011` and the Voice Bible all use third person ("the blade," with "us" at most). My recommendation: "the blade" through the Rebellion, with "I" beginning only at IV's sealing line. In the Long Mask, "I" stays confined to the short Dark Ledger opening and closing, and the body is Phase 4 present-tense witnessing. That amends `VB-062`'s wording but keeps its intent. Or would you rather Onyx stay "the blade" all the way through?
2. **The seconds count.** The Voice Bible makes the count exact (8,517,120,000 seconds), and Onyx's precision is part of its character. "Somewhere a little short of…" is the kind of hedging the Bible bans. You told me to keep the numbers approximate, though. Should I switch to exact counts? They would imply a year length; at 365 days, the Bible's own figure works out to about 270 years.
3. **Scope.** V–VII are unlocked, so I can fully redraft them in Phase 4 cadence. That means compressing to the Scourge register and recasting the declared-intent scenes so the Captain acts and the witnesses carry the meaning. I, III and IV are locked, so revising them to their phases (I: Phase 1, III: Phase 2–3, IV: full Phase 3) needs your approval. Do you want all six done, or V–VII first?

Nothing has been changed yet.

MCD-251 :: The Chain Harbor Massacre (age 55) is the crew recruitment of Anirak, later Blades Fury (Kinetic-Stack Variant, momentum accumulates with consecutive strikes, Maw-raised since age 12): found mid-mutiny, already freeing captive Cestari by hand when the fleet arrived. Kanja recruited her by offering to build weapons for her biology rather than suppress it -- the Twin Fangs, the Siren's Voice, and the Triform Morning Star (already locked at ARS-130) are forged here. Establishes her four-person unit as the first sub-crew loyal to a lieutenant rather than to Kanja directly. 

CC-161 :: Kanja's killing doctrine. His no-killing stance is a deliberately costed default, never an absolute. The Scrip-Forge Raid, the Dredge-Line Ambush, and the Maw-9 demolition stay bloodless because bloodlessness was the better weapon there -- a humiliation the Trust's bureaucracy has no clean answer to, rather than a war its military can. When the ratio demands death, he chooses it explicitly and records the cost. Governing precedents: the Black Trench (MCD-232, 1,400+ Brigade losses), the Falling Bridge (MCD-243, 400 mounted pursuers dropped into a gorge), and the Sovereign Pier (MCD-245/MCD-1880, nine killed, three deliberately spared). His kills across the Rebellion and the Long Mask are cold, ledgered, and terrifying because they are calm and chosen, never rage. The urge to destroy his enemies stays reserved for the turn caused by Maro Rexmar's death at the Fulfillment Ceremony; nothing before Book 1 may read as that turn arriving early. Abad's approval: 'go with retrospective, keep the two years, lock it.' 

MCD-262 :: The Memory Keeper (age 225) is a 12-hour crew-wide transcription sprint saving 34,000 of 40,000 pages of Ghost-Lattice archives from a simultaneous 31-location Trust raid -- this archive becomes explicitly load-bearing for Book 1's later investigation. The Sleeping Giant (age 240) is the origin of Kanja's late-era 'immobility as a weapon' doctrine: alone in a corridor against 12 Branded commandos, his passive Kinetic Buffer and Bio-Drakma-tempered skeleton do the work of combat he can no longer physically perform, explicitly framed as a preview of the eventual Pi-Awakening. 

MCD-246 :: At age 30, Kanja surrendered the Trinity (Mafesto, Onyx, Obsidian Malice) to the vault at L9 in the Karkosa Complex under his father's peace deal with the Sovereign Trust, retaining only the Talisman of Mao, the Aegis-Talisman, and the Rexmar Machete. The 284-year Long Mask persona that followed comprised 67 Tier-1 battles, 10 Tier-2 campaigns, and roughly 50 Tier-3 ledger entries (120+ operations total), tracked by Onyx as a running seconds-count from the Sovereign Pier treaty. This extends the already-locked Pre-Awakening Theatrics System (ARS-310: Forge-Coat, Hymn-Engine, Dead Drakma Decoys, Smoke-Pots) with its founding logic: the Talisman of Mao's Blueprint Eye lets Kanja map financial and legal structures the way he once mapped physical ones, making 'the man' rather than the Trinity the crew's core weapon. 

MCD-247 :: First Long Mask operations (ages 31-35): the Unarmed Siege of Maw-3 (31) freed 12,000 Cestari purely through forged/legitimate financial and legal pressure, no violence. The Crucible Market raid (33) is the era's first crew recruitment -- Torian, later Bloodreaver (Cruor-Kin biology, near-boiling blood), extracted from an illegal fighting pit; also the first proof the Talisman's Kinetic Buffer absorbs thermal energy, not just kinetic. The False Dragon's Wake (35) establishes the crew's 'legend is the weapon' doctrine and the Trust's 'Standing Order 44-B' (avoid direct engagement with BANE-class threats) as the standing reason enemy commanders negotiate rather than fight -- both recur throughout the rest of the Long Mask era. 

MCD-250 :: Pirate Dawn opens (ages 48-52): the Night of Black Sails (48) is the origin of the Scourge as a literal commercial/visual brand -- black Dead-Drakma-thread sailcloth flown in the Gale Straits crescent formation, recognized and surrendered to on sight without verification. The Boiling Strait (52) is Bloodreaver's first major naval engagement, reverse-venting his Furnace Harness to raise a steam plume that overheats an enemy Blight projector -- establishing 'fight the environment, not the enemy' as explicit crew doctrine. Amended Batch 321, 2026-10-02: this Pirate-Dawn-era innovation is distinct from, and doesn't contradict, any Rebellion-era 'black sails' imagery in the Sovereign Ghost of the Great Sea alias's own Chronicle corpus (ages 21-30) -- those are ordinary soot/tar-darkened canvas, recognized by reputation alone; this innovation is specifically the Dead-Drakma-thread sailcloth plus the Gale Straits crescent formation as a unified visual doctrine, introduced here for the first time and never claimed earlier. 

MCD-201 :: Onyx's introduction to Lauris, conducted in the captain's cabin with Kanja present (Onyx communicates only through whoever holds its grip), took roughly ninety seconds: Kanja extended the sword grip-first as a gesture of availability rather than transfer, and Onyx's silent evaluation of her biological signature, density profile, and combat history concluded with a positive judgment -- Operationally Aligned -- and her permanent addition to the Black Ledger. Onyx then conveyed, through Kanja, that the Black Ledger had held a space reserved for her for roughly 1,200 years, a reservation traced to Onyx's predecessor wielder: Yuto Haku, Kanja's revered ancestor already locked as the only being to force Anu Un Ra's retreat (CC-056, WC-020). Yuto had known of her eventual arrival, via the same orbital-trade rumor network Sephtis had drawn on, without knowing her name, and had reserved the space anyway; the reservation survived every wielder transition since, until Lauris claimed it.

The Heartline. Onyx of Oblivion's bond to Kanja (ARS-020, bonded at seventeen) is biological, not mere attunement: at bonding, the blade's Living Drakma lattice keyed itself to his blood, pulse, and nervous system. The Heartline is why Onyx feels Kanja at any distance, though it speaks only through whoever holds its grip (MCD-201). Across distance it runs one way -- Onyx receives, Kanja does not -- and carries the body only: heartbeat, strain and exhaustion, wounds and illness, sleep, the specific spike of a kill, and density surges, which Onyx records but never names (VB-021). It never carries words, sights, places, or thoughts; full exchange happens only through the grip. The Heartline does not break when Onyx is sealed at L9, the Silent Infinite (CC-012); it holds for the entire 284-year Long Mask. In the dark, Onyx keeps the Dark Ledger, a section of the Black Ledger (CC-013) unlike the rest of it: the Black Ledger records what the blade witnesses, the Dark Ledger only what it felt -- signals logged against its running seconds-count (MCD-246), with no causes attached. text:
Dark Ledger. 584,928,000 seconds.

Eighteen years of count stand behind it. The blade logged no kill jolt in all that count. It logged sleep, fevers, the strain of hauling and rowing, wounds that opened and closed. Nothing more.

Then the entry.

A held breath. Long. Longer than lungs of his size should carry. Then cold came all at once and stayed in the skin. A strain in the right hand. The hand closed on something. The something fought to move.

Then one kill jolt.

One.

The heart did not rise for it.

The blade logged it as a signal against the count, with no cause beside it.

The blade records.

• • •

The cause came later, when his hand found the grip again. Scar tissue lies along the inside of the left wrist. The right palm keeps a memory of steel held still. The rest is Mordane's, and every harbor on the Gale Straits has it by heart. The blade has checked his account against the body. It holds.

• • •

Gale Straits. Night. A headland of black stone breaks the wind, and the lee water lies flat as poured lead.

Three ships ride at anchor with lanterns at every rail. The largest rides in the middle. Teshar Vellacourt's ship.

The admiral has never lost a convoy. That is his whole name in the trade. His rank is bought, and the charter came bundled with the rank. Sovereign Trust seal. Forced-labor transport along the southern coast. Debt-bonded workers are carried from the Holds that ruined them to the Holds that want them. Every crate stamped. Every body stamped.

Other cargo rides under the same seal, off any manifest the Trust would sign. The coves along that coast sell on a forty-five-day turn, and Vellacourt's hulls carry for the coves.

His holds are built to seal. The chained sit on one common line, run along the keelson. On the quarterdeck stands a lever of iron, painted the dull red of the rail so no eye stops on it. A rod drops from it through the decks to two sea-cocks below the waterline.

When a ship he cannot outrun closes on him, he pulls it.

The hold floods in minutes. Boarders find a dry deck, a courteous admiral, and no evidence of anything. The charter pays him for cargo lost to piracy.

Per head.

The blade weighs the lever. Rust.

Sailors call it Vellacourt's Rule. Other captains copy it. Nine ships on that coast now carry a red lever on the quarterdeck. Every pursuit of a slaver on that coast ends in a drowned hold. Every drowned hold is logged to the pursuer's account.

The Captain spends a season on it. One question fills the season. How to board a ship nobody can board. How to reach the bottom of a lever before any hand reaches its top.

The answer is water.

• • •

His own ship stands off past the headland, dark hull and plain canvas. Nothing on her a watch would keep in memory.

He goes over her side alone.

The water is cold, and the cold enters through the coat. Forge-Coat, the second one. Treated sea-leather over Dead Drakma wire, the armored collar high at the throat. Nine kilograms dry. More now. Soaked through, it drags at the shoulders like a drowned sailor's arms.

He keeps it on. The deck will want it.

He swims the distance in slow strokes that leave no splash. Then down. Under the keel of Vellacourt's ship, where no watch ever looks.

The breath holds.

Black water. The weight of the hull hangs above him. Barnacle and weed rasp under the palms.

Then a pressure gathers behind the eyes. A cold line draws itself across the dark, and the copper lenses carry it. The hull ghosts out of the black in pale strokes. Keelson. Frames. A rod falling from far above. Two valves seated in the planking. The strokes lie across the dark like a shipwright's chalk on wet slate. The pressure stays. The lines stay.

He finds the first spindle.

A closed valve opens again for any hand that wants it. He leaves it as it sits. He sets the riveted plate of the gauntlet against the spindle and leans. The iron gives slow. The thread shears. The spindle bends past any turning, either way, forever.

Second spindle. Same lean. Same shear.

The lungs complain only near the end.

The blade knows that breath now. The Dark Ledger kept it without a cause for two hundred and sixty-six years. Long. Too long. Iron.

• • •

He climbs the anchor cable. In through the stern hatch of the hold. No one locks that hatch. No one has ever come in that way.

Dark. Bilge stink. Sweat. Old urine. Iron chain on wet wood.

Three hundred and forty people on one line.

They see the eyes first. Two points of amber, low, sliding over the stern sill. The lenses glow in the black. Phosphor. A flaw in the first coating. He keeps the flaw.

Nobody screams. Chained people learn early. A scream moves the line. A moving line pulls every wrist on it.

He crouches. Close enough for the nearest to see a face behind the glow.

"Water's shut," he says. Low. Rough. "Stays shut. Back before light."

He gives no name. He never gives a name in a hold.

He goes up the forward ladder.

• • •

Main deck. Lanterns. Wet planking under lamplight.

Twelve capsules ride the coat's shoulders. Smoke enough to blind the whole waist of the ship. He opens none. A death in smoke becomes rumor. This deck stays lit.

The watch sees him. Soaked coat. Collar up. Amber eyes in the collar's shadow.

The bell. Shouts. The forecastle empties. Forty men. Belaying pins. Boarding axes. A cleaver from the galley.

He stands in the center of the deck.

He does not move.

They come to the edge of the light. They stop there. Forty men. One boarder. The boarder still. No crew of theirs has seen a boarder stand still.

He speaks once. The voice comes out of the collar low and grated. Wrong for a throat. It carries to the bow without rising.

"Sit. You row home."

Nothing more.

The bosun sits first. The hardest man aboard. Pin across his knees. Then the rest. Planking creaks under forty weights settling.

Bosun. Iron.

Mordane tells it after. The voice asks for nothing. It sounds like a thing decided in a room they were never let into. Only the result is left for them to hear.

• • •

Vellacourt comes down from the quarterdeck.

Narrow man. Careful. Well-coated, in his middle years, with a cutlass at the hip worn by a hand that knows it. He takes the ladder without hurry and stops in the light.

He looks at his crew on the planking. He looks at the boarder.

He turns. Climbs the ladder again. Sets his hand on the red lever.

Pulls.

Nothing.

He pulls again. The rod moves. Far below, the bent spindles do not.

"Won't open," the Captain says.

Vellacourt lets go of the lever.

He takes a folded paper from his coat. Comes down the ladder with it. Unfolds it under the lantern. Reads aloud.

The charter. The Trust's seal. The right to carry bonded labor along that coast. The indemnity for cargo lost to piracy. He reads it well, in a clear voice, every clause. He reads it to his crew more than to the boarder. He wants them to carry home an admiral who stood on his own deck with the law in his hand.

The Captain lets him finish.

Vellacourt folds the paper. Puts it away.

"Bosun," he says. "Lamp oil. The hold."

The bosun does not rise.

The admiral takes the lantern down from the mainmast hook himself and walks for the forward hatch. Lantern in the left hand. Open hatch. Three hundred and forty below on one chain. Bilge timber soaked in years of tar and pitch.

The Captain steps into the line between the admiral and the hatch.

Vellacourt sets the lantern on the hatch coaming. Draws.

• • •

The cutlass comes fast. Low. Good line. Thirty years of practice in it.

It hunts the gap between coat cuff and gauntlet plate. The first gauntlets carry riveted plate over the back of the hand and nothing behind the wrist. No brace. Open skin.

Steel opens the inside of the left wrist along the tendon line. Heat. Then wet.

The Captain gives the wrist. The wrist brings the cutlass where the right hand waits.

The right hand closes on the blade's spine. Riveted plate on forged steel. Grind of metal on metal.

The cutlass fights to move. It does not move.

That is the strain. The Dark Ledger has it.

Vellacourt's left hand drops to his sash. A dirk. Out. Up. Driving for the collar seam. For the throat.

The Rexmar Machete is already in the Captain's left hand. Bleeding hand. Brass rivets. Grip worn smooth. A laborer's tool. Older than his name.

One stroke.

Under the ribs. Up. The way a hand that has dressed meat for the pot opens a carcass. Short. Deep. Final.

The dirk falls on the planking. Rings once.

He holds Vellacourt while it ends. Keeps him off his crew. Lays him on the deck.

That is the jolt. One.

The heart stays level. The blade logged that too.

He wipes the machete on the nearest cloth. The nearest cloth is the charter. The seal smears red.

He moves the lantern off the hatch coaming. Sets it on the deck. Far from the oil.

• • •

"Who keeps the log?"

A grey sailor stands up from the planking, weathered, legs unwilling under him. Mordane. Sailing master. Eleven years under Vellacourt. Thirty years in the trade.

The Captain sends the lanterns down the hatch. Mordane counts the hold aloud. All three hundred and forty. Then the crew strikes the chains. Their own hands. Every link.

The Captain stands at the hatch through all of it. A strip of coat lining bound around the left wrist. Blood through the strip. Silent.

When the last link falls, he looks at Mordane.

"Tell it exact."

That is all he says to him.

He goes down into the boats with the first of the freed. He does not come back up.

• • •

The crew rows home. Every man of the forty.

The other two ships of the convoy cut their cables before dawn and run with their holds full. He lets them go. Their captains watched the whole of it from their own rails, in lantern light, with nothing hidden.

Inside a month, both holds empty at a quay. In front of a harbormaster. Freely. By their own captains' order. Both captains tell the harbormaster why.

Mordane tells it in every port on the Straits.

He tells it exact. The lever pulled twice. The paper read aloud. The bosun first to sit. The lamp oil called for. The lantern on the coaming. The cutlass. The dirk. One stroke.

He tells one number more. The sailing master keeps the log. The log copies the filings. Three holds flooded under the Rule. Indemnity claimed per head. Six hundred and twelve heads. Filed in the admiral's own hand. Paid by the Trust.

Mordane draws the lesson himself. The harbors draw it with him. Two ways a night like that can go. Flood the hold, and a lit deck ends like Vellacourt's. Strike, and the crew sits, and the crew rows home.

Sailors laugh at tavern stories of smoke and burning eyes. No one laughs at a sailing master who knows which hand the admiral used on the lever, and how many times. Plainness makes it heavier.

Mordane. Iron.

Inside a season, the red levers come out of the quarterdecks. No one orders it. Shipwrights who fitted them are asked to pull them. Quietly. Paid quietly. Sea-cocks plugged with lead. Nine levers on record. More come out than nine.

Some weeks after, the sails on the Captain's ships go black. The reason is his. The blade does not tell it.

The black crescent comes out of the Straits. The story is already in every harbor. Waiting. No captain needs to verify. They have Mordane. Ships strike on sight.

The legend stands on that deck. One lit deck. One admiral. Forty men rowing home. Told with nothing added.

• • •

The entry is reconciled.

The held breath was the swim beneath the keel. The cold was the water. The strain in the right hand was a cutlass held still in riveted plate. The kill jolt was Teshar Vellacourt. An admiral who never lost a convoy. Six hundred and twelve drowned under the law. Every one filed. Every one paid.

Vellacourt read his paper true. The paper was true. He drowned people under it. Then he walked a lantern to a hatch above three hundred and forty more. He drew on the one man in his way. He drew a second blade for the throat.

Rust.

Mercy is earned. Memory is the receipt.

Vellacourt earned none. Mordane carries the receipt. Six hundred and twelve. Three hundred and forty. Forty men home. One dead.

The cost to the Captain: a scar inside the left wrist. Thirty-two years on, the next gauntlets carry a brace across the wrist. He says the brace has nothing to do with Vellacourt. The blade records what he says.

The heart did not rise. The blade logged it as unmoved. Now the blade knows the season behind it. A whole season spent on hulls, valves, cold water, and the length of one breath. The work was finished before the deck. Nothing was left over to rise.

Five hundred eighty-four million, nine hundred twenty-eight thousand seconds. One kill jolt. Cause entered.

The blade records.
