# Anirak Chronicle I: What Maw-11 Kept

*UNLOCKED DRAFT, PENDING ABAD'S APPROVAL, 2026-10-04. First entry of Anirak's Character Chronicle
series (Game Plan pitch 2, locked at Batch 372). Close-third on Anirak per `VB-065`. Kanja age 140,
the Long Mask, the Maw Cascade's inside job at Maw-11 (`MCD-264`). Her first marquee kill under
`MCD-1881`, a `CC-164` necessity kill fought at Warm. New named character: Gethin Brule, the tunnel
master of Maw-11, collision-checked against the full ledger and Chronicle corpus. Anirak, the Captain,
Ghostwind (Sylas), Edda, Hamund, and Odile reused. No child-safety issues. Not canon until approved.*

---

The table in the Captain's cabin was too small for the map. She drew it anyway.

Charcoal on the planks. A ring for the Slab. A square for the yard. A long bar for the pen block,
four tiers deep, under the hill. A spike of a line for the mast that stood over the pens.

She did not sit. She walked the table's edge while she drew, round and round, the charcoal never
lifting long.

Ghostwind leaned in the doorway. Sylas, twenty-nine, the wind-harness slack on his shoulders and the
disc on his breastbone ticking now and then as the weather shifted outside. He watched the lines go
down. The Captain stood at the stern window with his back to them both.

"Front gate." Her finger on it. "Yard. Slab. Three doors off the yard. Two go to the armories. One
goes down."

"Down where?"

"The tunnels. Staging, then the pens." She drew the tunnels. Not the main run. The other ones. The
drains under the staging floor. The old feed chute, bricked at the top and open at the bottom. The
gap behind the triage station where the wall had settled and nobody had cared. "Ninety-one steps from
the chute to the first grate. Dark the whole way."

"You walked it."

"I counted it."

He looked at the drawing a long while. Then at her.

"Every eye at Maw-11 knows your face."

"Every eye anywhere."

That was true. She had seen it in every harbor since Chain Harbor. Faces turned when she passed.
Stayed turned. She never knew which of them had chosen to.

The Captain spoke without turning from the window. The collar was off, so the voice came out plain,
low and rough.

"So you go in the front."

"Yes."

"And they all look at you."

"Yes."

"And nobody looks at him."

Ghostwind smiled at that, a little. He had a roll of oilcloth under his arm. He set it on the table
and opened it. Bronze reeds, thirty of them, each the length of a hand. A pen-worker could hide one
in a fist.

"Tuned to their mast," the Captain said. "Off the Trust's own books."

She picked one up. Blew across it once. No sound she could hear. The table hummed under her palms.
She knew that hum. It was the low one the crew sang at the oars. It was close to her own.

She set it down.

"They sing it in the pens," she said.

"They sing it. The weight comes off them. They walk."

She knew the weight. Every Branded under that mast knew it. Heavy in the limbs. Slow in the blood. A
body that could break iron, and could not lift its arms high enough to try.

"How long."

"Ghostwind needs an hour below. They need a quarter of one to learn the note." He turned at last.
"You hold the yard that long."

"Cost?"

"Don't stop moving."

• • •

Maw-11 sat in a fold of the coast hills, a day's sail south of the Brinewell roads. Grey stone. Low
walls. A regional house, small beside the great Maws of the capital. Three thousand eight hundred
Branded in its pens. A handful of bouts a month. A steady trade.

She came up the road at dusk with her three behind her. Edda. Hamund. Odile. No hoods. No stealth.

The smell reached her first. Before the walls. Before the gate. Lamp oil and old sweat. Wet straw
gone sour. Iron, and the copper underneath iron that is blood dried a long time. The smell had not
changed. It went into her nose and down into her chest and lay there.

The mast stood over the hill behind the walls, black against the last light. Taller than she
remembered. A thin pole with a box at the top. Nothing came off it that a person could see or hear.
She felt it all the same. A pressure behind the eyes. A drag in the shoulders. Faint, out here.
Stronger every step.

Her hands wanted to slow. She did not let them.

Two gate guards. Spears grounded. Lanterns on hooks.

The first one looked up. His face turned to her and stayed turned. His mouth opened. The spear-butt
slid on the stone and he caught it late.

The second one looked. Same.

She walked between them. Neither moved until she was past.

Behind her, Edda and Hamund took the gate. Odile put her back to the hinge post. The gate would not
close tonight.

• • •

The yard. Packed sand over stone. Raked smooth in rows. Lamps on poles at the corners. The Slab in
the middle, a raised floor of fitted blocks, stained dark in the seams. The smell of it stronger here.
Old blood in the sand. New blood on the Slab's edge from the afternoon's work.

Forty men in the yard. Slab crews at the reset carts, sweeping. Guards at the armory doors. A knot of
handlers at the water trough, cups in hand.

Every face found her.

Cups stopped halfway. Brooms stopped. The noise of the yard went out like a lamp in wind. They stood
with their faces on her, and the pull went out of her eyes and into them, and some of it came back.
She felt it come back. It always did. Forty men looking at her as if she were the only thing in the
world. She could not tell how much of that was hers.

Someone said it. Then several.

"Blades Fury."

She kept walking. Along the Slab's edge. Not toward anyone. Around.

The guards at the armories came off the doors. Eight of them. Spears and hook-poles. Then the
handlers from the trough, with clubs off the rack. Then the Slab crews with their iron reset bars.
Thirty, thirty-two. The rest stayed where they were and watched.

She read them as she walked.

The guards: drilled. They spread to flank. They would come together.

The trough handlers: bold with numbers, slow with clubs. They would come behind the guards.

The crews: afraid. They would come only if the others went first.

Her verdict was one sentence. Keep them all in the yard, and keep them all alive.

She let the Fangs down off her forearms. Chain ran through her fingers. The hook-swords hung at her
knees and swung there, cold.

The first guard came in fast with his spear low. She did not wait for him. She went to him.

A Fang went out on its chain and hooked his forearm behind the wrist. She pulled. The arm came across
his body, the spear with it, the point turned into the sand. Her free hand had already gone over her
shoulder. The Morning Star came off her back in its talon shape and caught the spear-shaft where the
arm had brought it. She twisted. The shaft left his hands. He went past her, empty, and sat down hard.

One.

The hook came back to her on its chain, and its weight came back with it, and she fed the weight into
the next throw.

The chains warmed. She felt it in the links where they crossed her fingers. Dull heat. Her heart
went up a step.

Two guards at once. She ran the Fangs in a figure-eight, left and right in turn, crossing in front of
her. The air moaned through the links. One hook took a spear out of a man's grip and threw it end
over end into the dark. The other opened a forearm to the bone. He dropped his pole and held the arm.

Two. Three.

Each strike landed and loaded the one after. Her body did not tire. It gathered. Every blow she gave
and every blow she took went into the next one, heavier, faster.

A hook-pole came at her from behind. She felt the air move. She stepped into the swing, inside the
hook, and took the shaft across her shoulder. The blow went into her and stayed in her. She turned
with it and gave it back through the Star into the man's thigh. He went down sideways.

Four.

The rest bunched. Six handlers with clubs, a guard on either end. They meant to rush her together.

She let her voice go.

It came from low in her throat, under hearing. The crystal nodes in the gorget took it up and laid
it out ahead of her like a blade of water. The handlers felt it in their chests first. Then in their
feet. The sand tilted. The lamps swung in their eyes though the lamps were still. The man in front
judged her six paces off and stepped back to be safe. She was four paces off. He stepped back into
the hooks.

She opened the Star's head wide and swept it through them. Clubs went out of hands, spinning. Men
went to their knees in the sand and stayed there with their heads down, sick, breathing hard. A
guard tried to rise. He looked at her, and his face held there. He sat back down.

No one came again.

She kept moving. Round the Slab. Round again. The men on the ground lay still. The ones still standing
at the edges stood still. Every face in the yard was turned to her.

The chains glowed now along their links. Dull amber. Her heart sat high and steady in her throat.

Warm. Not past it. She knew the line. She had lived on its near side every day since Chain Harbor.

• • •

She felt the chant before she heard it. She never heard it at all.

It came up through the stone under the sand. A hum below the floor of sound. It sat in her ribs the
way her own voice sat in other people's. Faint at first. Then more voices. Then many.

The pens were singing.

She knew what it was doing because her body told her. The drag behind her eyes was thinning. The weight
in her shoulders was going out of them. Down there, under the mast, three thousand eight hundred bodies
were lifting their arms for the first time in years. Down there, men who could break iron were
remembering it.

Ghostwind had found them. Ghostwind had given them the reeds.

She kept walking. Round the Slab.

Then the hum broke.

Not all of it. A piece. A hole torn in the low note, near the first grate. Voices stopping. Then
starting. Then stopping again.

Someone was at the grate. Someone the singers were afraid of.

She looked at the third door off the yard. The door that went down. It stood open. It had been shut
when she came in.

One man had not stayed to watch her. One man had gone below.

She knew who held the keys to that door.

She broke off. Her chains came up off the sand. She went through the door at a run, and the heat in
the links did not climb any higher.

• • •

Gethin Brule ran the tunnels at Maw-11. He had run them in her years there. He ran the staging. He
ran the armory keys. He ran the pens.

He was a free man. A careful one. He knew every Branded in his tunnels by their number, and every
number by its price. Nothing left his tunnels he had not counted.

He had been in the tunnels below when the singing started. He had felt it in the floor, the way she
had. He had known what it was. He had heard of the Blackout. Every tunnel master in the south had.

He did not run for the yard. He took a hook-pole off the staging rack and went toward the pens.

• • •

The tunnel. Stone close on both sides. The ceiling low enough that tall men stooped. Lamps far apart,
most of them out. Water running down the walls and pooling in the worn places of the floor. The
smell here was the pens' smell. She had slept in it.

Ninety-one steps from the old chute. She did not need the chute tonight. She counted from the staging
floor. Forty more.

The singing filled the dark. Low. Uneven. Holes in it, opening and closing.

The first grate. Iron bars set floor to ceiling, crossbars at waist and head height, a lamp on a
bracket beside it.

Brule stood at the bars with his back to her.

Beyond the grate, the first pen. Faces at the bars. Thin faces. Brands on the inner left forearms of
the hands gripping iron. A bronze reed in a fist here and there. Some of them still singing. Some
backed away from the bars, mouths shut.

One woman stood at the front. Grey-haired, her arms scarred to the elbow. She held a reed to her lips
and sang into it, and she did not step back.

Brule had the hook-pole set through the bars. The hook was at her throat.

"Stop," he said to her. "Stop that, or it goes in."

She sang.

Anirak read it in a breath.

The tunnel: narrow, wet, one man in it.

The man: one pole, hooked, set at a throat, his weight already leaning into it.

Her verdict was one sentence. He is killing her now.

She spoke from the dark, one time.

"Leave it. Walk."

He turned his head. The lamp lit her eyes, and his face stayed turned. For a heartbeat he only looked.
She saw him know her. She saw him put a number to her, and a price, and the price was nothing he
could pay.

"Anirak," he said.

Behind the bars, faces turned to her too. The singing faltered all along the grate. The low note
thinned toward nothing.

The grey woman's voice held. She sang louder. Others found the note again around her.

Brule's eyes went back to the woman.

His shoulders set to drive the pole.

The Fang left her hand. Four paces of chain. The hook took his forearm above the wrist. She pulled.
The arm came back out of the bars across his body, the pole with it, the hook scraping the iron. The
Star was already in her other hand. Its talons closed on the shaft. She twisted. The pole went
clattering down the tunnel.

He had a knife at his belt. He drew it.

He did not turn to her. He went back to the grate, low and fast, the knife up, his arm going through
the bars for the woman's belly.

The Star swung once. All the weight of the hall behind her, the yard, the guards, every blow she had
taken and given, came through her arm into the iron head. It met the side of his skull above the ear.
The bone gave like a plank under a dropped anvil. His head went into the bars. His body went down the
bars into the water on the floor.

The knife fell into the pen. The grey woman put her foot on it.

She sang through all of it.

• • •

Anirak stood a breath. Then she remembered and did not stand. She walked. Back and forth in front of
the grate, two steps each way, so the weight would not drain out of her while the hum built.

The faces behind the bars stayed on her. She kept her own face turned down the tunnel, away from them.
The singing found its depth again.

It filled the tunnel. It filled the stone. She felt it in her teeth. The drag behind her eyes was
gone entirely now. The weight was gone from her shoulders.

In the pen, a man put his hands on two bars. Took breath. Pulled.

The iron groaned. It bent outward. Rust burst off it in flakes. Then the crossbar sheared at its
seat with a crack like a mast going in a gale.

Others came to the bars beside him.

Ghostwind came out of the dark at the far end of the tunnel, the harness humming faintly on his back.
He looked at the body at the grate. He looked at her.

"Pens two through four are singing," he said. "Pen four's grates are already down."

"The yard's clear."

"Then they walk."

He was gone again, fast, the air sucking after him.

• • •

They walked.

Up through the staging tunnels and out the door to the yard. Grey faces, scarred arms, bare feet on
packed sand. They walked past the men still kneeling sick by the Slab, and none of those men moved.
They walked past the reset carts and the trough and the dark armory doors. They walked out through
the gate where Edda and Hamund stood aside to let them pass, and Odile kept her back to the hinge
post, and the gate stayed open.

Three thousand eight hundred.

Some of them looked at her as they passed. Their faces turned and stayed turned until the gate took
them. A few of them she knew. A scar. A way of walking. A number she had heard called across the sand.
They knew her too. They did not say her name. Out on the road, someone was already saying the other
one.

The grey woman passed last of her pen. She stopped in front of Anirak. She had the reed still in her
fist.

She held it up a moment. Then she put it in her shirt and walked on.

• • •

The Captain waited on the hill road beyond the gate, with the wagons and the crew. Coat on now. The
collar closed. The amber eyes burning dull in the dark of the hood.

The people went past him in a long grey river. He watched every one.

She came out last, her three behind her. Her chains hung cooling at her knees.

"Count," he said. The collar ground the word down to gravel.

"Three thousand eight hundred."

"And."

"One."

He looked at her a long moment. The pull went into him. She watched him feel it go, and put it aside,
and look at her hands.

"Who."

"The man with the keys. He had a hook at a singer's throat."

"Terms?"

"Once."

He nodded once. He turned back to the road and the river of people on it.

She stood beside him and did not stand still.

The mast stood over the empty pens behind them. Nothing came off it now that any of them could feel.

---

*Continuity notes (not narrative): dramatizes Maw-11 (`MCD-264`, Kanja age 140), the third of the
Maw Cascade's four liberations, for the first time anywhere. `MCD-264` locks it as an inside job using
Ghostwind's infiltration and a Hymn-Engine counter-frequency device, 3,800 freed, Maw-11 being
Anirak's former facility; this entry adds her part, which `MCD-264` does not name (flagged as a new
fact for the lock rule): she mapped Ghostwind's route from her own knowledge of the tunnels, and,
unable to go in unseen (`CC-112`), went in openly by the front gate as the visible draw, holding the
yard's guards and handlers while Ghostwind worked below. The counter-frequency device is rendered as
thirty bronze reeds tuned to the facility's suppression mast "off the Trust's own books" -- the
Calibration Theft's stolen manuals (`MCD-265`, age 108) -- carried in by Ghostwind and sung by the
pens themselves: the Hymn-Engine's synchronized-voice cancellation of Blight Frequency suppression
(`ARS-398`, `MCD-236`, `MCD-237`) under its precision-beam doctrine (`MCD-248`), here an inside job
in the literal sense. That the Maw's Branded are held under Blight Frequency suppression matches the
"Tether-managed levels" of `ARS-377` and the standard suppression of `MAW-131`; the bent and sheared
grates show freed Cestari at true biological density. The Calibration Theft precedes this (108); Anansi's
portable generator, the Frequency Vaccine (`MCD-265`, age 180), comes later and is not used. Ghostwind
at 29 (recruited at 19, age 130, `MCD-258`), with the Slipstream Harness and the Vane-Compass
(`ARS-409`); the Wind-Razors are not drawn. Her kill: Gethin Brule, a free tunnel master (a Tier 2
Backstage post per `MAW-077`, which runs tunnels, staging, and armories; handlers are "overwhelmingly"
Cestari, and Brule is one of the free exceptions), a `CC-164` necessity kill. He has a hook-pole set at
a singer's throat, is given terms once from the dark ("Leave it. Walk."), and is driving the hook when
First Payment strips the pole; he then draws a knife and goes back through the bars at her, and the
Morning Star kills him. He never turns on Anirak. Every yard fighter is disarmed or dropped and none
is killed: First Payment, Compound Interest, Siren's Draw, and Foreclosure (`ARS-441`), Foreclosure
lethal only to those who keep coming (`CC-164`), and no one keeps coming. Warm throughout: the chains
reach dull amber, her heart high and steady, and she breaks off the yard before her heat climbs further
(`ARS-441`, `ARS-373`); Fangs used at four paces, the low-to-middle reach; no sync, no active sonar. No
stillness: she paces the planning table, circles the Slab, and walks the grate while the hum builds,
the fiction showing Stack draining when she stops (`ARS-439`). Stack shown through sensation (blows
gathered and fed forward), never named. Her Voice felt in the body, shaped by the gorget into a forward
cone, the distance misjudgment putting a man inside the hooks (`ARS-438`, `ARS-411`); her kit on her
body as `ARS-439` sets it, the Star across her back. Her own hum recognized in the Hymn-Engine's low note
(`ARS-438`); the crew's oar-chant reference echoes the Hymn-Engine's work-chant origin (`MCD-236`). The
Siren shown only as faces turning and staying turned, with her doubt about it held unresolved (`CC-112`,
`VB-065`). The epithet "Blades Fury" in public use by Kanja 140; her name spoken only by Brule, one of
those who once held her, and withheld by the freed (`CC-163`). Brule's "number by its price" alludes to
the circuit's pricing of the Branded (`MAW-079`) without naming any debt of hers. Guards: no debtor,
brand, birth community, or age of hers is named or implied; her years at Maw-11 are left uncounted. Her
three (Edda, Hamund, Odile, `MCD-1890`) hold the front gate; they do not enter the pens, and none of
them is said to have been held at Maw-11. The Captain at 140, the Scourge register (Voice Bible Section
IV), "the Captain" throughout; Forge-Coat V3 era (`ARS-348`), the Breath Collar's ground-down command
voice (`ARS-351`), Sovereign Eyes V3's amber glow in the hood shadow (`ARS-350`); he takes no part in
the fighting. His "Struck it from the count" posture toward her Siren (`MCD-1883`) recurs. Onyx sealed,
absent (`MCD-246`). Brinewell (`MCD-255`) used as a sailing reference only; Maw-11 sits in the Southern
regional Maw network, numbered apart from the capital registry (`MAW-066`). Reserved threads
untouched: Hot/White and sync, Flood State, sonar, Sereth Vaul, Vestige, Ren, her three inside Ren's
field, the undead, her age.*

text:
SBD-040 | SBD document security escalates by clearance tier: SEALBLACK down through Level 4. The title 'Doctor' is retired for SBD medical/forensic staff in favor of 'Grave-Analyst.'

SBD-047 | Extends SBD-040/WC-007/ARS-399: the SBD enforces internal compliance through a tiered Scrip-Ledger disciplinary system layered onto ordinary personnel debt (extends WC-007's Metabolic Tether mechanics from subjects to staff). Level 1, Clinical Tone Failure -- using mythic/heroic language about a subject in official contexts -- draws a Metabolic Scrip-Fine, a 15% debt increase enforced biologically rather than merely on paper. Level 2, Repeated Subject Agency -- treating a subject's will or personhood as real in a way that could compromise operational distance -- draws a Cognitive Reset: administered amnestics erasing the preceding 24 hours, removing the 'Emotional Variance' leadership considers the actual risk. Level 3, Mythic Contamination -- sustained, willful departure from clinical doctrine -- draws reassignment to Expendable Asset status, pulling the offending agent out of personnel entirely and into the same experimental population used for Resonance Sequestration testing (extends MCD-1727's Conflict Map program with its actual human cost). The system is self-policing by design: agents fear their own Scrip-Ledger more reliably than they fear the subjects.

SBD-050 | Extends SBD-040: SBD field detachments are classified into four standing types, each keyed to a clearance tier rather than improvised per-operation. Level 4, Compliance Detachments -- general order-enforcement and site security, 12 to 20 personnel, tasked against baseline-through-Elite-Standard disruption (unrated civilians through roughly 500x) and authorized locally by any regional Grave-Analyst's sign-off. Level 3, Retrieval Detachments -- subject recovery, asset transport, and HVAH intake, 8 to 14 personnel, requiring the same regional Grave-Analyst authorization plus a logged Scrip-Ledger notation (extends SBD-047) since retrieval work routinely brushes the Clinical Tone standard. Level 2, Containment Detachments -- anomaly-class and Military-Standard engagement, 20 to 40 personnel scaling upward for confirmed OMEGA-PRIME-classified contact, authorized only through the office of the Grave-Analyst of record (currently Abbott Gage) with a mandatory Oracle Conflict Map cross-check (MCD-1727) before dispatch. SEALBLACK, the top tier -- direct action against politically sensitive, Titan-class, or root-architecture-adjacent targets -- is deliberately small, 6 to 8 personnel (matching the Fulfillment Ceremony wet-work team, MCD-091/092), and is never dispatched on regional authority alone. This sizing discipline is doctrine, not convenience: the Directorate's own institutional memory holds that a detachment large enough to be noticed is a detachment large enough to generate the exact anomalous-access pattern the Unmarked Fraction's own security depends on going undetected (CULT-051), so scale is suppressed deliberately at every tier above Compliance.

SBD-051 | Extends SBD-046/047/050/MCD-1727: authorization for a SEALBLACK-tier deployment requires two signatures, never one. The Executive Director (Ilona Corrance) or an explicitly named proxy provides operational authorization; the Grave-Analyst of record (Abbott Gage) provides technical clearance, confirming no active Conflict Flag exists in whichever of the six Oracle Conflict Map Domains (MCD-1727) the target falls under. If a Domain carries an active Conflict Flag, the deployment does not proceed on any delay -- it converts automatically to the 'Tighten' posture's Deception-by-Saturation model, substituting a Level 3 or lower detachment and a cover operation for the direct SEALBLACK action, since the Directorate's own doctrine treats a confirmed intelligence gap as disqualifying for its highest-authorization tier. Containment Detachments (Level 2) require only Grave-Analyst sign-off, without the Director's additional signature, unless the target intersects a SEALBLACK case file already open, in which case the higher bar applies retroactively. A detachment commander who proceeds without both signatures where required is, per SBD-047, guilty of Mythic Contamination by definition -- treating an operation's urgency as outweighing the Directorate's own process is exactly the kind of personal judgment the Scrip-Ledger system exists to price out.

SBD-052 | Extends MCD-1727/CULT-199: every detachment operation generates an after-action file under its personnel's real names and designations, filed first at the originating field office. On escalation to Director-level review -- automatic for any SEALBLACK operation, discretionary for Level 2 Containment -- the file passes through the Continuity Lock: proper names (of subjects, sites, and often the detachment's own operators) are stripped and replaced with code-designations before the file receives permanent status, and the original full-name draft is destroyed rather than merely sealed, on the theory that a destroyed record cannot later be recovered by whoever eventually breaches clearance to reach it. The redacted permanent copies are held at the Kesmara Continuity Vault; a small number of full-name shadow copies survive only in the personal, off-book records of whichever Grave-Analyst signed off (Abbott Gage's own such archive is referenced internally but never itself audited, since auditing it would require breaking the same Continuity Lock it exists to enforce). This is the specific mechanism by which, per MCD-1727's closing observation, 'even cleared archivists eventually lose the true names of what they guard' -- it is not organizational decay, it is designed obsolescence, executed one case file at a time.

SBD-058 | Named Containment Detachment (Level 2, extends SBD-050): 'the Coldline,' a standing 24-strong unit specializing in anomaly-class containment and extraction, built around rapid-cooling and structural-denial equipment rather than direct force -- doctrine developed specifically against thermal-permission entities such as Cinderhilt (MCD-1729), and adapted for use against the Verdigris and Sinkmark sites (SBD-054/055) it has also been tasked against. Its standard approach denies an anomaly its preferred failure mode -- denying collapse routes for a structural-collapse hazard, flash-cooling the air for a thermal one -- rather than attempting to destroy or restrain the anomaly directly, since direct engagement with an unconfirmed mechanism is doctrine-forbidden above Level 2 authorization. The Coldline reports through its own Grave-Analyst liaison rather than a field commander answering to the ordinary Compliance chain, reflecting its specialist, cross-regional deployment pattern; it has never operated at SEALBLACK tier, and its personnel doctrine explicitly bars it from anomaly-class targets that also carry a live political classification, on the theory that mixing the two invites exactly the kind of institutional error already documented at SBD-041 through 045.

SBD-059 | Named SEALBLACK wet-work cell (extends SBD-050/051): 'the Quiet Hand,' a 7-strong detachment distinct from the Fulfillment Ceremony wet-work team (MCD-091/092/1853), tasked against politically sensitive individual targets that do not require anomaly-handling expertise -- informants, defecting personnel, and figures whose removal or extraction cannot be traced to the Directorate. Unlike the Fulfillment Ceremony team, which operated once against a fixed, pre-planned target, the Quiet Hand is a standing detachment with rotating membership, authorized case by case under the full two-signature SEALBLACK protocol (SBD-051); its own after-action files are Continuity-Locked immediately upon filing rather than escalated for review, since its casework is considered maximally sensitive by category rather than by individual case. Internally, the Quiet Hand is understood to be the detachment leadership reaches for first when a Conflict Flag (MCD-1727) forces the 'Tighten' posture's Deception-by-Saturation model, precisely because a rotating, code-designated cell generates fewer traceable patterns than a larger or more consistent one.

SBD-060 | Named maintenance detachment (extends SBD-050/052, MCD-1727): 'the Lockstitch Detachment,' an 11-strong unit holding a clearance classification adjacent to but distinct from SEALBLACK, tasked with the physical maintenance of the sealed Oracle network's relay infrastructure and with executing Continuity Lock redaction sweeps against active case files as they escalate to permanent status. Lockstitch personnel are deliberately never briefed on the content of what they redact -- their training is purely mechanical, keyed to file structure and code-designation syntax rather than case substance -- so that the detachment most physically intimate with the Directorate's most sensitive records is also, by design, the one least capable of understanding what it is handling. This is the same 'Double-Blind' principle already locked at CULT-199, applied here to the personnel performing the redaction rather than to the archivists receiving the redacted product. The detachment answers directly to whichever Grave-Analyst holds split-custody KEY-B access (SBD-030) at a given time, currently Abbott Gage, and to no one else in the ordinary Compliance chain of command.

SBD-061 | Named Retrieval Detachment (Level 3, extends SBD-050): 'the Foundling Detachment,' a 12-strong unit specializing in HVAH asset recovery and subject transport -- the class of detachment Lauris Letitia was processed through on Directorate intake (MCD-175), and the same class elsewhere and unrelatedly tasked with routine subject relocation between SBD facilities. Its doctrine emphasizes non-destructive recovery and transport-condition documentation over speed, since a recovered HVAH asset's classification and value depend on an intact, undamaged assessment; a Foundling team that damages or kills a recoverable subject in the field is treated as a Level 1 Clinical Tone failure by default, regardless of circumstance, on the theory that a dead subject cannot be evaluated and an unevaluated subject is a wasted operation rather than a completed one. The Foundling Detachment carries no anomaly-handling authorization and defers automatically to a Containment Detachment (SBD-058) if a retrieval target proves to be anomaly-class rather than merely HVAH-classified.

ARS-397 | Extends ARS-300: SBD Dead Drakma Plate Armor is modular, effective against baseline-through-Elite Standard threats (25x-500x) and ineffective above Military Standard, non-self-repairing -- the direct material-property inverse of Kanja's self-repairing Living Drakma (ARS-010). Its structural weakness: Dead Drakma alloy resonates at a fixed frequency, and Kanja's Aegis-Talisman (ARS-050) broadcasts that exact frequency, causing sympathetic vibration across any Dead Drakma plate in range.

ARS-370 | Wrinkle 2, Voice/gaze synchronization (first integration Book 3, full expression Book 5): distinct from the always-on baseline gaze-capture (CC-112), this is the timing coordination between the Voice pulse and direct eye contact becoming biologically automatic as Fury escalates -- involuntary at Hot, consistent at White, and a single inseparable compound effect at Flood State. First involuntary occurrence (Book 3) unsettles Anirak briefly, since her own biology acted without her authorization; by Book 5 she doesn't register it at all.

ARS-443 | Anirak's Combination Codex. White-state combinations, Book 3 onward only (ARS-370): her combat ceiling through Book 4 (ARS-368). Fine control is reduced, the Fangs run near forge heat, and the Voice and her gaze fire together every time. Her shapes get bigger and more committed. | Called Debt. Both Fangs wrap one opponent and she pulls the two chains against each other, twisting his frame in torsion until one point in it gives. The torsion is released before any three-second hold, so it stays distinct from the Flood-State thermal failure point (ARS-372). It is the White-state breaker for a single hard target. | The Long Note. The chains have sung one long note at speed since the Chain Harbor yard (MCD-1883). At White, at near-forge heat, she fuses that note with the Voice's hum into one wall of sound within her Fang reach, and the enemies inside it lose balance, distance, and direction at the same moment. The locked cone figures stand. Abad's approval: 'draft Anirak's Combination Codex next' / 'keep going, lock the Codex when the review is clean and connecting logically. if not, it NEVER passes.'

ARS-447 | Anirak's Combination Codex. Tide Line crew combinations (MCD-1890), each built on the partner's locked kit. Each is run below Flood State; once she reaches it, the crew works around her instinct (ARS-444): | Double Draw (with Stormbreaker). Her chain-pull drags a target into the Equinox's gravity corona, which pulls the struck target into the hit rather than knocking it away (ARS-417). The target is pulled twice, from two directions, by two different physics. | Mark and Collect (with Voidbreaker). He embeds a Void-Marker dart behind the target and folds to it (ARS-419), and his displacement-strike staggers the target forward into her Fang radius. She holds the Voice until his strike lands and he folds back out to a dart off her cone's line, so the Voice never catches him or spoils the exact position his strike needs. | Two Storms (with Zora). Zora's Scream is a 5-meter sonic-boom cone that ruptures eardrums and breaks balance (ARS-420). The cone throws outward from the point of impact, and inside it Anirak's own acoustic sea-sense (ARS-367) would be deafened, so Zora strikes from Anirak's side of the target, throwing the cone away from her, and only after the Fangs have pulled clear. Zora steps in only after the Voice pulse has passed, so she is never in the cone when it fires. The order is fixed: the Voice goes first, so its vertigo has the target off-balance before the Scream lands, and no one can brace against the second hit. The crew drills the order until it is instinct. | The Eastern Passage (with Edda, Hamund, and Odile). This is the formation from Chain Harbor, where three freed prisoners held the passage at her back so she could work (MCD-1883). Her core holds the line, and she never has to stop. It is the oldest combination in the Codex, built before any of the others. Abad's approval: 'draft Anirak's Combination Codex next' / 'keep going, lock the Codex when the review is clean and connecting logically. if not, it NEVER passes.'

ARS-446 | Anirak's Combination Codex. Partner combinations. | Storm and Depth (with Ren). This is their locked pairing, "Surface Storm / Deep Pressure" (CC-114). Her Fangs cut a target's structure, and then Ren's active field (+200% load within about 15 meters, CC-101) collapses it under its own weight. His field strips her gaze from everyone inside it (CC-112), and its load falls on her too if she stays inside it, so she clears the radius before it closes. It is also why he is the one partner who sees her clearly. | Joint Account (with Lauris, before Book 5 only, ARS-374). Lauris's Triad-Lock breaches become failure points that Anirak's Debt Collection pulls open in the following second. Lauris grows quieter and Anirak louder, and no instrument can track both. Abad's approval: 'draft Anirak's Combination Codex next' / 'keep going, lock the Codex when the review is clean and connecting logically. if not, it NEVER passes.'

ARS-445 | Anirak's Combination Codex. Undersea combinations. She has more torque in denser water (CC-113), the water carries her Voice through the gorget, and her sea-sense runs ambient, becoming active sonar only in Book 5 (ARS-371). | The Drowning Spiral. Underwater, a full-body rotation drives both chains in one spiral that drags a swimmer inward into the Fangs. Denser water gives her more torque (CC-113). | Black-Water Lantern. The Lantern-Star's strobe (ARS-411) is a locked Ever-Haunt countermeasure (CULT-197), and in black water it is the only light. She strobes it to scatter the lower tiers of the Ever-Haunt and to blind and disorient anything that hunts by sight. The outcome of her engagement with Sereth Vaul stays reserved (MCD-1892). Abad's approval: 'draft Anirak's Combination Codex next' / 'keep going, lock the Codex when the review is clean and connecting logically. if not, it NEVER passes.'

CC-114 | Anirak and Ren (Abyss) are established as a deliberate tactical/relational pairing -- 'Surface Storm' (Anirak's kinetic, rotational output) and 'Deep Pressure' (Ren's gravitational field) -- complementary both in combat (her blades shred structure, his field collapses the weakened structure under its own augmented weight) and as a sibling-like bond: Anirak positioned herself as his protector without formal assignment, recognizing a body the world wasn't built for.

CC-101 | Abyss (Ren Oshaal), deeper physiology: his Negative-Density Variant biology generates a localized gravitational-pressure field -- passive (~5m radius, +30% gravitational load), active (~15m radius, +200% load), and the Depth-Charge (field compressed to ~1m, approximating deep-ocean crush pressure, costing ~6 hours' recovery). Age ~45 (the crew's youngest adult recruit; Pyro, roughly 24-36 at Book 1, is younger), personal density ~150x, carries no weapons -- his field is his arsenal, moderated by Kanja-built Dead Drakma gravitational-compensator boots and a field-moderating mesh vest for close proximity to allies. Origin: a deep-ocean pressure-adapted community on the Jicome continental shelf; sent to the surface at 16 after his field's output exceeded his settlement's structural tolerance at 14; recruited by Sephtis.

ARS-372 | Wrinkle 4, chain thermal transfer at Flood State: the Twin Fangs run at forge-adjacent temperature at Flood State; two chain wraps sustained three seconds on the same contact point structurally weakens (not burns through) the material there, creating a failure point Ren learns to target without either of them naming the mechanism explicitly.

ARS-369 | Wrinkle 1, Flood State (Book 5 Tide Line exclusively, MCD-1889 -- the series' longest sustained engagement): no engagement before Book 5 lasts long enough to push Anirak past White. At Flood State the Chain-Strike doctrine's techniques persist only as biological instinct, no longer intentional choices. Ren's role shifts correspondingly from finisher to full aftermath-radius manager, neutralizing what she's disoriented and clearing targets so she doesn't have to stop. Red Beard (commanding the Line front per MCD-221) responds to her reaching Flood State by silently increasing his own operational distance by 30 meters, at the single moment the Tide Line's shore phase meets the Line's flank -- the one time he stands within sight of her at Flood State.

MCD-259 | The Parley of the Raptor's Nest (age 155) recruits Stormreaver (Kairo, aerial biology with the forged Zephyr-Frame flight harness and Dual-Spectrum Insight Lenses), the only recruitment achieved through zero violence and initiated by the recruit's own choice after three years' observation; he becomes the crew's explicit moral-compass/mediator. The Archive Fire (age 170) has Ghostwind remove only the physical locks from sealed Trust archives (leaving the records themselves untouched), letting suppressed rebellion-era history spread uncontrollably through academia. The Iron Carnival (age 185) is a full-theatrical, zero-violence garrison evacuation at Fort Gallan enabling an 11-hour unopposed study of new Trust hardware.

MCD-260 | At the Second Century Mark (age 200), Trust Governor Maren Tallis negotiates a 12-year truce recognizing the Scourge's economy has outgrown Trust taxation; this battle is also where the Talisman of Mao's Stage 2-to-3 transition (the 'Governor's Shackle') is named explicitly for the first time, with an in-text 114-year countdown to Pi-Awakening (200+114=314, consistent with the already-locked age-314 threshold). The Generational Test (age 205) is the first battle where Kanja, visibly slowed, delegates combat entirely to an Avatar (Stormbreaker) rather than fighting himself -- the turning point the text marks as 'from here forward, the Avatars fought, the Captain directed.'

MCD-261 | The Breath That Broke the Blockade (age 210) recruits Soulreaver Zora (26, Atmospheric Pressure Variant, fisherman's daughter), whose grief-driven wind ability is weaponized into a 60-knot corridor breaking a 20-warship blockade; equipment forged specifically to let her fight without needing to grieve: the Scream, Lung-Collapse grenades, the Gale-Shield. The Cartographer's War (age 215) counters a Trust attempt to legally erase 47 settlements (120,000 people) from official maps by distributing superior charts before the ratification deadline.

MCD-262 | The Memory Keeper (age 225) is a 12-hour crew-wide transcription sprint saving 34,000 of 40,000 pages of Ghost-Lattice archives from a simultaneous 31-location Trust raid -- this archive becomes explicitly load-bearing for Book 1's later investigation. The Sleeping Giant (age 240) is the origin of Kanja's late-era 'immobility as a weapon' doctrine: alone in a corridor against 12 Branded commandos, his passive Kinetic Buffer and Bio-Drakma-tempered skeleton do the work of the mobile combat he can no longer physically perform (he still walks, climbs, grips, and grounds a blow through the Forge-Coat; he no longer dodges, turns fast, or runs), explicitly framed as a preview of the eventual Pi-Awakening.

MCD-263 | The Orphan's Harbor (age 250): Kanja consolidates 220 years of accumulated war orphans into a permanent sanctuary, Stormshelter Cove (already locked as Sovereign Trust Domain territory at MCD-110/MAW-033; this adds physical detail -- a basalt-cliff, deep-water inlet -- and layers the new institution onto the existing site without contradicting it), housing 2,000 children within 5 years. The Orphan's Harbor becomes the Ghost-Lattice's primary talent pipeline -- three-quarters of its couriers, forgers, and analysts in the era's final decades are Harbor graduates.

MCD-266 | Tier-2 Campaign C6, the Merchant Accord (ages 80-200): a 120-year campaign transforming the Scourge brand into a parallel commercial government -- the First Charter (80, 37 vessels, 15% protection rate vs. the Trust's 40-60% taxation, elected merchant council), the Tariff War (120, 17 independent commercial docks built in response to punitive Trust tariffs, which are repealed within 5 years), the Currency Standard (155, the Coin-Weight Raid's corrected Scrip formalized as the alliance's official currency, ~500,000 notes/year), and the Mutual Defense Compact (200, alongside Governor Tallis's truce) -- converting the alliance into a full maritime confederation with its own currency, governance, infrastructure, and defense force.

MCD-269 | The Shimmer Incident (age 282) is the first externally-documented sign of Kanja's body itself changing -- a light-bending distortion field around him, observed and measured by a Trust patrol -- as the Governor's Shackle approaches its final stages; near this same location, a Trust survey team separately investigates an ancient Karesian cavern-system heritage site already known as 'the Living Gate' (the same Living Gate later activated as T.D.K.'s containment mechanism at Pyro's birth, age ~290 -- this predates that event and establishes it as a real, ancient physical location rather than something built from nothing). The Cestari Overture (age 285) is Red Beard's (Tarn Cestari) first contact via the Brand-Line, a multi-year correspondence opening 29 years ahead of his already-locked Book 1 defection.

MCD-270 | The Birth of Fire (age 290): Pyro's natural birth and the Dhar-Kael imprinting bond completing between him and the juvenile Varkul, Varruk, and Sorya (already locked in detail) occur with Kanja required to stay 12km away so the Talisman's output doesn't disrupt the bonding frequencies -- consistent with, and adding texture to, the already-locked birth/Living Gate timeline (MCD-022, MCD-131/132). The Last Lighthouse (age 295) is Kanja's otherwise-inexplicable capture of the Gilded Lighthouse, whose ancient Living Drakma cladding resonates with the Governor's Shackle and eases his weight briefly -- already consistent with the locked CC-005/MCD-060/061 identification of the Lighthouse as the future Pi-Awakening site.

input.content:
# Anirak Chronicle II: The Second Harness

*UNLOCKED DRAFT, PENDING ABAD'S APPROVAL, 2026-10-04. Second entry of Anirak's Character Chronicle
series (Game Plan pitch 3, locked at Batch 372). Close-third on Anirak per `VB-065`. The Long Mask,
roughly Kanja 175, after Maw-11 (`MCD-264`) and before Ren comes aboard. A Sealbound Directorate
Retrieval Detachment (`SBD-050`, `SBD-061`) comes for a subject of its own and brings a damping rig
built against her Stack. Notable register, no kill. New named characters: Ardith (the subject) and
Grave-Analyst Ambry Pruett (the rig's maker), both collision-checked against the full ledger and
Chronicle corpus. Anirak, Edda, Hamund, and Odile reused. No child-safety issues. Not canon until
approved.*

---

Tideglass at night. A free port. The Scourge's mark painted small on the harbor-master's door, and the
Trust's tax-house shuttered three streets back for longer than most of the dockhands had been alive.

Rain on slate. Tar smell off the boat sheds. Kelp rotting on the slip. Lamps in the tavern windows
along the front, and the water black between the piers.

She lay awake in the loft over the net-maker's shop. She could not have said what woke her.

Then she could.

A hull in the harbor. Out past the second pier, low in the water, no lamp. She felt it the way she
felt weather. A weight sitting in the swell where no weight had been at dusk. Oars, muffled, dipping
slow. Then stopping.

She was down the ladder with the chains in her hands before the oars stopped.

• • •

The woman was called Ardith. Twenty, or near it. She had come into Tideglass nine days before on a
salt barge, under a tarp, with a number cut into the skin behind her ear and no other thing she would
talk about. The harbor council had put her in the rooms over the chandler's. The crew had told the
council the rooms were watched.

They were. Edda had the door. Hamund had the lane. Odile had the roof across the way.

Anirak came round the corner of the chandler's at a run and saw it all in one look.

Twelve of them. Grey oilcloth over dull plate. No marks. Six already at the chandler's door, two of
those on the stair, and the door open. Edda down on one knee on the step, a hand to her head, blood in
her hair. Six more in the lane mouth facing Hamund, close-packed, in no hurry.

Two of the six in the lane carried a long bundle between them. Canvas over something that clinked.

Odile dropped off the roof across the way into the lane behind them. Hamund stepped up beside her.

On the stair, a voice. Ardith's. One word, and then a hand over it.

Read: twelve in a narrow lane, rain on the stones, one door, one stair, a boat out in the dark.

The six on the stair: taking her now.

The six in the lane: waiting. For something. For her.

Verdict: the stair first, and the waiting ones are the trap.

She went for the stair.

• • •

The six in the lane let her through.

That was the wrong thing for them to do. She saw it as she passed them and could not stop. Stopping
cost her. She went past them toward the door with every face in the lane turned on her, and none of the
six moved a hand.

The first man on the step had a short club in one hand and a coil of leather strap in the other. A Fang
went out on its chain and took the club arm behind the wrist. She pulled. The arm came across his body.
The Star came off her back and its talons took the club. Gone. He sat down on the step.

The weight of it came back up her arms. The chains began to warm.

The second man on the step. A strap swung at her head. She ducked under it and fed the turn into the
second Fang. The hook took his belt and she threw him off the step into the gutter.

The stair. Four more on it, and the top of it, and the door to the rooms.

Behind her, the canvas came off the bundle.

• • •

She heard it before she felt it. Iron weights clinking on cords. A whirring. Then the thing came down
over her shoulders from behind.

A net. Heavy. Thick bands of quilted leather stitched in a lattice, every band packed tight with lead
shot. It dropped over her head and shoulders and arms and the chains, and the six from the lane were
already round her on the stair-foot, each with a cord in his fists, and they leaned back on the cords
all at once.

The net closed.

She drove an elbow back. It sank into a band. The shot inside shifted and swallowed the blow. Nothing
came back up her arm. Nothing.

She drove the Star's haft into the lattice. Same. The blow went into the lead and died there. A dead
blow. No ring. No weight returned.

She tried to turn. The cords held. Six men leaning their whole weight on six cords from six sides. She
could move a hand's breadth any way. No more.

The heat began to go out of the chains.

She felt it go. Down her arms. Out of her shoulders. Out of her chest. A cracked jar draining in the
rain. Every blow she had banked since the step leaking away, and nothing she could do with her body
would put any of it back.

A hood came down over her head. Coarse cloth. Wet. It cut off the lamps.

She stood in the dark, held still, in a harness made for her.

They harnessed me. So the blows wouldn't stack.

• • •

Outside the hood, a calm voice. Close. Not one of the cord-men.

"Hold tension. She will try the hands first, then the hips. Do not answer either."

Another voice, rougher. "She's quiet."

"She is draining. Look at the chain."

She knew that voice's kind. No heat in it. Every word chosen. A man reading a gauge.

"Stair team?"

"Subject secured. Moving to the water."

"Then we hold her four minutes and go."

On the stair above her, boots, and something dragged. A muffled sound through a hand. Going down the
other side. Going toward the boat.

The calm voice spoke again, nearer. To her, this time.

"Anirak." He said it the way a clerk reads a name off a docket. "Do not exert yourself. Exertion inside
the rig only drains you faster. No one here is authorized to injure you. In four minutes we will be
gone."

She stood still. She had to. Every breath of stillness bled her more.

Four minutes was long enough for a boat to clear the harbor mouth.

• • •

Her hands were caught. Her hips were caught. Her eyes were covered.

Her throat was not.

They had built the rig against the blows. Against the eyes. A Directorate gauge-man reads what a file
tells him to read, and her file said Kinetic-Stack.

She let her voice go.

Low. Under hearing. Into the gorget at her throat, and the crystal nodes took it up even through the wet
cloth of the hood, and laid it out ahead of her.

Forward. Where she faced. Where two of the six stood on the cords.

She felt it land in them. Not in her ears. In the cords. The tension on the forward lines wavered. One
cord went slack in a jerk, then tight again, then slack. A man went to his knees on wet stone. She heard
him retch.

Behind her, the calm voice. "Forward lines. Hold. Hold."

The forward line went slack again.

A hand's breadth became an arm's length.

She turned into the slack. Hard. All her weight. The net came round with her, the lead bands swinging
out on their stitching. The cords on the far side snapped taut with her turn, and the men on them came
off their feet.

Movement. Only that. Her own weight, swung.

It came back up her arms.

Small. A single coin of heat in the chains. Then she turned the other way, and the cords on that side
came taut, and the men holding them came stumbling in, and that was two. Three.

She was not hitting anything. The net ate every blow. So she did not hit. She pulled. The men on the
cords were holding her by the cords. The cords held them to her. Every turn she made dragged one of them
across the stones and every drag came back up her arms.

The chains were warm again under the bands.

Somewhere outside the hood, Hamund's voice. "Left cord!"

A blow. A man's grunt. The left cord went dead. Then Odile's. "Right!" The right one too.

Her three, on the cord-men. They did not reach for the net. They knew better. They held the line around
her and took the cords off one by one, so she never had to stop.

She ripped one arm up through the slack lattice. Got a hand to the hood. Tore it off.

Lamps. Rain. The lane.

Every face in the lane on her.

The calm voice was a thin man in grey oilcloth standing three paces back from it all, out of reach of
any cord. He had a slate in one hand and a stylus in the other. He was not holding a weapon. His face
had turned to her with all the rest. He looked at her as if she were the only thing in the world. He
looked down at his slate. Then back.

She went through the last of the lattice. The lead bands fell round her feet on the stones.

The men who had held the cords were down, or backing off, hands open. Not one of them came at her.

The thin man did not run. He did not come at her either. He wrote something.

• • •

She did not stop for him.

The lane. The slip. The end of the second pier, at a dead run, the chains hot and singing.

Out past the harbor mouth, a hull under sail.

She felt it before she saw it. A long keel, bigger than the rowboat. A cutter running before the land
breeze, heeled, every sail drawing. The rowboat bumping empty at its stern on a towline.

She stood at the end of the pier. She did not stand. She paced it, three strides each way. Rain on the
planks. The weight in her arms and nowhere to put it.

The sea told her the rest. The cutter's hull went out and out across the swell. Faster than anything
that swims. Farther every breath.

She could have gone into the water. She would have caught nothing.

The keel went over the edge of what she could feel. Then there was only the swell.

• • •

When she came back up the lane, the detachment was gone. Over the seawall and down to a second boat she
never heard. Twelve men. Every one of them on his feet or carried. No one dead.

The net lay in the lane where it had fallen. Edda was sitting on the chandler's step with a rag to her
head. Odile was holding the rag. Hamund stood over the net.

He kicked it. It clinked.

"They made that for you."

"Yes."

"How long, to make a thing like that?"

She looked down at it. The bands. The stitching. Twelve men drilled on six cords until they could close
it on a moving body in one breath. A hood. A count of minutes.

"Long."

"Who?"

She thought of the thin man with the slate. A man reading a gauge. He had stood three paces off the
whole time and never once been in reach. He had watched the rig work. He had watched it fail. He had
written all of it down.

"The one who wrote," she said.

Odile looked up. "Gone too."

"He'll build another."

None of them answered that.

Anirak picked up the net. It was heavy, the lead dragging in every band. She carried it to the end of
the slip and threw it in the harbor. It went down fast.

That was nothing. They had it on the slate.

port under the Merchant Accord (`MCD-266`). The detachment is a twelve-strong Sealbound Directorate

Foundling class's non-destructive recovery (`SBD-061`, "a team that damages or kills a recoverable
subject in the field" fails Clinical Tone), which is why no one on either side dies: the detachment
never threatens a life, so under `CC-164` Anirak has no necessity kill to make, and she kills no one.

unstated, and she is not recovered. The rig (new fact, flagged for the lock rule): a weighted net of
leather bands packed with lead shot, held by six men on six cords, with a hood. It is built against her
Stack as the SBD classifies it (Kinetic-Stack Variant, `CC-122`): the shot swallows every strike and
returns no impact, so nothing is banked (`ARS-367`, `ARS-439` -- Stack counts landed strikes and
absorbed impacts), and the cords hold her still, so what she has banked drains (`ARS-439`, the root of
`ARS-373`'s no-stillness doctrine). The hood answers the Siren (`CC-112`). It is the second harness:
her Chain Harbor damping harness (`MCD-1883`, "They harnessed me. So the blows wouldn't stack.") is the
first, and the line recurs in her head. It fails on what it was not built against: her Voice is her own
throat's hum, carried and shaped by the gorget into a forward cone (`ARS-438`), and the hood does not
stop it; the vertigo slackens the forward cords; she turns into the slack and banks Stack from her own
weight dragging the cord-men (impact absorbed and landed in the pull, Debt Collection's logic,
`ARS-440`); her three take the cords off one by one so she never stops, the Eastern Passage formation
(`ARS-447`). Warm throughout: the chains warm, drain, warm again, and the engagement ends within
minutes. The design survives: Grave-Analyst Ambry Pruett, its maker, records the rig's work and failure
on a slate; the after-action file runs under real names at the field office (`SBD-052`); Anirak sinks
the physical net, which costs the Directorate nothing. "He'll build another" is her belief, not a
locked future: no future use of the rig is reserved or implied. Pruett reads her name off her file
(`CC-163`: SBD field files name her). Grave-Analyst is the SBD's title for its medical and forensic
staff (`SBD-040`); a regional Grave-Analyst authorizes Level 3 work (`SBD-050`). Her three: Edda takes a
scalp wound on the door, the only injury of note; none is lost (reserved). Her sea-sense is ambient only
(`ARS-367`, `ARS-371`): she feels hulls and weather, no active sonar. Her undersea speed (`CC-113`) is
weighed and rejected against a cutter running before the wind. Reserved threads untouched: Hot/White and
sync, Flood State, sonar, Sereth Vaul, Vestige, Ren and his field, her origin's open questions, the
undead, her age. Tech level: oars, sail, lead shot, leather; nothing beyond the pre-industrial world.*

# Lauris Chronicle XCVIII: The Weight Nobody Else Would Stand Under

*Locked canon, Batch 300, 2026-09-18 (`MCD-1715`). Ninety-eighth entry in Lauris Letitia's own
Chronicle series, Strand W. A stakes-free entry pairing Lauris with Abyss (Ren Oshaal, `CC-101`),
the crew's youngest adult recruit -- she becomes his preferred practice partner for controlling his
Negative-Density Variant field's active-range output, since her own biology tolerates standing
inside it without the discomfort most of the crew experience. Puts `CC-134`'s combat-joy trait on
the page as the pleasure of testing a genuine physical limit safely, alongside her established
witness psychology's patience with someone isolated by their own capability. Corrected Batch 334,
2026-10-02: "fifteen-percent" corrected to "thirty-percent" gravitational load. No new named
characters.*

-----

*Archive fragment, present-day, undated by her own habit: "Ren asked, the first time, whether it
hurt. It did not. I told him so, and he did not believe me, so I stood there again until he did."*

Ren Oshaal is, by a wide margin, the youngest adult recruit this crew has taken on,
and I have observed that this fact sits on him less as a distinction than as a mild, chronic
inconvenience, the way a smaller man might resent being handed the lightest end of every load out of
someone else's misplaced consideration. His field is his arsenal and, by his own admission to me on
more than one occasion, also the reason most of the crew keep a careful, unspoken distance from him
even at rest -- a passive thirty-percent increase in gravitational load is a mild discomfort to
most; his active range, which he must practice controlling if he is ever to trust it in an
engagement, is considerably less mild, and volunteers for that practice are, understandably, scarce.

Lauris volunteered on the second week she noticed no one else had.

"It will not hurt me," she told him, the first time, with the specific flatness she reserves for
facts she does not expect to be believed on the strength of her word alone. He did not believe her.
She stood inside the active radius anyway, for the better part of an hour, while he brought the field
up in increments and watched her for any sign of strain that did not come, and by the end of that
hour I am told he had stopped watching her for signs of strain and started, instead, simply watching
the field itself, the way an artisan watches a tool finally behaving the way the diagrams always
promised it would.

I have since sat in on perhaps a dozen of these sessions, and I want to record what I have observed
of them honestly, because I think a reader unfamiliar with either of them might assume this is
charity on her part, extended downward to the crew's most isolated member out of some general
largesse. It is not charity. She has told me, plainly, that she enjoys it -- the specific, rare
pleasure of a body built without compromise being asked to actually meet something that tests it,
rather than simply outlasting whatever is put in front of it. Most threats this crew faces, she has
said, she survives through capacity so far in excess of the demand that there is no honest contest in
it at all. Ren's field, at its higher settings, is close enough to her own tolerances that standing
inside it is, for her, something closer to genuine exertion than most of what she does in a given
year, and she has told me she finds that scarcity worth seeking out on its own account, entirely
apart from what it does for him.

What it does for him, though I do not think either of them would frame it this way to the other, is
considerable. He was sent to the surface at sixteen because his own settlement could no longer bear
the structural cost of standing near him, and I have come to understand, across the years I have
watched him, that a great deal of what makes him careful, and quiet, and slower than most of this
crew to accept an offered kindness, traces back to that particular exile -- to having been, for the
first sixteen years of his life, a danger his own people loved him despite rather than because of.
Lauris did not ask him about any of that directly, the evening I am recording here, some months into
their sessions. She simply asked him to bring the field up one increment further than he had tried
before, and stood inside it without flinching while he did, and afterward, catching his breath before
she had needed to catch her own, he said, "You are not afraid of it."

"No," she said. "I have found very little in six thousand years that frightens me in the way I think
you mean. I have found that this makes me useful to people who need something to stand against
without breaking, more than it makes me remarkable."

He considered that for a while, in the particular stillness I have learned is his version of careful
arithmetic, and then said, "It is strange, having something to push against that pushes back the
right amount."

"I know the feeling," she told him. "I have gone most of my life without it, myself."

I do not think either of them meant that exchange as more than the plain trade of two facts. I have
come, nonetheless, to think it is the truest thing either has said to the other across a dozen
sessions of steadily increasing weight -- that a crew built from people the world found too much to
hold has, in this small unremarkable corner of it, produced exactly the kind of company each of them
had been missing without knowing to ask for it.

# Anirak Chronicle III: The Body the World Was Not Built For

*UNLOCKED DRAFT, PENDING ABAD'S APPROVAL, 2026-10-04. Third entry of Anirak's Character Chronicle
series (Game Plan pitch 1, locked at Batch 372), closing the launch wave. Close-third on Anirak per
`VB-065`. The late Long Mask, roughly Kanja 300. Ren (Abyss, Ren Oshaal) comes aboard an adult,
already recruited by Sephtis, and she takes him as her charge unasked, the undated origin of their
pairing (`CC-114`). Notable register, no kill, no fight. No new named characters. Anirak, Ren, Edda,
Hamund, and Odile reused; Sephtis and the Captain referred to, not on the page. No child-safety
issues. Not canon until approved.*

---

He came aboard on the morning launch, in fog.

She felt the launch before she saw it. A small hull riding low. Lower than six oarsmen and a cargo of
water casks should ride it. As if one more cask sat in the bottom of it, a cask of lead.

The launch came alongside. The oarsmen shipped their oars fast and kept to the far gunwale, all six of
them, crowded together on the one side so the boat listed. In the stern, a young man sat alone with a
sea-bag on his knees.

Hamund, at the rail beside her, said it under his breath. "Sephtis's."

Word had come the week before. Sephtis had found someone on the shelf islands. Sephtis was sending him
out.

The young man came up the side ladder. The rungs creaked under him. Every one. The ladder was oak and
had held men in full plate. It creaked under him as if he were three.

He stepped onto the deck.

The planks groaned. A long, low sound, deep in the wood, the sound a hull makes in a heavy sea. The
deck was flat calm.

The men nearest the ladder stepped back. Not far. A few paces. They did not mean anything by it. Their
bodies did it for them. Something in the air around him leaned on them, and they leaned away.

He saw them do it. His face did not change. He had seen it before.

• • •

They gave him a berth in the forward hold, alone, near the keel where the timbers were thickest. The
bosun did that. Nobody told him to.

By the end of the first day there was a shape on the deck that followed the young man everywhere.

A ring. Five paces across. Empty.

Where he walked, the ring walked with him. Men coiling line drifted out of it. Men at the pumps found
reasons to stand at the other pump. At the evening meal the crew sat close along the benches amidships,
elbow to elbow, and he took his bowl to the bow and sat on the anchor housing with the ring around him
and the dark coming on.

The planks under the anchor housing groaned all through the meal. Not loud. Steady. A ship talking to
itself about a weight.

His name was Ren. Somebody had heard it from the launch crew.

• • •

She watched him for three days.

Read: the young man ate alone. Slept alone. Worked the pumps alone, at the hours nobody else took. He
moved through the ship slowly and set his feet down carefully, the way a man walks on ice. He never
went below the waist deck. Somebody had told him the lower timbers were older.

He did not complain. He did not ask anyone to stand nearer. He did not ask for anything.

Her three watched her watch him. Edda said nothing. Odile said nothing. Hamund said, on the second
night, "They're afraid of him."

"No. They're heavy near him."

"Same thing, to a body."

She had no answer to that.

On the third evening he looked up from the bow. Across the waist of the ship, across the benches and
the crew between them, to where she stood at the mainmast.

His face turned to her and stayed.

The same as every face. The pull went out of her eyes and into him, and the little that came back came
back the way it always did, and she could not tell what in it was his.

He looked away. It took him a moment. She watched him do it.

• • •

She walked across the deck to the bow.

The crew on the benches turned to watch her go, all of them, the way they always did. She went past
the end of the benches. Past the foremast. To the edge of the ring.

She stepped into it.

The weight came down on her at once. Not a blow. A load. As if the air had grown a hand and set it flat
on her shoulders and pressed. Her knees took it. Her spine took it. The chains on her forearms went
heavier by a third and hung straight down, swinging less. The plank under her boot gave a groan of its
own.

She took another step. Then another. Each one set down harder than the one before it. Her heart rose a
little with the work of it.

He was watching her come. She saw his face. She saw the moment she crossed into the weight, because
something in his face went.

The pull went out of it.

It was the only word she had. He had been looking at her the way everyone looked at her. Fixed. Held.
Then she was inside the ring, under the weight, three paces from him, and he was only looking at her.
His eyes moved. Down to the chains. To her boots on the groaning planks. Back to her face. Off to the
sea, once, and back again, because he chose to bring them back.

She stood very still a moment and watched him do that.

Nobody had ever looked away from her and then come back.

• • •

"You'll want to step back," he said. Quiet. He did not get up. "It is heavy, this close."

"Yes."

"Most people step back."

"I saw."

She sat down on the deck beside the anchor housing, an arm's length from him. The weight sat down with
her. It pressed her into the planks. The planks groaned under the two of them together, one long low
note.

He looked at her for a while. She let him. She had nothing to measure it against.

"Does it hurt you?" he said.

"It's heavy."

"That isn't an answer."

"It's the answer."

He almost smiled. Then didn't. He looked down at the bowl in his hands.

"At home they built the walls thicker for me," he said. "Then thicker again. Then there wasn't any wall
thick enough."

She said nothing. She did not ask where home was. He did not ask her anything at all.

Out on the benches, the crew had gone back to their bowls. Her three sat at the end of the nearest
bench, outside the ring, the way everyone sat outside the ring. Hamund was watching. He caught her eye
and held it, and his face did what every face did, and she looked away from him first.

• • •

She ate at the bow after that.

Every evening. Inside the ring. The weight on her shoulders through the whole meal, and the planks
groaning their low note under two bowls instead of one. She did not explain it to anyone. Nobody asked
her to.

In the mornings she worked the pumps at his hours. She walked the waist deck with him when he walked
it, on the side nearest the crew, so that the men coiling line looked at her instead of at the empty
space around him. Faces turned to her and stayed. That was the use of it. A ring that walks with a
woman everyone watches is a ring nobody counts.

On the fifth day a deckhand came too close behind him with a cask on his shoulder, misjudged the
weight, and went to one knee in it, the cask rolling. The man swore at Ren. Loud. The whole waist heard.

She was there before the cask stopped rolling. She did not touch the deckhand. She stood between them,
inside the weight, with the chains hanging heavy at her knees, and looked at him.

His face turned to her and stayed.

"Go round," she said.

He went round. He did it wide.

Ren had not moved. He was looking at her. She knew the difference now. She could feel it, the way she
felt a hull in the dark. Inside the ring, his look was only his.

"I didn't ask you to do that," he said.

"No."

He waited. She did not give him more.

• • •

On the ninth day, word came forward from the stern. The Captain wanted the young man's measure. Feet.
Chest. The weight of him. There would be boots. A vest.

Ren listened to the bosun say it from the edge of the ring. Then he looked at her.

"Boots," he said.

"He builds for the body you have," she said. "He doesn't take any of it away."

He thought about that for a long time, in the stillness that she was learning was the way he counted.

"How do you know?"

She held up one wrist. The chain ran from the cuff to the Fang that hung at her knee, and the links
were warm from her pulse, and heavier than they should be, inside the weight.

He looked at it. Then at her face. Then away to the sea, and back.

That night she lay in her hammock and listened to the ship. The groan in the forward timbers went on
past midnight, low and even. A weight the hull had learned to carry.

She fell asleep counting it.

---

*Continuity notes (not narrative): closes Anirak's launch wave (Game Plan pitches 2, 3, 1 in
chronological order). The late Long Mask, roughly Kanja 300, within the last ~29 years before Book 1;
`CC-101` dates only Ren's surfacing at sixteen, his age when he comes aboard is not stated (he is an
adult), and the Captain's age is not stated in the narrative. Ren (Abyss, Ren Oshaal, `CC-066`,
`CC-101`, `CC-138`): his passive field (+30% load within about 5 m) shown as the groaning planks and
ladder, the listing launch, the crew stepping back, and a five-pace empty ring that follows him; no
active field and no Depth-Charge; no compensator boots or vest yet, so his load is unmoderated, and the
ninth-day measuring for "boots" and "a vest" seeds the Kanja-built Dead Drakma gravitational-compensator
boots and field-moderating mesh vest of `CC-101` without showing them. Recruited by Sephtis (`CC-101`),
off the page; Sephtis is openly with the crew in these years (`MCD-195`, `MCD-206`), which is why word
of him comes ahead of the launch. "Shelf islands" stays within `CC-101`'s Jicome continental-shelf
origin and `CC-138`'s remote-island finding without naming either. His "At home they built the walls
thicker for me" restates `CC-101`'s exile (his field exceeding his settlement's structural tolerance)
and `MCD-1715`'s "a danger his own people loved him despite"; neither of them asks the other's origin,
so `CC-163`'s open questions (whether her community was Vael Kem, `MCD-041`, `MCD-1896`) stay closed.
The Siren (`CC-112`): from across the deck his face is caught like every face; inside his radius the
pull is stripped and he sees her clearly, "the one known exception." It is shown through his eyes
moving and returning by choice, never named as a mechanism. Her three stay outside the ring the whole
time (Hamund's face caught as always), so the reserved payoff -- her three inside Ren's field,
stripped of the Siren and still hers -- is untouched. The load falls on her too (`ARS-446`): chains
heavier, knees and spine taking it; she sits and stands inside the passive field only, consistent with
`ARS-446`'s clearing of the active radius, and with `MCD-1715` (Lauris later his practice partner for
the active range, which Anirak does not stand in). She takes him as her charge unasked (`CC-114`:
"Anirak positioned herself as his protector without formal assignment, recognizing a body the world
wasn't built for"); the title echoes that rule. No fight, no kill; `CC-164` not engaged. Her stillness
inside the ring is at rest, outside any engagement; `ARS-373`'s no-stillness doctrine governs combat.
Her heart "rose a little with the work" of walking under load, short of any Fury state. The Captain is
referred to only through a measuring request carried by the bosun, consistent with the late Long Mask's
"the Avatars fought, the Captain directed" (`MCD-260`, `MCD-271`). Her age is never stated. Reserved
threads untouched: Hot/White and sync, Flood State, sonar, Sereth Vaul, Vestige, her origin's open
questions, the undead, the loss of any of her three.*

series (Game Plan pitch 3, locked at Batch 372). Close-third on Anirak per `VB-065`. The Long Mask,

Retrieval Detachment (`SBD-050`, `SBD-061`) comes for a subject of its own and brings a damping rig
