text:
=== anirak-chronicle-i-what-maw-11-kept.md

The table in the Captain's cabin was too small for the map. She drew it anyway.

Charcoal on the planks. A ring for the Slab. A square for the yard. A long bar for the pen block, four
tiers deep, under the hill. One hard stroke for the mast above the pens, and a small square at its top
for the box.

She walked the table's edge while she drew. Round and round. The charcoal lifted only to move.

Ghostwind leaned in the doorway. Sylas, twenty-nine, the harness slack on his shoulders, the disc on
his breastbone ticking as the weather shifted outside. The Captain stood at the stern window, his back
to them both.

"Front gate." Her finger on it. "Yard. Slab. Three doors off the yard. Two to the armories. One down."

She drew the tunnels. The old ways under the main run. Drains beneath the staging floor. A feed chute, bricked at the yard end, open on the hillside. A gap behind the triage station where the wall had settled.

"Ninety-one steps, chute to first grate. Dark all the way."

Ghostwind studied the lines a long while. Then her face.

"They'll know you at the gate."

"They know me everywhere."

He set a roll of oilcloth on the table and opened it. Bronze reeds, thirty, each as long as a forearm,
weighted at the foot. Ghostwind lifted one and hummed down it. The table
shook under her fingers as she passed, a buzz under hearing.

Ghostwind set it down.

The Captain turned from the window. Shirt open at the throat. The voice rough and low.

"Hold the yard an hour."

"Cost?"

"Don't stop moving."

• • •

Maw-11 sat in a fold of the southern coast hills. Grey stone. Low walls. A regional Maw, small beside
the Grand Maws. Three thousand eight hundred held behind its walls.

She came up the road at dusk, her three behind her. Edda. Hamund. Odile. No hoods. The Captain's
wagons waited on the hill road below the gate.

The smell reached her before the walls did. Lamp oil and old sweat. Wet straw gone sour. Iron, and
the copper under iron that is blood dried a long time. It went into her nose and down into her chest
and lay there.

The mast stood over the hill behind the walls, black against the last light. Taller than she
remembered. A thin pole. A box at the top, its face turned down toward the pen block.

She knew what came off it. She had carried it in her arms for years, in that place. Slow blood. Heavy
limbs. Arms that could not lift high enough to try a grate. Tonight it touched nothing of her.

Two gate guards. Spears grounded. Lanterns on hooks.

The first looked up. His face turned to her and stayed. The spear-butt slid on the stone. He caught it
late.

The second looked. The same.

She walked between them. Neither moved until she was past.

Edda and Hamund took the gate behind her. Odile set her back to the hinge post.

• • •

The yard. Packed sand over stone, raked smooth in rows. Lamps on poles at the corners. The Slab in the
middle, a raised floor of fitted blocks, the seams stained dark. Blood in the sand. Blood on the Slab's edge,
the afternoon's, not yet swept.

Forty men. Slab crews at the reset carts with brooms and iron bars. Guards at the armory doors, free men in the Maw's pay. Wardens
at the water trough, cups in hand, free men hired to the clubs.

Every face found her.

Cups stopped halfway to mouths. Brooms stopped. The noise of the yard went out. Forty faces held on her,
and she could not tell how much of that was hers.

Someone said it. Then several.

"Blades Fury."

She kept walking. Along the Slab's edge. Around it.

The guards came off the armory doors. Eight. Spears and hook-poles. The wardens came behind them with
clubs off the rack, twelve of them, bunched, clubs held too tight. The Slab crews stayed at the
carts, bars in their fists, watching.

She read them as she walked.

Guards: drilled. Spreading to flank. They would come together.

Wardens: they would come behind the guards.

Crews: they would come only if the rest went first.

Nobody in this yard has to die.

Hold them here. All of them alive.

She let the Fangs down off her forearms. Chain ran through her fingers. The hook-swords hung at her
knees and swung there, cold.

The lead guard came fast, spear low.

A Fang went out on its chain and hooked the haft below his hands. She pulled. The haft turned across
his hips and dragged him a step off his line. Her other hand had already gone over her shoulder. The
Morning Star came off her back with its talons open and caught the shaft at the hook. She wrenched. The
spear left him. He went past her empty-handed and fell on his side in the sand.

The pull came back up her arm heavier than she had sent it. She fed it into the next throw.

The links warmed where they crossed her fingers. Dull heat. Her heart went up a step.

Two guards at once. She ran the Fangs in a figure-eight, left and right in turn, crossing before her.
The air moaned through the links. One hook took a spear from a man's grip and threw it end over end
into the dark. The other opened a forearm to the bone. He dropped his pole and clutched the arm.

Each strike came back up her arms heavier than she sent it. Her shoulders loosened. The next throw went
out faster than the last.

A hook-pole came at her back. She felt the air move and stepped into the swing, inside the hook, and
took the shaft across her shoulder. It went into her and stayed in her. She turned with it and gave it
back through the Star into the man's thigh. He went down sideways.

The wardens bunched. Twelve, the last guards at the ends. They meant to rush her together.

She let her voice go.

Low in her throat. Under hearing. The crystal nodes in the gorget took it up and laid it out before
her, a wedge of it, forward.

The front rank's hands went to their chests. A man swayed. Another planted his club in the sand and
leaned on it. The man at the center stepped back to where he looked clear. He stood braced half a pace inside the
reach. The figure-eight came round and found him.

She opened the Star's head wide and swept it through them. Clubs spun out of hands. Men went to their
knees, heads down, retching into the sand, and stayed there. A guard tried to rise. He swayed, and sat
back down.

No one came again.

She kept moving. Round the Slab. Round again. The men on the ground lay where they fell, breathing. Every face in the yard
was on her.

The chains glowed along their links. Dull amber. Her heart sat raised and steady.

• • •

She felt it in the stone. A buzz in the teeth, under hearing. Up through the sand into her boots, into her knees, into her
ribs. A few voices. Then more. Then many.

The pens were singing.

Ghostwind had found them. Ghostwind had put the reeds in their hands.

Up on the mast, the box began to tick. A sound like a cooling stove. Then a whine, high and thin, that
set the yard's dogs barking somewhere behind the armories.

Down there the weight would be coming off. Down there every pen would be lifting its arms.

She kept walking. Round the Slab.

Then a hole tore in the low note. Voices stopping. Starting. Stopping again.

Someone was at the grate.

The third door off the yard stood a hand's width open. It had been shut when she came in. Lamp-light
below it, moving away.

She knew who held the key to that door.

She broke off. The chains came up off the sand. She went through the door at a run, the heat in the
links steady, climbing no higher.

• • •

Gethin Tamber ran the tunnels at Maw-11. He had run them in her years there. The staging. The armory
keys. The pens.

A free man. A careful one. Nothing left his tunnels uncounted.

Every tunnel
master in the south had heard of the Blackout.

He had come up to look at the yard, then gone back down the inner way from the armories to the
staging floor. The staging rack inside the door held the
hook-poles. She passed it at a run. One hook was gone.

• • •

The tunnel. Stone close on both sides. The ceiling low enough that tall men stooped. Lamps far apart,
most of them out. Water down the walls, pooling in the worn places of the floor. The pens' smell. She
had slept in it.

The chute was ninety-one steps from the first grate. She came from the staging floor instead. Forty
from there.

The singing filled the dark. Low. Uneven. Holes opening in it and closing.

The first grate. Iron bars floor to ceiling, crossbars at waist and head height, a lamp on a bracket.

Tamber stood at the bars with his back to her.

Beyond the grate, the first pen. Faces at the bars. Thin faces. Brands on the inner left forearms of the
hands that gripped iron. A bronze reed in a fist here and there. Mouths open on the low note. Two men
backed from the bars, mouths shut.

One woman at the front. Grey-haired, arms scarred to the elbow. She held a reed to her lips and sang
into it and kept her place.

Tamber had the hook-pole through the bars. The hook was at her throat.

"Stop," he said. "Stop that, or it goes in."

She sang.

Anirak came down the last ten paces still moving, the Fangs swinging at her knees.

One man. One pole, hooked, set at a throat. His weight set behind it.

He will drive it.

She spoke from the dark, once.

"Leave it. Walk."

He turned his head. The lamp caught her eyes. His face held on her. For a heartbeat he only looked. She
saw him know her. She saw him measure the four paces, the chain, the dark between, and come up short.

"Anirak," he said.

Beyond the bars, faces turned toward her as well. The singing faltered all along the grate. The low note
thinned.

The grey woman's voice held. Louder. Others found the note again around her.

She shifted her weight, step to step, the chains swaying. Tamber's eyes went back to the woman.

His shoulders set to drive the hook.

The Fang left her hand. Four paces of chain. The hook took his forearm above the wrist. She pulled. The
arm came back out of the bars and across his body, the pole with it, iron scraping iron. The Star was in
her other hand. Its talons closed on the shaft. She twisted. The pole went clattering down the tunnel.

The Fang came free. He had a knife at his belt. He drew it.

His face stayed on the grate. He went back to it, low and fast, knife up, his arm going through the bars
for the woman's belly.

The Star swung once. Everything she had gathered in the yard came through her arm into the Star's head.
It met the side of his skull above the ear. The bone gave like a plank under a dropped anvil. His head
struck the bars. His body slid down them into the water on the floor.

The knife fell into the pen. The grey woman put her foot on it.

She sang through all of it.

• • •

Anirak walked. Two steps each way before the grate. She turned
her face down the tunnel, from the bars. The singing found its depth again.

It filled the tunnel. It filled the stone. She felt it in her teeth.

Far above, through rock, a crack. Like a cask-stave splitting. Then the thin whine stopped.

In the pen, a man put his hands on two bars and pulled.

The iron groaned. It bent outward. Flakes of rust burst off it. The crossbar sheared at its seat.

Others came to the bars beside him.

Ghostwind came out of the dark at the tunnel's far end, the harness humming faint on his back. He looked
at the body at the grate. He looked at her.

"Two through four are singing. Four's grates are down."

"Yard's clear."

"Then they walk."

He was gone, the air sucking after him.

• • •

They walked.

Up through the staging tunnels and out the door into the yard. The staging hands came up out of the
tunnels with them. Grey faces, scarred arms, bare feet on
packed sand. Past the guards and wardens still sitting in the sand by the Slab. None of them rose. At the reset
carts the Slab crews set their iron bars down on the sand and fell in with the rest. Past the trough and the dark armory doors. Out through the gate. Edda and Hamund stood aside. Odile kept
her back to the hinge post. The gate stood open.

Three thousand eight hundred.

Some of them looked at her as they passed. Faces turned and held until the gate took them. A few she
knew. A scar. A way of walking. A face she had seen across the sand. None of them said a name. Out on the road someone was already shouting "Blades Fury."

The grey woman came last of her pen. She stopped before Anirak, the reed still in her fist.

She held it up a moment. Then she put it inside her shirt and walked on.

• • •

The Captain stood on the hill road beyond the gate, with the wagons and the crew. Coat on now. Collar
closed. The amber eyes burning dull in the dark of the hood. He was watching every face that passed
when she came up beside him, her three behind her, the chains cooling at her knees.

"Count." The collar ground it to gravel.

"Three thousand eight hundred."

"And."

"One."

His eyes held on her a beat. Then went to her hands.

"Who."

"The man with the keys. Hook at a singer's throat."

"Terms?"

"Once."

He nodded once and looked back to the road.

She waited beside him, shifting foot to foot. The chains swayed at her knees.

Behind them the mast stood over the empty pens. The box at its top hung split down the face, and cold.

=== anirak-chronicle-ii-the-second-harness.md

Tideglass at night. A free port. The Scourge's mark painted small on the harbor-master's door. The
Trust's tax-house three streets back, shuttered since the Sweep.

Rain on slate. Tar off the boat sheds. Kelp rotting on the slip. Lamps in the tavern windows along the
front, and the water black between the piers.

She lay awake in the loft over the net-maker's shop, and the sea told her why.

Hulls. Small ones, close, inside the harbor. One working oars, slow, quiet. One lying still. Out past
the mouth, something long and heavy, holding against the swell.

She was down the ladder with the chains in her hands and the Star across her back before the oars went quiet.

• • •

The woman was called Ardith. Twenty, or near it. She had come into Tideglass nine days before on a salt
barge, under a tarp, with a number cut into the skin behind her ear and nothing else she would talk
about. The harbor council had put her in the rooms over the chandler's. The crew had told the council
they would watch the rooms.

Edda had the door. Hamund had the lane. Odile had the roof across the way.

Anirak came round the corner of the chandler's at a run and took it in at one look.

Grey oilcloth over dull plate. No marks.

Edda down on one knee against the wall beside the door, a hand to her head, blood in her hair. A club lay on the flags
beside her.

The chandler's door open on a flagged entry, a stair going up from the back of it. Two of them at the
foot of the stair. Four more up it, near the top, and
Hamund and Odile on the stair below those four, pressing up. Staves cracking on the crew's
blades in the narrow well.

Six more in the lane mouth, close-packed, in no hurry. Two of them held a long canvas bundle between
them that clinked when they shifted it.

Behind the six, alone, a thin man in the same grey with a slate in one hand and a stylus in the other.

The stair. The two at its foot. Those first.

The six in the lane parted and let her through.

Too easy. She saw it as she passed them. Stopping would cost the stair.

The first man at the stair-foot swung a weighted strap low, for her arm. She took it on the cuff of her
left forearm. The strap wrapped the chain. She turned her wrist and reeled, and the strap brought him with
it, into her shoulder, and her shoulder put him into the wall. He slid down it.

The weight of him came back up her arm.

The second man crouched to come in low. A Fang went out on its chain along the flags and hooked his
ankle. She pulled. His leg went out from under him. His head met the bottom step.

The links began to warm across her fingers.

Behind her, iron weights clinked on cords. A whirring. Canvas falling away.

• • •

It came down over her from behind.

A net. Heavy. Thick bands of quilted leather stitched in a lattice, every band packed tight with lead
shot, mail under the leather. Weighted cords at its rim. It dropped over her head and shoulders, over
her arms and the chains, and the six from the lane were round her before it settled, each with a cord
in his fists, and they leaned back on the cords together.

The lattice drew tight. It pinned her arms to her sides and pressed the Fangs flat against her thighs.

She drove an elbow back. It sank into a band. The shot shifted and swallowed the blow. The blow died in
the lead and came back up her arm as nothing at all.

She ground a Fang's edge against the band across her hip. Leather parted. Mail under it. The edge
skidded.

The net's crown cinched as the six leaned back. A hood sewn into it came down over her face, coarse,
sodden. Cold water ran down her neck. It closed over her mouth and her throat, the
gorget and all. The lamps went out.

She could move a hand's breadth any way. No more.

Her heart slowed. She let it, to keep her head. The links cooled with it under the bands. The
weight she had gathered began to leak out of her arms. Down. Out through her shoulders. Out of her
chest. Water from a cracked jar. Every breath of stillness took more of it.

They harnessed me. So the blows wouldn't stack.

• • •

On the stair above her, blades on staves. Hamund's grunt. Odile's breath hissing through her teeth. Then a muffled
sound through a hand, and boots going up and away, across the rooms over her head, and a shutter banging
open at the back of the building, the side over the water.

Hamund's voice. "Window! They're out the back!"

Outside the hood, close, a calm voice. From behind the cords.

"Hold tension. Four minutes."

A stylus scratching on slate, close behind the cords.

A man reading a tide-mark. No heat in it. Every word chosen.

Another, rougher. "She's stopped pulling."

Then, nearer. To her.

"Anirak." The way a clerk reads a name off a docket. "Do not exert yourself. No one here is authorized
to injure you."

She could not move enough. Every breath of it bled her more.

Her voice was under the wet cloth, ready. She held it.

Hamund and Odile were on the stair, before her. In the line it would take. On a stair.

She held it.

Boots on the steps, coming down fast. Hamund. Odile. Past her, one on either side. To the cords at her
flanks.

Two cords in front of her, heavy, one either side of the stair foot. Nothing on the steps. Edda's
boot scraping the flags, behind her, out past the door.

She let it go.

Low. Under hearing. It went out through the wet cloth, forward.

It reached the two before her. She felt it reach them, down the cords. The forward lines shuddered.
One went slack in a jerk. Then tight. Then slack. A man retching on the flags.

Behind her, the calm voice, a half-beat late. "The hood --"

They built it against a sound.

"Forward lines. Hold."

The forward lines went slack again.

The slack came. An arm's length.

She turned into the slack. Hard. All her weight. The net came round with her, the lead bands swinging
out on their stitching. The cords on the far side snapped taut, and a man's whole weight hit the end of
his.

That came back up her arms.

She turned the other way. Another cord came taut. Another man's weight hit the end of it and came
stumbling in across the stones.

That came back up her arms too.

Her heart came up. The links warmed again under the bands.

"Left cord!" Hamund. A blow. A grunt. The left cord went dead.

"Right!" Odile. The right one too.

Her two, on the cord-men. They held the ground around her and took the
cords off her one at a time.

She worked one arm up through the slack lattice. Got a hand to the crown cord. Tore the hood back.

Lamps through the open door. Rain. The lane.

Every face in the lane on her.

The thin man stood three paces back from all of it. The slate in one hand, the stylus in the other. No
weapon. His face held on her with all the rest. He looked down at his slate. Looked up.

She went out through the last of the lattice. The bands fell round her feet on the stones.

The cord-men were down, or backing off with their hands open. Not one of them came at her.

The thin man stayed where he was, three paces back.

She went past him.

• • •

The lane. The slip. The end of the second pier, at a dead run, the chains warm and singing.

Out past the mouth, the oar-beat had stopped against something heavy. As her feet hit the last planks,
the wake under it deepened. It gathered way before a stiff land breeze.

She set a foot on the last pile and looked at the swell.

Too far. Too fast.

At the end of the pier she paced. Three strides each way. Rain on the planks. The weight in her arms and
nowhere to spend it.

The keel went out past the point. Then the swell took it, and there was only the swell.

• • •

Hamund met her at the head of the slip.

"Four went with her. Rest over the seawall, carrying their own. The boat under it." He wiped rain off his face. "Thirteen
in all. Nobody dead."

She had felt that second hull from the loft. She had let it go for the keel.

They walked back up the lane together.

The net lay across the chandler's threshold where it fell. Edda sat on the chandler's step with a rag to her head. Odile held
the rag.

Hamund kicked the net. It clinked.

"They made that for you."

"Yes."

"How long, a thing like that?"

She looked down at it. The bands. The mail. The stitching. Six men drilled on six cords until they could
close it on a moving body in one breath. A hood sewn in, soaked to stop a sound.

"Long."

"Who?"

"The one with the slate."

Odile looked up. "Gone."

"It's on his slate."

She picked the net up. The lead dragged in every band. She carried it to the end of the slip and threw it
in the harbor. It went down fast.

Upstairs in the chandler's rooms, the bed was still made. A cup of water on the sill. The back shutter
hung open on the rain.

She stood in the doorway and looked at the cup.

Then she went down to the harbor council's night clerk, and said the name while he wrote it down. Ardith.
Twenty, or near it. A number behind the ear. Taken.

=== anirak-chronicle-iii-the-body-the-world-was-not-built-for.md

He came aboard on the morning launch, in fog.

She felt the launch before she saw it. A small hull answering the swell slow, like a laden boat. Six
oarsmen laboring at it as if one more cask sat in the bottom of it, a cask of lead.

The launch came alongside. The oarsmen shipped their oars fast and crowded to the far gunwale, all six,
so the boat listed. In the stern a young man sat alone with a sea-bag on his knees.

Hamund, at the rail beside her, said it under his breath. "The one from the islands."

Word had come the week before. Someone had been found on the shelf islands and was being sent out.

The young man came up the side ladder. The rungs creaked under him, every one, as if he weighed a third
again what he looked.

He stepped onto the deck.

The planks groaned. A long low sound deep in the wood, the sound a hull makes in a heavy sea. The deck
lay flat calm.

The men nearest the ladder stepped back a few paces. Their bodies did it for them. Something in the air
around him leaned on them, and they leaned away.

He watched them do it. His face stayed as it was. He had seen it before, by the look of him.

• • •

The bosun cleared him a berth under the forecastle, on deck, by the anchor housing. Nobody told him to.

By the end of the first day a shape followed the young man everywhere on the deck.

A ring. A dozen paces across. Empty.

Where he walked, the ring walked with him. Men coiling line drifted out of it. Men at the pumps found
reasons to work the other pump. At the evening meal the crew sat close along the benches amidships,
elbow to elbow. He took his bowl to the bow and sat on the anchor housing with the ring around him and
the dark coming on.

The planks under the anchor housing groaned through the meal. Low. Steady. A ship talking to itself
about a weight.

His name was Ren. Somebody had it from the launch crew.

• • •

She watched him for three days.

The young man ate alone. Slept alone. Worked the pumps alone, at the hours nobody else took. He moved
through the ship slowly and set his feet down with care, the way a man walks on ice.

He made no complaint. He asked nobody to stand nearer. He asked for nothing.

Her three watched her watch him. Edda said nothing. Odile said nothing. Hamund said, on the second
night, "They're afraid of him."

"They're heavy near him."

"Same thing, to a body."

She had no answer to that.

On the third evening he looked up from the bow. Across the waist of the ship, across the benches and the
crew between them, to where she stood at the mainmast.

He looked at her. Then at the sea. Then back at her.

She waited for his face to set and hold, the way every face set and held. It stayed loose. His eyes
went to her chains. To her hands. Back to her face. Off to the sea again. Back.

Every time, they came back. Loose.

Faces had left her before. The Captain's, at Chain Harbor and since, to her hands. They came back set.

A man alone in a ring nobody would cross. A man who looked at her, and looked away, and looked back.

Go and stand in it.

• • •

She walked across the deck to the bow.

The crew on the benches turned to watch her go, all of them, faces holding on her the whole length of
the deck. She passed the end of the benches. Passed the foremast. Came to the edge of the ring.

She stepped into it.

The weight came down on her at once. A load, flat and even. As if the air had grown a hand and set it on
her shoulders and pressed. Her knees took it. Her spine took it. The chains on her forearms hung heavier
and swung less. The plank under her boot gave a groan of its own.

She took another step. Each one the same weight. Her heart lifted a little with the work of it.

He watched her come. His eyes moved the whole way. Down to the chains. To her boots on the groaning
planks. Back to her face.

• • •

"You will want to step back," he said. Quiet. He stayed seated. "It is heavy, this close."

"Yes."

"Most people step back."

"I saw."

She did not sit. Sitting under a weight was the harness again. She stood an arm's length from him with
her bowl in her hand and ate on her feet, shifting her weight from one foot to the other, the load riding
down through her into the planks. The planks groaned under the two of them together, one long low note.

He looked at her for a while. She let him. She had nothing to measure it against.

"Does it hurt you?" he said.

"It's heavy."

"That is not an answer."

"It's all of it."

He almost smiled. He looked down at the bowl in his hands.

"At home they built the walls thicker for me," he said. "Then thicker again. Then there was no wall thick
enough."

She did not ask where home was.

Out on the benches the crew had gone back to their bowls. Her three sat at the end of the nearest bench,
outside the ring, where everyone sat. Hamund was watching. He caught her eye, and his face set and held
the way every face did, and she looked away from him first.

• • •

She ate at the bow after that.

Every evening. Inside the ring, on her feet, the weight on her shoulders through the whole meal, the
planks groaning their low note under two bowls. She explained it to no one. Nobody asked.

In the mornings she worked the pumps at his hours. She walked the waist deck with him when he walked it,
on the side nearest the crew. The men coiling line looked up as she passed, and their faces turned to her
and held, and the ring went by beside her unremarked.

On the fifth day a deckhand cut too close behind him with a cask on his shoulder, misjudged the weight,
and went to one knee in it, the cask rolling. He scrambled back out over the ring's edge on his hands and
knees and stood up outside it, swearing at Ren. Loud. The whole waist heard.

Swearing at a man for the weight he was born with.

She stepped out of the ring and stood in front of the deckhand, the chains hanging at her knees.

His face turned to her and held.

"Go round," she said.

He went round. He went wide.

She stepped back into the weight. Ren had not moved. He was looking at her.

"I did not ask you to do that," he said.

"No."

He waited. She gave him nothing more.

• • •

On the ninth day, word came forward from the stern. The Captain wanted the young man's measure. Feet.
Chest. The weight of him. There would be boots. A vest.

Ren listened to the bosun say it from the edge of the ring. Then he looked at her.

"A vest," he said. "To make me less."

"To let people near when you want them near."

He thought about that a long time, in the stillness that she was learning was the way he counted.

"How do you know what he builds?"

She held up one wrist. The chain ran from the cuff to the Fang at her knee. The links hung cool and
heavier than they should, inside the weight.

"He measured my heart," she said. "Then he built these to it."

He looked at the chain. Then at her face. Then away to the sea, and back.

That night, in her hammock, she listened to the ship. The groan in the forward timbers went on past
midnight, low and even. A weight the hull had learned to carry.

She fell asleep counting it.

Anirak's first wave is clean: all three Chronicles have passed independent review. Chronicle I took five rounds, II six, and III four. Before presenting I/II/III I made a few small wording changes after their last clean review. Every change was taken from that review's own optional list, and none adds a fact. All three are committed and pushed, still marked unlocked. Here they are in full, in story order.

# Anirak Chronicle I: What Maw-11 Kept

*Kanja 140, the Long Mask: the Maw Cascade's inside job at Maw-11 (`MCD-264`). Her first marquee kill.*

The table in the Captain's cabin was too small for the map. She drew it anyway.

Charcoal on the planks. A ring for the Slab. A square for the yard. A long bar for the pen block, four tiers deep, under the hill. One hard stroke for the mast above the pens, and a small square at its top for the box.

She walked the table's edge while she drew. Round and round. The charcoal lifted only to move.

Ghostwind leaned in the doorway. Sylas, twenty-nine, the harness slack on his shoulders, the disc on his breastbone ticking as the weather shifted outside. The Captain stood at the stern window, his back to them both.

"Front gate." Her finger on it. "Yard. Slab. Three doors off the yard. Two to the armories. One down."

She drew the tunnels. The old ways under the main run. Drains beneath the staging floor. A feed chute, bricked at the yard end, open on the hillside. A gap behind the triage station where the wall had settled.

"Ninety-one steps, chute to first grate. Dark all the way."

Ghostwind studied the lines a long while. Then her face.

"They'll know you at the gate."

"They know me everywhere."

He set a roll of oilcloth on the table and opened it. Bronze reeds, thirty, each as long as a forearm, weighted at the foot. Ghostwind lifted one and hummed down it. The table shook under her fingers as she passed, a buzz under hearing.

Ghostwind set it down.

The Captain turned from the window. Shirt open at the throat. The voice rough and low.

"Hold the yard an hour."

"Cost?"

"Don't stop moving."

• • •

Maw-11 sat in a fold of the southern coast hills. Grey stone. Low walls. A regional Maw, small beside the Grand Maws. Three thousand eight hundred held behind its walls.

She came up the road at dusk, her three behind her. Edda. Hamund. Odile. No hoods. The Captain's wagons waited on the hill road below the gate.

The smell reached her before the walls did. Lamp oil and old sweat. Wet straw gone sour. Iron, and the copper under iron that is blood dried a long time. It went into her nose and down into her chest and lay there.

The mast stood over the hill behind the walls, black against the last light. Taller than she remembered. A thin pole. A box at the top, its face turned down toward the pen block.

She knew what came off it. She had carried it in her arms for years, in that place. Slow blood. Heavy limbs. Arms that could not lift high enough to try a grate. Tonight it touched nothing of her.

Two gate guards. Spears grounded. Lanterns on hooks.

The first looked up. His face turned to her and stayed. The spear-butt slid on the stone. He caught it late.

The second looked. The same.

She walked between them. Neither moved until she was past.

Edda and Hamund took the gate behind her. Odile set her back to the hinge post.

• • •

The yard. Packed sand over stone, raked smooth in rows. Lamps on poles at the corners. The Slab in the middle, a raised floor of fitted blocks, the seams stained dark. Blood in the sand. Blood on the Slab's edge, the afternoon's, not yet swept.

Forty men. Slab crews at the reset carts with brooms and iron bars. Guards at the armory doors, free men in the Maw's pay. Wardens at the water trough, cups in hand, free men hired to the clubs.

Every face found her.

Cups stopped halfway to mouths. Brooms stopped. The noise of the yard went out. Forty faces held on her, and she could not tell how much of that was hers.

Someone said it. Then several.

"Blades Fury."

She kept walking. Along the Slab's edge. Around it.

The guards came off the armory doors. Eight. Spears and hook-poles. The wardens came behind them with clubs off the rack, twelve of them, bunched, clubs held too tight. The Slab crews stayed at the carts, bars in their fists, watching.

She read them as she walked.

Guards: drilled. Spreading to flank. They would come together.

Wardens: they would come behind the guards.

Crews: they would come only if the rest went first.

Nobody in this yard has to die.

Hold them here. All of them alive.

She let the Fangs down off her forearms. Chain ran through her fingers. The hook-swords hung at her knees and swung there, cold.

The lead guard came fast, spear low.

A Fang went out on its chain and hooked the haft below his hands. She pulled. The haft turned across his hips and dragged him a step off his line. Her other hand had already gone over her shoulder. The Morning Star came off her back with its talons open and caught the shaft at the hook. She wrenched. The spear left him. He went past her empty-handed and fell on his side in the sand.

The pull came back up her arm heavier than she had sent it. She fed it into the next throw.

The links warmed where they crossed her fingers. Dull heat. Her heart went up a step.

Two guards at once. She ran the Fangs in a figure-eight, left and right in turn, crossing before her. The air moaned through the links. One hook took a spear from a man's grip and threw it end over end into the dark. The other opened a forearm to the bone. He dropped his pole and clutched the arm.

Each strike came back up her arms heavier than she sent it. Her shoulders loosened. The next throw went out faster than the last.

A hook-pole came at her back. She felt the air move and stepped into the swing, inside the hook, and took the shaft across her shoulder. It went into her and stayed in her. She turned with it and gave it back through the Star into the man's thigh. He went down sideways.

The wardens bunched. Twelve, the last guards at the ends. They meant to rush her together.

She let her voice go.

Low in her throat. Under hearing. The crystal nodes in the gorget took it up and laid it out before her, a wedge of it, forward.

The front rank's hands went to their chests. A man swayed. Another planted his club in the sand and leaned on it. The man at the center stepped back to where he looked clear. He stood braced half a pace inside the reach. The figure-eight came round and found him.

She opened the Star's head wide and swept it through them. Clubs spun out of hands. Men went to their knees, heads down, retching into the sand, and stayed there. A guard tried to rise. He swayed, and sat back down.

No one came again.

She kept moving. Round the Slab. Round again. The men on the ground lay where they fell, breathing. Every face in the yard was on her.

The chains glowed along their links. Dull amber. Her heart sat raised and steady.

• • •

She felt it in the stone. A buzz in the teeth, under hearing. Up through the sand into her boots, into her knees, into her ribs. A few voices. Then more. Then many.

The pens were singing.

Ghostwind had found them. Ghostwind had put the reeds in their hands.

Up on the mast, the box began to tick. A sound like a cooling stove. Then a whine, high and thin, that set the yard's dogs barking somewhere behind the armories.

Down there the weight would be coming off. Down there every pen would be lifting its arms.

She kept walking. Round the Slab.

Then a hole tore in the low note. Voices stopping. Starting. Stopping again.

Someone was at the grate.

The third door off the yard stood a hand's width open. It had been shut when she came in. Lamp-light below it, moving away.

She knew who held the key to that door.

She broke off. The chains came up off the sand. She went through the door at a run, the heat in the links steady, climbing no higher.

• • •

Gethin Tamber ran the tunnels at Maw-11. He had run them in her years there. The staging. The armory keys. The pens.

A free man. A careful one. Nothing left his tunnels uncounted.

Every tunnel master in the south had heard of the Blackout.

He had come up to look at the yard, then gone back down the inner way from the armories to the staging floor. The staging rack inside the door held the hook-poles. She passed it at a run. One hook was gone.

• • •

The tunnel. Stone close on both sides. The ceiling low enough that tall men stooped. Lamps far apart, most of them out. Water down the walls, pooling in the worn places of the floor. The pens' smell. She had slept in it.

The chute was ninety-one steps from the first grate. She came from the staging floor instead. Forty from there.

The singing filled the dark. Low. Uneven. Holes opening in it and closing.

The first grate. Iron bars floor to ceiling, crossbars at waist and head height, a lamp on a bracket.

Tamber stood at the bars with his back to her.

Beyond the grate, the first pen. Faces at the bars. Thin faces. Brands on the inner left forearms of the hands that gripped iron. A bronze reed in a fist here and there. Mouths open on the low note. Two men backed from the bars, mouths shut.

One woman at the front. Grey-haired, arms scarred to the elbow. She held a reed to her lips and sang into it and kept her place.

Tamber had the hook-pole through the bars. The hook was at her throat.

"Stop," he said. "Stop that, or it goes in."

She sang.

Anirak came down the last ten paces still moving, the Fangs swinging at her knees.

One man. One pole, hooked, set at a throat. His weight set behind it.

He will drive it.

She spoke from the dark, once.

"Leave it. Walk."

He turned his head. The lamp caught her eyes. His face held on her. For a heartbeat he only looked. She saw him know her. She saw him measure the four paces, the chain, the dark between, and come up short.

"Anirak," he said.

Beyond the bars, faces turned toward her as well. The singing faltered all along the grate. The low note thinned.

The grey woman's voice held. Louder. Others found the note again around her.

She shifted her weight, step to step, the chains swaying. Tamber's eyes went back to the woman.

His shoulders set to drive the hook.

The Fang left her hand. Four paces of chain. The hook took his forearm above the wrist. She pulled. The arm came back out of the bars and across his body, the pole with it, iron scraping iron. The Star was in her other hand. Its talons closed on the shaft. She twisted. The pole went clattering down the tunnel.

The Fang came free. He had a knife at his belt. He drew it.

His face stayed on the grate. He went back to it, low and fast, knife up, his arm going through the bars for the woman's belly.

The Star swung once. Everything she had gathered in the yard came through her arm into the Star's head. It met the side of his skull above the ear. The bone gave like a plank under a dropped anvil. His head struck the bars. His body slid down them into the water on the floor.

The knife fell into the pen. The grey woman put her foot on it.

She sang through all of it.

• • •

Anirak walked. Two steps each way before the grate. She turned her face down the tunnel, from the bars. The singing found its depth again.

It filled the tunnel. It filled the stone. She felt it in her teeth.

Far above, through rock, a crack. Like a cask-stave splitting. Then the thin whine stopped.

In the pen, a man put his hands on two bars and pulled.

The iron groaned. It bent outward. Flakes of rust burst off it. The crossbar sheared at its seat.

Others came to the bars beside him.

Ghostwind came out of the dark at the tunnel's far end, the harness humming faint on his back. He looked at the body at the grate. He looked at her.

"Two through four are singing. Four's grates are down."

"Yard's clear."

"Then they walk."

He was gone, the air sucking after him.

• • •

They walked.

Up through the staging tunnels and out the door into the yard. The staging hands came up out of the tunnels with them. Grey faces, scarred arms, bare feet on packed sand. Past the guards and wardens still sitting in the sand by the Slab. None of them rose. At the reset carts the Slab crews set their iron bars down on the sand and fell in with the rest. Past the trough and the dark armory doors. Out through the gate. Edda and Hamund stood aside. Odile kept her back to the hinge post. The gate stood open.

Three thousand eight hundred.

Some of them looked at her as they passed. Faces turned and held until the gate took them. A few she knew. A scar. A way of walking. A face she had seen across the sand. None of them said a name. Out on the road someone was already shouting "Blades Fury."

The grey woman came last of her pen. She stopped before Anirak, the reed still in her fist.

She held it up a moment. Then she put it inside her shirt and walked on.

• • •

The Captain stood on the hill road beyond the gate, with the wagons and the crew. Coat on now. Collar closed. The amber eyes burning dull in the dark of the hood. He was watching every face that passed when she came up beside him, her three behind her, the chains cooling at her knees.

"Count." The collar ground it to gravel.

"Three thousand eight hundred."

"And."

"One."

His eyes held on her a beat. Then went to her hands.

"Who."

"The man with the keys. Hook at a singer's throat."

"Terms?"

"Once."

He nodded once and looked back to the road.

She waited beside him, shifting foot to foot. The chains swayed at her knees.

Behind them the mast stood over the empty pens. The box at its top hung split down the face, and cold.

# Anirak Chronicle II: The Second Harness

*Roughly Kanja 175, the Long Mask, after Maw-11 and before Ren. No kill.*

Tideglass at night. A free port. The Scourge's mark painted small on the harbor-master's door. The Trust's tax-house three streets back, shuttered since the Sweep.

Rain on slate. Tar off the boat sheds. Kelp rotting on the slip. Lamps in the tavern windows along the front, and the water black between the piers.

She lay awake in the loft over the net-maker's shop, and the sea told her why.

Hulls. Small ones, close, inside the harbor. One working oars, slow, quiet. One lying still. Out past the mouth, something long and heavy, holding against the swell.

She was down the ladder with the chains in her hands and the Star across her back before the oars went quiet.

• • •

The woman was called Ardith. Twenty, or near it. She had come into Tideglass nine days before on a salt barge, under a tarp, with a number cut into the skin behind her ear and nothing else she would talk about. The harbor council had put her in the rooms over the chandler's. The crew had told the council they would watch the rooms.

Edda had the door. Hamund had the lane. Odile had the roof across the way.

Anirak came round the corner of the chandler's at a run and took it in at one look.

Grey oilcloth over dull plate. No marks.

Edda down on one knee against the wall beside the door, a hand to her head, blood in her hair. A club lay on the flags beside her.

The chandler's door open on a flagged entry, a stair going up from the back of it. Two of them at the foot of the stair. Four more up it, near the top, and Hamund and Odile on the stair below those four, pressing up. Staves cracking on the crew's blades in the narrow well.

Six more in the lane mouth, close-packed, in no hurry. Two of them held a long canvas bundle between them that clinked when they shifted it.

Behind the six, alone, a thin man in the same grey with a slate in one hand and a stylus in the other.

The stair. The two at its foot. Those first.

The six in the lane parted and let her through.

Too easy. She saw it as she passed them. Stopping would cost the stair.

The first man at the stair-foot swung a weighted strap low, for her arm. She took it on the cuff of her left forearm. The strap wrapped the chain. She turned her wrist and reeled, and the strap brought him with it, into her shoulder, and her shoulder put him into the wall. He slid down it.

The weight of him came back up her arm.

The second man crouched to come in low. A Fang went out on its chain along the flags and hooked his ankle. She pulled. His leg went out from under him. His head met the bottom step.

The links began to warm across her fingers.

Behind her, iron weights clinked on cords. A whirring. Canvas falling away.

• • •

It came down over her from behind.

A net. Heavy. Thick bands of quilted leather stitched in a lattice, every band packed tight with lead shot, mail under the leather. Weighted cords at its rim. It dropped over her head and shoulders, over her arms and the chains, and the six from the lane were round her before it settled, each with a cord in his fists, and they leaned back on the cords together.

The lattice drew tight. It pinned her arms to her sides and pressed the Fangs flat against her thighs.

She drove an elbow back. It sank into a band. The shot shifted and swallowed the blow. The blow died in the lead and came back up her arm as nothing at all.

She ground a Fang's edge against the band across her hip. Leather parted. Mail under it. The edge skidded.

The net's crown cinched as the six leaned back. A hood sewn into it came down over her face, coarse, sodden. Cold water ran down her neck. It closed over her mouth and her throat, the gorget and all. The lamps went out.

She could move a hand's breadth any way. No more.

Her heart slowed. She let it, to keep her head. The links cooled with it under the bands. The weight she had gathered began to leak out of her arms. Down. Out through her shoulders. Out of her chest. Water from a cracked jar. Every breath of stillness took more of it.

They harnessed me. So the blows wouldn't stack.

• • •

On the stair above her, blades on staves. Hamund's grunt. Odile's breath hissing through her teeth. Then a muffled sound through a hand, and boots going up and away, across the rooms over her head, and a shutter banging open at the back of the building, the side over the water.

Hamund's voice. "Window! They're out the back!"

Outside the hood, close, a calm voice. From behind the cords.

"Hold tension. Four minutes."

A stylus scratching on slate, close behind the cords.

A man reading a tide-mark. No heat in it. Every word chosen.

Another, rougher. "She's stopped pulling."

Then, nearer. To her.

"Anirak." The way a clerk reads a name off a docket. "Do not exert yourself. No one here is authorized to injure you."

She could not move enough. Every breath of it bled her more.

Her voice was under the wet cloth, ready. She held it.

Hamund and Odile were on the stair, before her. In the line it would take. On a stair.

She held it.

Boots on the steps, coming down fast. Hamund. Odile. Past her, one on either side. To the cords at her flanks.

Two cords in front of her, heavy, one either side of the stair foot. Nothing on the steps. Edda's boot scraping the flags, behind her, out past the door.

She let it go.

Low. Under hearing. It went out through the wet cloth, forward.

It reached the two before her. She felt it reach them, down the cords. The forward lines shuddered. One went slack in a jerk. Then tight. Then slack. A man retching on the flags.

Behind her, the calm voice, a half-beat late. "The hood --"

They built it against a sound.

"Forward lines. Hold."

The forward lines went slack again.

The slack came. An arm's length.

She turned into the slack. Hard. All her weight. The net came round with her, the lead bands swinging out on their stitching. The cords on the far side snapped taut, and a man's whole weight hit the end of his.

That came back up her arms.

She turned the other way. Another cord came taut. Another man's weight hit the end of it and came stumbling in across the stones.

That came back up her arms too.

Her heart came up. The links warmed again under the bands.

"Left cord!" Hamund. A blow. A grunt. The left cord went dead.

"Right!" Odile. The right one too.

Her two, on the cord-men. They held the ground around her and took the cords off her one at a time.

She worked one arm up through the slack lattice. Got a hand to the crown cord. Tore the hood back.

Lamps through the open door. Rain. The lane.

Every face in the lane on her.

The thin man stood three paces back from all of it. The slate in one hand, the stylus in the other. No weapon. His face held on her with all the rest. He looked down at his slate. Looked up.

She went out through the last of the lattice. The bands fell round her feet on the stones.

The cord-men were down, or backing off with their hands open. Not one of them came at her.

The thin man stayed where he was, three paces back.

She went past him.

• • •

The lane. The slip. The end of the second pier, at a dead run, the chains warm and singing.

Out past the mouth, the oar-beat had stopped against something heavy. As her feet hit the last planks, the wake under it deepened. It gathered way before a stiff land breeze.

She set a foot on the last pile and looked at the swell.

Too far. Too fast.

At the end of the pier she paced. Three strides each way. Rain on the planks. The weight in her arms and nowhere to spend it.

The keel went out past the point. Then the swell took it, and there was only the swell.

• • •

Hamund met her at the head of the slip.

"Four went with her. Rest over the seawall, carrying their own. The boat under it." He wiped rain off his face. "Thirteen in all. Nobody dead."

She had felt that second hull from the loft. She had let it go for the keel.

They walked back up the lane together.

The net lay across the chandler's threshold where it fell. Edda sat on the chandler's step with a rag to her head. Odile held the rag.

Hamund kicked the net. It clinked.

"They made that for you."

"Yes."

"How long, a thing like that?"

She looked down at it. The bands. The mail. The stitching. Six men drilled on six cords until they could close it on a moving body in one breath. A hood sewn in, soaked to stop a sound.

"Long."

"Who?"

"The one with the slate."

Odile looked up. "Gone."

"It's on his slate."

She picked the net up. The lead dragged in every band. She carried it to the end of the slip and threw it in the harbor. It went down fast.

Upstairs in the chandler's rooms, the bed was still made. A cup of water on the sill. The back shutter hung open on the rain.

She stood in the doorway and looked at the cup.

Then she went down to the harbor council's night clerk, and said the name while he wrote it down. Ardith. Twenty, or near it. A number behind the ear. Taken.

# Anirak Chronicle III: The Body the World Was Not Built For

*Roughly Kanja 300, late in the Long Mask. Ren comes aboard. No kill, no fight.*

He came aboard on the morning launch, in fog.

She felt the launch before she saw it. A small hull answering the swell slow, like a laden boat. Six oarsmen laboring at it as if one more cask sat in the bottom of it, a cask of lead.

The launch came alongside. The oarsmen shipped their oars fast and crowded to the far gunwale, all six, so the boat listed. In the stern a young man sat alone with a sea-bag on his knees.

Hamund, at the rail beside her, said it under his breath. "The one from the islands."

Word had come the week before. Someone had been found on the shelf islands and was being sent out.

The young man came up the side ladder. The rungs creaked under him, every one, as if he weighed a third again what he looked.

He stepped onto the deck.

The planks groaned. A long low sound deep in the wood, the sound a hull makes in a heavy sea. The deck lay flat calm.

The men nearest the ladder stepped back a few paces. Their bodies did it for them. Something in the air around him leaned on them, and they leaned away.

He watched them do it. His face stayed as it was. He had seen it before, by the look of him.

• • •

The bosun cleared him a berth under the forecastle, on deck, by the anchor housing. Nobody told him to.

By the end of the first day a shape followed the young man everywhere on the deck.

A ring. A dozen paces across. Empty.

Where he walked, the ring walked with him. Men coiling line drifted out of it. Men at the pumps found reasons to work the other pump. At the evening meal the crew sat close along the benches amidships, elbow to elbow. He took his bowl to the bow and sat on the anchor housing with the ring around him and the dark coming on.

The planks under the anchor housing groaned through the meal. Low. Steady. A ship talking to itself about a weight.

His name was Ren. Somebody had it from the launch crew.

• • •

She watched him for three days.

The young man ate alone. Slept alone. Worked the pumps alone, at the hours nobody else took. He moved through the ship slowly and set his feet down with care, the way a man walks on ice.

He made no complaint. He asked nobody to stand nearer. He asked for nothing.

Her three watched her watch him. Edda said nothing. Odile said nothing. Hamund said, on the second night, "They're afraid of him."

"They're heavy near him."

"Same thing, to a body."

She had no answer to that.

On the third evening he looked up from the bow. Across the waist of the ship, across the benches and the crew between them, to where she stood at the mainmast.

He looked at her. Then at the sea. Then back at her.

She waited for his face to set and hold, the way every face set and held. It stayed loose. His eyes went to her chains. To her hands. Back to her face. Off to the sea again. Back.

Every time, they came back. Loose.

Faces had left her before. The Captain's, at Chain Harbor and since, to her hands. They came back set.

A man alone in a ring nobody would cross. A man who looked at her, and looked away, and looked back.

Go and stand in it.

• • •

She walked across the deck to the bow.

The crew on the benches turned to watch her go, all of them, faces holding on her the whole length of the deck. She passed the end of the benches. Passed the foremast. Came to the edge of the ring.

She stepped into it.

The weight came down on her at once. A load, flat and even. As if the air had grown a hand and set it on her shoulders and pressed. Her knees took it. Her spine took it. The chains on her forearms hung heavier and swung less. The plank under her boot gave a groan of its own.

She took another step. Each one the same weight. Her heart lifted a little with the work of it.

He watched her come. His eyes moved the whole way. Down to the chains. To her boots on the groaning planks. Back to her face.

• • •

"You will want to step back," he said. Quiet. He stayed seated. "It is heavy, this close."

"Yes."

"Most people step back."

"I saw."

She did not sit. Sitting under a weight was the harness again. She stood an arm's length from him with her bowl in her hand and ate on her feet, shifting her weight from one foot to the other, the load riding down through her into the planks. The planks groaned under the two of them together, one long low note.

He looked at her for a while. She let him. She had nothing to measure it against.

"Does it hurt you?" he said.

"It's heavy."

"That is not an answer."

"It's all of it."

He almost smiled. He looked down at the bowl in his hands.

"At home they built the walls thicker for me," he said. "Then thicker again. Then there was no wall thick enough."

She did not ask where home was.

Out on the benches the crew had gone back to their bowls. Her three sat at the end of the nearest bench, outside the ring, where everyone sat. Hamund was watching. He caught her eye, and his face set and held the way every face did, and she looked away from him first.

• • •

She ate at the bow after that.

Every evening. Inside the ring, on her feet, the weight on her shoulders through the whole meal, the planks groaning their low note under two bowls. She explained it to no one. Nobody asked.

In the mornings she worked the pumps at his hours. She walked the waist deck with him when he walked it, on the side nearest the crew. The men coiling line looked up as she passed, and their faces turned to her and held, and the ring went by beside her unremarked.

On the fifth day a deckhand cut too close behind him with a cask on his shoulder, misjudged the weight, and went to one knee in it, the cask rolling. He scrambled back out over the ring's edge on his hands and knees and stood up outside it, swearing at Ren. Loud. The whole waist heard.

Swearing at a man for the weight he was born with.

She stepped out of the ring and stood in front of the deckhand, the chains hanging at her knees.

His face turned to her and held.

"Go round," she said.

He went round. He went wide.

She stepped back into the weight. Ren had not moved. He was looking at her.

"I did not ask you to do that," he said.

"No."

He waited. She gave him nothing more.

• • •

On the ninth day, word came forward from the stern. The Captain wanted the young man's measure. Feet. Chest. The weight of him. There would be boots. A vest.

Ren listened to the bosun say it from the edge of the ring. Then he looked at her.

"A vest," he said. "To make me less."

"To let people near when you want them near."

He thought about that a long time, in the stillness that she was learning was the way he counted.

"How do you know what he builds?"

She held up one wrist. The chain ran from the cuff to the Fang at her knee. The links hung cool and heavier than they should, inside the weight.

"He measured my heart," she said. "Then he built these to it."

He looked at the chain. Then at her face. Then away to the sea, and back.

That night, in her hammock, she listened to the ship. The groan in the forward timbers went on past midnight, low and even. A weight the hull had learned to carry.

She fell asleep counting it.

LEDGER = "canon-ledger.json"

SOURCE = ("Anirak Game Plan (docs/lords-of-cian/character-profiles/anirak.md, Section 3), approved "

d = json.load(open(LEDGER, encoding="utf-8"))
ids = {r["id"] for r in d["rules"]}
t = open(DRAFT, encoding="utf-8").read()

def para(rid, cat):
    m = re.search(r"\*\*" + rid + r" \(new, " + cat + r"\)\.\*\* (.*?)\n\n", t, re.S)
    return " ".join(m.group(1).split()).replace("`", "")

def amend_text(rid):
    m = re.search(r"- \*\*`" + rid + r"`\.\*\* (.*?)(?=\n- \*\*|\n\n)", t, re.S)
    return " ".join(m.group(1).split()).replace("`", "")

assert "VB-065" not in ids
d["rules"].append({"id": "VB-065", "category": "voice-bible",
                   "statement": para("VB-065", "voice-bible") + " " + APPROVAL,

R = {r["id"]: r for r in d["rules"]}
for rid in ("VB-020",):
    a = amend_text(rid)
    m = re.match(r'"(.*)" becomes "(.*)"$', a)
    old, new = m.group(1), m.group(2)

## **2026-08-15 — Jicome/Rexmar reading changed (supersedes Phase 0 item 1); uncle character role confirmed**

Two decisions from the canon-ledger session, both confirmed by Abad, both affecting open items in this roadmap directly.

**Jicome definition changed.** Phase 0 item 1 below ("Jicome / Sovereign Trust Domain naming — DECIDED... same territory, two names") is superseded. Abad chose the richer Rexmar material instead: Jicome is Haku's unified kingdom, a Rex mainland (the Regional Atlas's original JI region, capital Rexhaven) plus a Mar archipelago (a separate archipelago, not the Astral Archipelago), held by the Rexmar line after Haku. The Sovereign Trust Domain (Karkosa, Stormshelter Cove, Maw-7 Slab) is now a **separate, distinct territory**, not Jicome under another name. Full resolution logged as CONFLICT-004 in claude/canon-ledger.json; MCD-110 and MCD-111 corrected there, original text preserved inline as superseded.

This directly reopens Phase 1 item 7 below (the Jicome canon note that was supposed to go into Master Canon Decisions) — the note that gets written now needs to reflect this corrected reading, not the original Phase 0 verdict.

It also puts Phase 1 item 5 (Southern Seaboard theater definition) in question, not resolved. The original definition assumed Jicome and the Sovereign Trust Domain were the same place; now that they're separate, it's unclear whether "Southern Seaboard" means Jicome's coastline, the Sovereign Trust Domain's coastline, or both together. Flagged as MCD-112 (FLAGGED status, not LOCKED) in the ledger. Needs Abad's direct ruling before Phase 1 item 5 proceeds — this blocks Chronicle 1 per this roadmap's own dependency chain.

**Uncle character, role confirmed.** The "uncle" character flagged as an open item below (a Rexmar-line figure, secretly allied with Kanja but a bitter rival on the surface) is Kanja's co-conspirator, revealed in a specific chapter timed just before "someone big" dies. Confirmed by Abad 2026-08-15, logged as CHAR-002 in the ledger. Still undeveloped beyond this: no name, no physical description, no specific chapter placement, no identity for the "someone big," no established relationship to Maro Rexmar. Only urgent to build out now if he appears in Chronicle 1 specifically — same conditional as before, the role is settled but the character isn't built.

## **2026-08-09 — Scope narrowed to Chronicle 1 (Chronicle XXIII) only**

Abad's instruction: focus exclusively on Chronicle 1. Everything else set aside until further notice.

This does not remove the Phase 1 canon-lock prerequisites — the atlas dedup, RA grid code, Southern Seaboard definition, and Jicome/Sovereign Trust Domain canon note are still needed before Corvin drafts Chronicle 1, since they were never chronicle-specific fixes. What changes: Chronicles XXIV and XXV, the \~35-location Gazetteer expansion, and any work not directly required to get Chronicle 1 to a draftable state are paused, not abandoned. They resume once Chronicle 1 is through Isolde and in Abad's hands.

Still open and specific to getting Chronicle 1 draftable:

  - Phase 1 items 2-7 (atlas dedup, RA grid code, Southern Seaboard definition, Jicome canon note) — blocked on browser bridge access, and items 5/7 now additionally depend on the 2026-08-15 Jicome reading change above.
  - The uncle character decision — role now confirmed (see 2026-08-15 update above); only blocking if the character appears in Chronicle 1 specifically, and only the full build-out (name, description, placement) remains undone.
  - Book 1 structural outline scoping — relevant if Chronicle 1's events overlap Book 1's opening (the Fulfillment Ceremony falls at the end of the Long Mask era, so this needs checking against where Chronicle XXIII actually falls in the timeline).

## **2026-08-08, later — Kanja profile origin corrected. Read this before touching Kanja's backstory again.**

The first delivered cut of the Kanja Personality Bible invented an origin (a dockworker's epiphany at eighteen, a 750-year-old uncle explaining the family's decline at a birthday feast) instead of using the real Book 1 canon, which already existed in Drive and answers this completely. Abad caught it and pointed back to the Lore Vault folder (1ju89lRxrCXhnjFEcZip9Hse3r2QogcDe). Corrected. The real material, confirmed across MASTER CANON DECISIONS.docx, the Session Locks section within it, --THE PITCH COLLECTION- MY RIVAL'S DISTANCE--, Pitch Bible, and Beloved\_and\_Blade\_Ronin\_Victims.docx:

  - Kanja is a prince. His father, Maro Rexmar, is a king. Kanja's Rebellion (ages 18-30, against the Sovereign Trust, not the SBD) was winning: 22 victories in 12 years, 6 of them battles the Directorate itself classified as unwinnable.
  - **The Sovereign Pier Accords**, negotiated in secret roughly 296 years before Book 1 opens: Maro Rexmar and Aethelgard Verehimu (Ozmund's father) traded the end of Kanja's rebellion for Aethelgard's future recognition of Maro as sovereign King of Jicome, plus an alliance against the Shattered Kingdoms. This, not a birthday lecture, is why Kanja's father was able to convince him to stand down from a war he was winning. Kanja surrendered the Trinity (Mafesto, Onyx, Obsidian Malice) into L9 and put on the Long Mask to wait out the deal.
  - **The Fulfillment Ceremony is Book 1's opening event** (per Master Canon's own "BOOK 1 STRUCTURE: THE DEPOSED KING" section: "Opening: Murder scene. Two kings dead."). Aethelgard, king for one month, was about to crown Maro sovereign King of Jicome, fulfilling the Accords 284 years after Kanja put on the mask. At the ceremony, three contracted assassins, the Three Ronin, killed both kings: Decimus Korr ("the Silence") cleared the guards, an unnamed infiltrator ("the Ghost") had already been inside for weeks, and Serai Noth ("the Blade") killed both kings in 1.6 seconds. An SBD wet-work team sanitized the scene within four minutes. Ozmund rejects the crown the murder leaves him, hires Ezio to investigate, this is Book 1.
  - The pitch material's own line for Kanja: "The 284-year performance was the longest undercover operation in history, and it ended one day too late."
  - Kanja and Ozmund are cousins through their mothers, Val Saeryn Kareth and Val Mirel Kareth (Karesian war-sisters), not through their fathers. Their fathers' shared murder is the origin wound both sons carry into Book 3's confrontation ("You are becoming the thing our fathers died to prevent" / "Our fathers' way got them both killed," Master Canon's own locked line, both right, both wrong).

Corrected sections III and IV of 00\_Kanja\_Psychological\_Profile.docx to run on this material, retitled Section IV from "The Interrupted Boy" to "One Day Too Late," enriched the Ozmund passage in Section IX with the shared-murder/Book-3-rift material, and updated Rule 6 and the "What Kanja Wants" closing to match. Rendered to PDF and checked page by page before redelivering. This is now the second time this session that not searching the Lore Vault folder thoroughly enough produced work that had to be redone — the geography audit undercounted the manuscript's actual "Eastern Seaboard" instances earlier the same day, and this profile invented an origin that Drive already had an answer for. Both times the fix was to go back to source documents already sitting in the folder rather than infer or invent. Treat the Lore Vault folder as the source of truth before drafting anything else for this project, including future chronicle drafts.

**Uncle character, role now confirmed** — see the 2026-08-15 update at the top of this document. The paragraph that used to sit here describing this as fully open is superseded; the narrative role is settled, only the full character build-out remains.

**VB-067**. Account types and reliability. Each protagonist's series is to be complemented over time by at least one entry of each further account type available in that protagonist's world. **VB-067**. Account types and reliability. Each protagonist's series is to be complemented over time by at least one entry of each further account type available in that protagonist's world. (1) The Series: the protagonist's own named series (VB-066), reliable whoever narrates it. For Kanja, the Series is his Alias entries, the manuscript Chronicles I-VIII, and the Kanja-version track (VB-026), which is the home of his Onyx accounts (VB-062); its Long Mask Onyx accounts are reconstructed retrospectively (VB-062, ARS-437). From this rule's lock onward, each new entry's header labels its account type and its teller ("teller: none" for close-third or neutral narration); the narrative never labels its own reliability. Entries locked before this rule are read as reliable (the Series, under the narration rule above) unless their rule marks a claim as contested (as SBD-041 does for the SBD's Pyro file), and are not relabeled. input.description: Research psychology of told accounts
input.prompt:
Research task for a fiction-writing project. Do NOT edit any repository files and do not run git. Use web search and your own knowledge; cite real sources (author, year, title) for every claim you rely on, and flag anything you are unsure of.

Goal: a research brief that a novelist will turn into rules for writing in-world "accounts" -- stories about events told by characters, in realistic conversational settings. Accounts come in these types: (a) a protagonist's own narrated series (reliable); (b) a Comrade Account told by an ally (good faith, partial, bounded by what they saw); (c) an Adversary Account told by an enemy (bent by interest); (d) a Dossier, an institutional record by an intelligence bureau or state (fallible by design, bureaucratic misreadings); (e) Hearsay, told at a remove by civilians/bystanders through rumor and legend drift. Tellers can be informed, uninformed, mistaken, or deliberately lying to someone who doesn't know better.

Cover, concretely and with craft-usable detail:
1. Structure of oral conversational narrative: Labov & Waletzky (abstract, orientation, complicating action, evaluation, resolution, coda); Labov's reportability and evaluation devices; co-narration and group storytelling (Ochs & Capps "Living Narrative"; Norrick); story rounds and topping ("second stories", Sacks); how listeners interrupt, challenge, demand sources, repair.
2. Rumor and legend transmission: Allport & Postman (leveling, sharpening, assimilation); Bartlett's serial reproduction; Rosnow / DiFonzo & Bordia (rumor under anxiety and ambiguity, credibility); Shibutani ("improvised news"); urban-legend features (friend-of-a-friend, Brunvand); how numbers, names, and dates drift; how legends attach to famous figures.
3. Gossip: Dunbar; social function, reputation, in-group policing; who is allowed to tell what.
4. Deception in conversation: DePaulo's cue research, Vrij (verbal cues, cognitive load, strategic use of evidence), Interpersonal Deception Theory (Buller & Burgoon), Reality Monitoring / Criteria-Based Content Analysis (truthful accounts have more sensory/contextual detail, admitted memory gaps, spontaneous corrections; liars rehearse, are over-structured, avoid self-deprecation), how a liar adapts to an uninformed vs. a skeptical listener, how lies get embellished on retelling.
5. Memory and eyewitness distortion: Loftus misinformation effect, weapon focus, stress and memory, confabulation, source-monitoring errors, retelling effects (Marsh & Tversky: retellings are tailored to audience and purpose).
6. Setting-specific talk: bar/tavern talk; barbershop talk; street-corner society (Whyte "Street Corner Society", Liebow "Tally's Corner", Elijah Anderson "Code of the Street", "A Place on the Corner"); runners and numbers games; locker-room / male peer-group talk and status display (and its performative exaggeration); sports-crowd talk during an event; family dinner-table narratives (Ochs & Taylor, "Father knows best" dynamics); workplace break talk (docks, factory); soldiers' war stories and veterans' talk (who speaks, who stays silent, why); sailors' yarns; elders' storytelling to children; market talk. For each: who is present, status hierarchy, turn-taking norms, what is reportable, typical openings and closers, how challenge works, typical exaggerations.
7. Institutional writing: intelligence-report conventions (estimative language, confidence levels, Sherman Kent's "Words of Estimative Probability", source grading like the Admiralty/NATO A1-F6 system), police/incident report voice, bureaucratic passive voice and how institutions misread through their own categories.
8. Enemy/adversary narratives: self-justification (Tavris & Aronson "Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me)"), cognitive dissonance, saving face, how defeated commanders tell defeats.

Deliver a structured brief (aim for 3,000-5,000 words) with, for each section, (i) key findings, (ii) concrete markers a writer can use on the page (phrasings, structural moves, tells), (iii) sources. End with a one-page "matrix": for each teller state (informed / uninformed / mistaken / deliberately lying) the observable markers in speech. Return the brief as your final message.

Once both come back, I'll draft the account craft standard: for each account type and each setting, the structure of the telling, who's present, how the talk flows, and the speech markers of an informed, uninformed, mistaken or lying teller. Any new place or role names will be collision-checked, the whole draft goes through the Gate, and I'll present it to you before anything locks. that research on psychology needs to be comprehensive and it needs to be very thorough so what is the established number of sources Gathering or intelligence gathering that will make this a meta-analysis more effective? I don't know if I'm expressing myself correctly but if I'm not you may begin a line of questioning to clear up any ambiguity

Your question was clear. The short answer is that a meta-analysis isn't defined by a number of sources. It's a statistical method: it pools the measured results of many studies on one narrow question into a single combined estimate. What you're describing is closer to a systematic review of the evidence. Since we're turning findings into craft rules rather than running new statistics, the most rigorous move is to build on meta-analyses that already exist, and many do in these areas:

- **Spotting liars:** one review pooled 206 studies and found people catch lies only about 54% of the time.
- **Signs of lying:** another examined 158 possible signs across 120 groups of people studied.
- **How memory distorts under stress:** pooled studies on how stress and a visible weapon degrade what witnesses remember.

On how many sources is enough, the established benchmarks are:

- **Cochrane:** the standard handbook for these reviews sets no minimum. It does say the tests for publication bias (studies that never got published, skewing the picture) need at least about 10 studies.
- **Research practice:** in general, findings that rest on one or two studies are treated as weak, and findings that hold up across several independent groups are treated as strong.

So here's the standard I'm setting for this research:

- **Eight areas, researched separately and in parallel:**
  1. how people tell stories out loud
  2. how rumor and legend spread
  3. gossip and reputation
  4. deception and how liars talk
  5. how memory and retelling distort events
  6. the settings: bar, corner, barbershop, locker room, sports crowd, dinner table, dock break, soldiers' war stories, sailors' yarns
  7. how institutions write reports
  8. how enemies justify themselves
- **At least 12 sources per area, about 100 in total.** Existing meta-analyses and systematic reviews come first, then major primary studies, then the classic field studies (for example, the long-term street-corner studies).
- **Every finding graded** strong, moderate, or contested, and only strong or moderate findings become rules.
- **Two independent sources for every rule,** or one meta-analysis.

The first, lighter research agent is still running, and its result will serve as an overview. The eight deeper agents are starting now. Tell me if you meant something different and I'll redirect them.

Dunbar 1996/2004 (social-bonding function; proportion of conversation that is social); Foster 2004 review "Research on gossip: taxonomy, methods, and future directions"; Robbins & Karan 2020 "Who gossips and how in everyday life?"; Feinberg, Willer, Stellar & Keltner 2012 (prosocial gossip); Beersma & Van Kleef 2011/2012 (motives); Giardini & Wittek 2019 (Oxford Handbook of Gossip and Reputation); Baumeister, Zhang & Vohs 2004 (gossip as cultural learning); Gluckman 1963 (gossip and scandal, group boundary); Wert & Salovey 2004 (social comparison); Sommerfeld et al. 2007 (gossip and indirect reciprocity); research on who has the right to gossip about whom, insider/outsider boundaries, gossip about the powerful vs the low-status, gossip in tight-knit communities (villages, crews, neighborhoods), gossip as policing of norms, and how gossip handles absent third parties. Include evidence on gender differences only where well-supported, and flag stereotypes that are NOT supported.

METHOD STANDARD (mandatory):
- At least 12 distinct sources; prioritize meta-analyses and systematic reviews where they exist, then influential primary studies, then classic theory/ethnography. Use web search to verify citations; give author, year, title, venue, and a URL or DOI where you can find one. Never invent a citation; if you cannot verify one, mark it [unverified].

Findings (numbered), each with: the finding, evidence grade, sources, and "On the page" -- concrete markers a novelist can use (who opens gossip, lowered voices, hedges like "I didn't hear it from me", testing the listener, how the absent party is named or not named), written so they apply in a pre-industrial fantasy world as well as a 1960s-90s American city.

input.description: Domain 4: deception in talk
input.prompt:
Evidence-synthesis research for a fiction project. Write ONE file only: /home/user/Lords-of-Cian-Knowledge-Core/research/accounts-psychology/04-deception.md. Do not edit any other file and do not run git.

DOMAIN: How people lie in conversation and how listeners do or don't catch it. Meta-analyses first: DePaulo et al. 2003 "Cues to deception" (Psychological Bulletin); Bond & DePaulo 2006 "Accuracy of deception judgments"; Hartwig & Bond 2011/2014 (why lie-catchers fail; cue validity); Hauch et al. 2015 (computer-based linguistic cues meta-analysis) and Hauch et al. 2016 (verbal-cues training); Oberlader et al. 2016 (CBCA/Reality Monitoring meta-analysis); Amado et al. 2016 (CBCA in children/adults); Vrij et al. (cognitive load approach; Vrij, Fisher & Blank 2017; verifiability approach, Nahari); Strategic Use of Evidence (Granhag & Hartwig); Interpersonal Deception Theory (Buller & Burgoon 1996) and its critiques; Truth-Default Theory (Levine 2014, 2020) and truth bias; prevalence of lying (Serota, Levine & Boster 2010 "few prolific liars"); how liars plan and rehearse, over-structuring, less self-correction, fewer admitted memory gaps, less sensory/contextual detail, how liars embed lies in truth ("embedded lies", Leins et al.), how lies get embellished across retellings, lying to uninformed vs skeptical listeners, persuasion tactics (Cialdini only as relevant). Flag popular myths NOT supported by evidence (gaze aversion, fidgeting).

- At least 12 distinct sources; prioritize meta-analyses and systematic reviews, then influential primary studies. Use web search to verify citations; give author, year, title, venue, and a URL or DOI where you can find one. Never invent a citation; if you cannot verify one, mark it [unverified].
